descriptors.title: Water as an environmental resource
descriptors.description: classification of environmental resources and the way that water connects and changes places as it moves through environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students enter Year 7 Geography from the F–6 HASS curriculum. They have a working understanding of basic geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnections, scale, sustainability, change), can identify natural and managed environments, and have located Australia within the Asia-Pacific region. They have not previously encountered formal resource classification frameworks or the concept of the hydrological cycle as an agent of landscape change.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how water is classified as an environmental resource and how its movement through environments connects and changes places.

nodes.label: Resource classification framework
nodes.checkpoint: Students can classify environmental resources as renewable, non-renewable or continuous and give examples of each type.
criteria: Classifies water in at least three forms (e.g. surface water, groundwater, water vapour, salt water, ice) using the renewable/non-renewable/continuous framework and justifies each classification.
Explains the defining characteristic that distinguishes renewable resources from continuous resources.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot accurately apply the three-category framework, they will misclassify water in its various forms throughout the rest of the unit, undermining analysis of sustainability, distribution and management strategies in K01–K03.

width.minimum: Students classify at least two examples of each resource type and explain the defining characteristic that places each in its category.
width.typical: Students use the three-category framework to classify a range of environmental resources including water in different forms, fossil fuels, solar energy and timber, explaining the basis for each classification.
wider: Examine contested classifications — e.g. is groundwater renewable or non-renewable given recharge timescales? Where does 'fossil water' sit in the framework?
Compare this classification to alternative frameworks (e.g. natural capital, ecosystem services) and evaluate which is more useful for decision-making
Investigate how resource classification has changed over time as technology has enabled previously inaccessible resources to be used

modes.reason: Students frequently confuse 'continuous' (always available, e.g. solar, wind) with 'renewable' (regenerates within a human timeframe, e.g. timber, fish). A consolidation pass using targeted sorting exercises with explicit feedback on the continuous/renewable distinction resolves this before it propagates.
Widening to contested and edge cases (fossil water, geothermal, unconventional gas) builds genuine understanding of the classification logic rather than memorised category membership.

nodes.label: Water movement and place connection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how water moving through environments connects places, using geographical terminology for different water forms and pathways.
criteria: Names and distinguishes at least three forms of water (e.g. groundwater, surface water, soil moisture, salt water, ice) and their pathways through environments.
Explains, using a specific example, how water movement connects at least two places — identifying what is carried, transferred or affected.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding water movement as a connective process between places is the conceptual foundation for K02 (distribution and sustainability) and K03 (values). Without this spatial understanding, students treat water as a static resource rather than a dynamic system.

width.minimum: Students trace at least one water pathway (e.g. surface water in a river system, groundwater movement) and explain how it connects two or more places.
width.typical: Students explain how groundwater, surface water and soil moisture move through environments, identifying at least two ways this movement connects places — including the role of water as a potential resource when it exists as salt water, ice or water vapour.
wider: Map a river catchment at multiple scales, tracing how upstream and downstream places are connected through water movement and identifying human modifications to that flow
Investigate the Great Artesian Basin as a case study of groundwater connecting geographically distant places across long timeframes
Examine how climate systems (ENSO, Indian Ocean Dipole) affect the distribution of water movement across Australia, connecting meteorological patterns to water availability in different places

modes.reason: Students often confuse 'water connects places' with simple transport (water flows downstream). The reasoning scaffold needed is: water moves → carries materials, energy and consequences → downstream/down-gradient places are affected by upstream/up-gradient conditions. Diagramming catchment connections explicitly supports this.
Widening to different water movement types — surface, sub-surface, atmospheric — and different scales prevents students from overgeneralising from river examples.

nodes.label: Environmental, economic and social effects of water movement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain environmental, economic or social effects of water as it connects places, using a specific Australian example.
criteria: Identifies a specific case of water movement connecting places and explains at least one environmental, economic or social effect with reference to the geographical processes involved.
Distinguishes between beneficial and adverse effects of the same water movement for at least one example.

width.minimum: Students explain one effect type (environmental, economic or social) of water movement connecting places, supported by a specific example.
width.typical: Students explain environmental, economic and social effects of water movement across two or more examples, including at least one case where water connection produces both beneficial and adverse effects for different groups.
wider: Examine the Snowy Mountains Hydroelectric Scheme — compare environmental effects of water diversion (reduced flows in the Snowy and Murrumbidgee rivers) with economic effects (power generation and irrigation)

Investigate the Mutitjulu Waterhole as a case where the social and cultural effects of water connectivity are primary — connecting this to prior understanding of First Nations relationships to Country
Research the Ord River Irrigation Area, examining how engineered water movement produced economic effects for some groups and adverse social/environmental effects for others

modes.reason: The three effect types (environmental, economic, social) are best understood comparatively across contexts. Using multiple case studies prevents students from conflating the framework with a single example.

nodes.label: Moving water as an agent of landscape change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how moving water changes places through erosion, deposition and related geomorphological processes.
criteria: Explains at least one way moving water changes the physical characteristics of a place, identifying the process involved.
Uses appropriate geographical terminology (e.g. erosion, deposition, runoff, valley) to describe water-driven landscape change.

width.minimum: Students explain at least one process by which moving water changes the physical landscape of a place (e.g. erosion cutting valleys, soil erosion).
width.typical: Students explain how moving water causes erosion and deposition, identifying examples of landforms created by water movement and explaining the conditions that intensify these processes.
wider: Investigate a specific landform created by water action (e.g. river gorge, alluvial plain, delta, coastal cliff) and trace the process sequence that produced it
Examine how land use change (clearing, urban surfaces) alters water movement and intensifies erosion processes
Compare water-driven landscape change rates across different climate zones — arid Australia vs monsoonal tropics vs temperate coasts

modes.reason: Students tend to describe outcomes (valleys exist) without explaining the process chain (water energy → rock/soil disaggregation → transport → deposition elsewhere). Explicitly scaffolding the process sequence — energy source, material acted on, transport, deposition site — grounds the explanation.

nodes.label: Integration: water as classifier, connector and change agent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how water is classified as an environmental resource and how its movement through environments connects and changes places — applying the classification framework, connectivity concept and change processes to a specific geographical context.
criteria: Produces an explanation of a specific water-related context that applies the resource classification framework, explains a connection between places, and identifies a change process.
Uses accurate geographical terminology throughout and names specific places, water forms and processes.

width.minimum: Students produce an explanation that draws on at least two of the three concepts (classification, connection, change) for a specific water-related geographical context.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated explanation of a water-related geographical context that applies the resource classification framework, traces the connectivity between places, and identifies a change process — making explicit the relationship between the three concepts.
wider: Apply all three concepts simultaneously to a complex case: e.g. the Murray-Darling Basin as a system where water classification (competing uses and scarcity), connectivity (rivers linking states and ecosystems) and change (salinity, erosion, altered flow regimes) operate together

Evaluate a real or proposed water management intervention using the three-concept framework to assess what it changes about classification (access), connectivity (flow alteration) and physical change (erosion, sedimentation)

modes.reason: The three concepts in this descriptor — classification, connection and change — are typically taught as sequential nodes but the descriptor requires them to work together in explanation. The integration node is where students practise moving between the three simultaneously rather than applying each in isolation.

descriptors.title: Water distribution and sustainability
descriptors.description: the location and distribution of water resources in Australia, their implications, and strategies to manage the sustainability of water
descriptors.knowledge: Students have completed AC9HG7K01 — they can classify water as a renewable/continuous/non-renewable resource, trace water movement connecting places, and explain environmental, economic and social effects. They can locate Australia broadly but have not previously examined the spatial distribution of Australia's water resources or the concept of sustainability applied specifically to water.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the location and distribution of water resources in Australia, their implications for people, and strategies to manage water sustainability.

nodes.label: Locating and representing Australia's water resources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the location of Australia's major water resources (surface water and groundwater) and describe the pattern of their distribution.
criteria: Represents the location of at least two types of Australian water resource on a map, applying appropriate cartographic conventions.
Describes the distributional pattern of water resources across Australia, identifying which regions have greater or lesser access.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot accurately read or produce a distribution map will be unable to engage with the implications analysis in nodes 2–3. Spatial literacy with distribution maps is the foundation for the rest of this standard.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two types of water resource location in Australia (e.g. surface water in a river system, a major groundwater basin) and describe a basic distributional pattern.
width.typical: Students represent the location of Australia's surface water (rivers, lakes, reservoirs) and groundwater (aquifers, the Great Artesian Basin) on a map and describe the uneven distribution of these resources across the continent.
wider: Analyse temporal variation — represent not just where water is located but how availability changes seasonally and across drought/flood cycles using historical data
Compare Australia's water resource distribution with a country in Asia with contrasting distribution (e.g. Japan, India) to identify what makes Australia's distribution distinctive
Examine the difference between 'water exists here' and 'water is accessible here' — mapping accessible versus total water resources

modes.reason: Constructing and reading distribution maps requires repeated practice with cartographic conventions. Students who have only seen maps need guided practice constructing one before interpreting distribution patterns.

nodes.label: Causes and factors of water variability and scarcity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between physical and economic causes of water scarcity, and explain factors that contribute to variability in water resources.
criteria: Distinguishes between a physical cause and an economic cause of water scarcity in Australia, using an example for each.
Identifies at least two factors (e.g. climate, topography, seasonality) that contribute to variability in Australia's water resources and explains how each operates.
nodes.hinge_reason: Confusing physical and economic causes of scarcity leads to mismatched strategy evaluation in node 4 — students recommend engineering solutions for economic scarcity or policy solutions for physical scarcity without examining fit. The cause-strategy match is the core analytical move in this standard.

width.minimum: Students identify at least one physical cause and one economic cause of water scarcity, and name at least two factors contributing to variability.
width.typical: Students explain physical causes (absolute shortage — climate, geography), economic causes (inadequate development of water infrastructure) and use-based causes (competing demands) of water scarcity, and explain factors such as location, climate, topography, seasonality and evaporation that contribute to variability in water resources.
wider: Compare a place experiencing physical water scarcity (e.g. remote arid Australia) with a place experiencing economic water scarcity (e.g. parts of developing Asia) — examine whether the same strategies are effective for both
Investigate the role of climate variability (ENSO) as a driver of temporal variability in Australia's water resources, using historical records
Analyse how population growth and changing land use interact with natural variability to compound water scarcity

modes.reason: The three cause types (physical, economic, use-based) are commonly collapsed into a single 'not enough water' explanation. Explicitly scaffolding the causal chain — what is scarce vs what limits access vs who uses how much — grounds the distinction before strategy evaluation.
Comparing physical and economic scarcity in different contexts (arid Australia vs under-resourced communities with available water) resolves the misconception that scarcity is purely about quantity.

nodes.label: Implications of distribution for people
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain implications of Australia's water distribution for people in different settlement types, including people in rural and remote places.
criteria: Explains at least two implications of water distribution for people in a specific rural or remote place, connecting the resource distribution pattern to a lived consequence.
Compares water access in at least two different settlement types (e.g. urban vs remote), identifying a key difference in implication.

width.minimum: Students explain at least one implication of Australia's water distribution for people in rural or remote places.
width.typical: Students compare access to water for people in urban, rural, and remote/very remote settlements, explaining how the distribution of water resources creates different levels of access and different implications for health, economic activity and daily life.
wider: Examine a specific remote community's water access story — e.g. a remote Indigenous community dependent on bore water — and identify the compounding social, economic and health implications
Analyse how virtual water trade affects which populations bear the real burden of water-intensive production
Compare historical and current water access in a growing peri-urban area to show how rapid population growth alters implications

modes.reason: Urban students may assume water is reliably available everywhere. Widening to rural, remote and very remote contexts — especially Indigenous communities with limited water infrastructure — builds genuine understanding of distributional inequity.

nodes.label: Strategies for water sustainability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a water management strategy may improve the sustainability of water resources, identifying the problem it addresses and trade-offs involved.
criteria: Explains how at least one water management strategy addresses a specific sustainability problem, naming the cause of the problem and how the strategy targets it.
Identifies at least one reason water sustainability is difficult to manage, such as shared uses, competing demands or supply variability.

width.minimum: Students explain one water management strategy and identify the problem it addresses.
width.typical: Students examine at least two strategies (e.g. grey water recycling, stormwater harvesting, desalination, inter-regional transfer, demand reduction) and explain how each addresses a specific cause of water scarcity or sustainability problem, including shared/competing uses as a reason sustainability is difficult.
wider: Evaluate a strategy against criteria — effectiveness, cost, environmental impact, equity of access — and argue for or against its applicability to a specific Australian context
Compare desalination (capital-intensive, supply-side) with demand management (behavioural, demand-side) — examine which approach better addresses water sustainability and under what conditions
Research virtual water trade as a strategy — examine how food import/export decisions can reduce or increase a country's effective water demand

modes.reason: Students often default to a single 'save water' solution. Widening across supply-side (desalination, transfer), demand-side (recycling, reduction) and governance (trade, pricing) strategies builds understanding that no single approach solves sustainability.

nodes.label: Integration: distribution, implications and management
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain the location and distribution of water resources in Australia, their implications for people, and strategies to manage water sustainability — integrating spatial, social and management analysis.
criteria: Produces an explanation of a specific Australian water context that addresses distribution, implications for people, and a management strategy.
Uses geographical concepts (distribution, sustainability, variability, scarcity) accurately throughout the explanation.

width.minimum: Students produce an explanation that connects Australia's water distribution to at least one implication for people and one management strategy.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated analysis of an Australian water management case that addresses: where water resources are distributed, implications of that distribution for a specific population, why sustainability is difficult, and how a strategy attempts to address the problem.
wider: Develop a case study of the Murray-Darling Basin as an integration of all four elements: distribution (water location and variability), implications (competing users including agriculture, urban users, environment), sustainability challenge (over-allocation, salinity), and management response (the Basin Plan, water trading)
Compare the Murray-Darling case with a contrasting case in Asia (e.g. Mekong Delta water management) to identify universal versus context-specific sustainability challenges

modes.reason: The standard brings together spatial representation, causal analysis, equity implications, and strategy evaluation. The integration node practises weaving these threads into a coherent geographical explanation rather than presenting them as separate analyses.

descriptors.title: Values of water
descriptors.description: the economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value of water for people, including First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students have completed K01 and K02 — they can classify water resources, trace water movement connecting places, and explain distribution and sustainability. Those nodes treat water primarily as a physical and economic resource. This standard introduces the cultural, spiritual and aesthetic dimensions of water value, which require a different conceptual lens.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value of water for people, including First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Framework of water values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic values of water and give an example of each.
criteria: Names and distinguishes economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic values of water, providing a concrete example for each.
Identifies a water body or waterway that holds more than one type of value and explains how each applies.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish the four value types — particularly conflating cultural and spiritual, or treating economic value as the only 'real' value — will struggle to explain First Nations relationships to Country/water in node 2, which requires understanding non-economic values as primary rather than supplementary.

width.minimum: Students define each value type and provide at least one concrete example.
width.typical: Students explain each of the four value types (economic, cultural, spiritual, aesthetic) and provide examples drawn from Australian and Asian contexts, recognising that a single water body may hold multiple value types simultaneously.
wider: Examine how the four value types can conflict — e.g. a river's economic value (irrigation) may conflict with its spiritual value for First Nations communities — and consider how such conflicts are mediated
Compare how values attributed to water differ across cultures — e.g. the aesthetic value of a waterfall in Japanese culture vs an Australian National Park listing for the same feature type
Explore how a value type can be 'discovered' or recognised — e.g. aesthetic value formalised through World Heritage listing

modes.reason: The economic/non-economic distinction needs explicit scaffolding. Many students default to economic explanations. A structured reasoning approach that requires students to explain each value type on its own terms — not as a secondary consideration after economics — addresses this.
Widening to cases where non-economic values are primary (spiritual significance, aesthetic listing) gives students examples where the framework applies without defaulting to economic framing.

nodes.label: First Nations Australians and multilayered water values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the multilayered meanings of water for First Nations Australians — material, cultural and spiritual — using specific examples of rivers, waterways, waterholes or other water features.
criteria: Explains at least two dimensions of water significance (material, cultural, spiritual) for First Nations Australians using a specific water feature as an example.
Describes the relationship between water and Country/Place identity for at least one First Nations community.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat First Nations water values as merely 'cultural enrichment' (supplementary to economic value) will not be able to explain why water management decisions that prioritise economic value can cause profound harm to First Nations communities. This understanding is foundational to K07 (cultural connectedness to place).

width.minimum: Students explain that water features hold material, cultural and spiritual significance for First Nations Australians, supported by at least one specific example.
width.typical: Students discuss the multilayered meanings (material, cultural and spiritual wellbeing) associated with rivers, waterways, waterholes, human-made wells, seas, lakes, soaks and springs for First Nations Australians, explaining how these meanings are connected to Country/Place and to social identity.
wider: Examine the Mutitjulu Waterhole — its material significance as a water source, cultural significance in Anangu Tjukurpa, and spiritual significance as a living Dreaming site — as a case study of integrated multilayered meaning
Research how water-sharing protocols and custodianship responsibilities reflect the relationship between First Nations peoples and water features
Examine how dispossession and land management changes have affected First Nations Australians' relationship with water features, and current efforts to restore cultural access

modes.reason: Students need scaffolding to understand that material, cultural and spiritual dimensions are simultaneously present — not alternatives — in First Nations relationships to water. A case study approach where all three dimensions are traced in the same water feature makes this concrete.

Using multiple water feature types (waterhole, river, coastal waterway, soak) broadens understanding beyond a single exemplar and reveals that multilayered water values operate across all water forms, not just iconic sites.

nodes.label: Economic value of water: irrigation and food production
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the economic value of water for irrigation-based communities and industries, using a comparison between an Australian and an Asian example.
criteria: Explains the economic role of water in an irrigation-based region using a specific Australian example.
Compares at least one similarity and one difference in how irrigation shapes economic life in an Australian and an Asian context.

width.minimum: Students explain the economic value of water for one irrigation case study.
width.typical: Students examine and compare places in Australia and a country in Asia that have economies and communities based on irrigation — e.g. the Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area in NSW and the Mekong Delta in Vietnam — identifying similarities and differences in how irrigation shapes economic and community life.
wider: Analyse the virtual water embedded in food exports from irrigation regions — calculate the 'water cost' of traded agricultural products and consider what this means for water sustainability
Compare the economic value of irrigation water with the economic value of water for urban use — how are competing economic values prioritised and by whom?

Examine historical case studies where irrigation dramatically changed regional economies and societies (e.g. development of the Ord River, transformation of the MIA) and evaluate the costs and benefits

modes.reason: Comparing Australian and Asian irrigation cases prevents students from treating economic water value as a purely domestic story. The Mekong Delta case also shows water's economic value in a different national and cultural context.

nodes.label: Aesthetic and cultural value of water: heritage and tourism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the aesthetic and cultural value of water features through examples of World Heritage or national park listings in Australia and Asia.
criteria: Explains the aesthetic or cultural value of a water feature in Australia or Asia, including why it has been formally recognised through listing or protected status.
Describes at least one way aesthetic or spiritual value of water differs between two cultural contexts.

width.minimum: Students explain the aesthetic or cultural value of one water-related heritage or protected site.
width.typical: Students examine bays, rivers, waterfalls or lakes in Australia and in countries of Asia that have been listed as World Heritage sites or national parks for their aesthetic and cultural value, explaining what features generate these values and how listing reflects them.
wider: Examine how aesthetic value of a water feature generates economic value through tourism — is aesthetic value independent of or connected to economic value?

Investigate the spiritual significance of water in an Asian culture (e.g. the Ganges in Hindu practice, sacred lakes in Tibetan Buddhism) and compare the nature of that significance with Australian First Nations examples
Analyse how the criteria for World Heritage listing reflect particular cultural frameworks for 'outstanding universal value' and consider whose values are centred

modes.reason: The elaborations explicitly call for Asian examples. Widening to include spiritual significance in Asian cultures (not just aesthetic/heritage) builds fuller understanding of non-economic water values across diverse cultural contexts.

nodes.label: Integration: multiple values in tension and context
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain the economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value of water for people — applying the four-value framework to a specific case and recognising where values coexist or conflict.
criteria: Applies at least three of the four value types to a specific water feature or management case, explaining each.
Identifies at least one point of tension between different values held by different groups for the same water feature.

width.minimum: Students apply at least two value types to a specific water-related context, explaining each value's source and how they relate.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated explanation of a specific water feature or water management case that identifies economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic values, explains how these are expressed by different groups, and considers whether and how they coexist or conflict.
wider: Analyse a water management decision (e.g. a proposed dam, a river restoration project) using the four-value framework — identify which values are advanced, which are compromised, and for which communities

Apply the framework to a case involving First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous water users — e.g. the Darling/Baaka River, the Daintree, or a local river — to assess whose values inform decision-making and whose are marginalised

modes.reason: The four value types are taught separately but the descriptor requires students to apply them together. The integration node practises the analytical move of seeing a single water context through all four lenses simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Hydrological and atmospheric hazards
descriptors.description: the causes and impacts of an atmospheric or hydrological hazard, and responses from communities and governments
descriptors.knowledge: Students have completed K01–K03 — they understand water as an environmental resource, can explain water distribution and sustainability, and know that water movement causes environmental change. They have basic knowledge of climate and weather from primary school but have not previously studied hazard processes in depth or examined governmental and community response frameworks.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the causes and impacts of an atmospheric or hydrological hazard and responses from communities and governments.

nodes.label: Hazard environmental processes and causes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the environmental processes that cause an atmospheric or hydrological hazard, using accurate geographical terminology.
criteria: Explains the environmental process causing the selected hazard, identifying at least two conditions required for the hazard to occur.
Uses accurate geographical terminology (e.g. low pressure system, storm surge, soil saturation, drought threshold) to describe the process.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot explain the causal process will conflate hazard with outcome (treat flooding as the cause rather than the consequence of specific hydrometeorological conditions). This undermines impact analysis — if the cause is unclear, the link between process and impact cannot be made.

width.minimum: Students explain the key environmental process causing one selected hazard (e.g. drought, flood, tropical cyclone, storm).
width.typical: Students explain the environmental processes that cause at least one atmospheric hazard (e.g. tropical cyclone) and one hydrological hazard (e.g. flood or drought), distinguishing the different process chains involved.
wider: Examine how multiple atmospheric and hydrological processes interact — e.g. how drought (soil moisture deficit, reduced vegetation) intensifies flooding when rain finally arrives
Investigate the role of climate variability (ENSO, Indian Ocean Dipole) as a driver of both drought and flood risk in Australia, tracing the oceanic-atmospheric process chain
Compare the atmospheric processes causing tropical cyclones versus east coast lows, identifying what makes each distinctive in process terms

modes.reason: Explicitly scaffolding the process chain — atmospheric/hydrological conditions → triggering event → hazard manifestation — prevents students from describing weather events without explaining their geographical causes.

nodes.label: Factors influencing hazard impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the impacts of a hazard on people and the environment are influenced by environmental, social or economic factors.
criteria: Identifies at least two different types of factor (environmental, social, economic) that influence the impact of the selected hazard.
Explains, using a specific example, how one social or economic factor increases or decreases hazard impact.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand that impact is influenced by context factors will default to 'bigger hazard = bigger impact' reasoning. This blocks sophisticated analysis of community and government responses — if impact were purely a function of hazard magnitude, differentiated responses would make no sense.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two factors that influence the impact of their selected hazard and explain how each affects the severity of impact.
width.typical: Students explain how environmental factors (landform, vegetation, climate), social factors (population density, community preparedness, marginalised groups) and economic factors (infrastructure quality, insurance coverage, economic base) influence hazard impacts, applying these to a specific case study.
wider: Compare the same type of hazard (e.g. flood) in two very different contexts — e.g. a developed country city vs a rural developing country region — to isolate how social and economic factors drive differential impact
Examine how exposure and vulnerability differ for different population groups within the same hazard event — who is most affected and why
Analyse a historical Australian hazard event (e.g. 2011 Queensland floods, 2019–20 Black Summer) to map environmental, social and economic factors onto actual impact patterns

modes.reason: Comparing the same hazard type across different social/economic contexts is the most direct way to demonstrate that factors beyond the hazard process determine impact. Without this comparison, students struggle to see social and economic factors as causal.

nodes.label: Community and government responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe examples of community and government responses to a hazard at the local scale, explaining what made some responses effective.
criteria: Identifies at least one community and one government response to the selected hazard, using a specific Australian example.
Explains at least one factor that contributed to a response being effective or ineffective.

width.minimum: Students identify at least one community response and one government response to a hazard, and identify a factor that contributed to one being effective.
width.typical: Students identify examples of responses to a hazard from the community and government at the local scale, and identify practices that increased response effectiveness — drawing on a specific Australian hazard case.
wider: Compare local community responses with state and federal government responses to the same event — examine how coordination (or its absence) affected outcomes
Examine formal and informal community responses — official emergency services vs community networks, social media coordination, volunteer organisations — and evaluate relative effectiveness

Investigate how First Nations knowledge contributes to community hazard responses (e.g. fire management as drought/flood risk reduction) and why such knowledge is sometimes overlooked in official response frameworks

modes.reason: Widening beyond a single response example to include community and government responses at different scales, and formal and informal responses, builds a richer understanding of the response landscape.

nodes.label: Prevention, mitigation and preparedness framework
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply the prevention, mitigation and preparedness framework to explain how community and government responses can reduce hazard impact.
criteria: Distinguishes prevention, mitigation and preparedness as three distinct principles, providing an example of each from the selected hazard case.
Explains how at least one response reduces hazard impact by reference to one of the three principles.

width.minimum: Students distinguish prevention, mitigation and preparedness and apply each to one response example.
width.typical: Students reflect on the principles of prevention, mitigation and preparedness in responses from community and government to explain how impact can be reduced — applying all three principles to responses in their selected hazard case study.
wider: Evaluate the relative effectiveness of prevention vs mitigation vs preparedness in the context of a hazard that cannot be prevented (e.g. tropical cyclone) vs one where prevention is possible (e.g. some types of flood management through land use planning)
Examine the trade-offs between investing in prevention/mitigation infrastructure and funding post-disaster response — what factors influence this decision?
Compare the prevention-mitigation-preparedness framework applied to the same hazard type in two countries with different governance systems

modes.reason: The three-principle framework is a conceptual tool for organising responses — students need practice applying it analytically, not just defining each term. Scaffolding that requires students to classify a range of responses into the framework builds this analytical use.

nodes.label: Integration: causes, impacts and responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain the causes and impacts of an atmospheric or hydrological hazard and responses from communities and governments — integrating process analysis, impact factors and response framework.
criteria: Produces an integrated explanation of a hazard event that addresses causes, impact factors and at least one response, using accurate geographical terminology throughout.
Explicitly connects at least one response to a prevention, mitigation or preparedness principle.

width.minimum: Students produce an explanation of a selected hazard that addresses causes, at least two impact factors, and at least one community or government response.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated explanation of a hazard case that traces: the environmental process causing the hazard, how environmental/social/economic factors shaped its impact, specific community and government responses, and how prevention, mitigation or preparedness principles inform those responses.
wider: Develop a hazard management recommendation for a specific Australian place, applying all four elements of the integrated framework and drawing on evidence from the case study
Compare two hazard cases (one atmospheric, one hydrological) to examine whether the causes, impact factors and response types share common patterns or differ fundamentally

modes.reason: The four nodes in this standard cover distinct analytical components (process, impact factors, response examples, response framework). The integration node practises synthesising these into a coherent geographic explanation rather than four separate answers.

descriptors.title: Liveability decisions
descriptors.description: factors that influence the decisions people make about where to live, including perceptions of the liveability of places and the influence of environmental quality
descriptors.knowledge: Students enter the liveability unit having completed the water unit (K01–K04). They understand that places have environmental, economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic dimensions of value, and that water distribution creates differential access for populations in different settlement types. They have not previously encountered the concept of 'liveability' or the objective/subjective measurement distinction.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain factors that influence where people live, including perceptions of liveability and the influence of environmental quality.

nodes.label: Factors influencing residential location decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain multiple types of factors (economic, cultural, spiritual, aesthetic) that influence decisions about where to live.
criteria: Identifies at least three different factor types (economic, cultural, spiritual, aesthetic) influencing residential location decisions, with an example for each.
Explains how one non-economic factor can be the primary reason for a residential location decision.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish multiple factor types will default to economic explanations for all residential decisions. This blocks understanding of cultural and spiritual factors in K07 (First Nations connectedness) and prevents meaningful liveability measurement analysis in node 2.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two different types of factor and explain how each influences a residential location decision.
width.typical: Students explain economic factors (employment, industries in remote places), cultural factors (connection for cultural groups), spiritual factors (meanings attributed to places) and aesthetic factors (urban amenity, 'tree change') that influence where people choose to live.
wider: Analyse a migration case study — e.g. sea change/tree change movements in Australia — mapping which factor types predominate and which populations make these moves
Examine forced vs voluntary movement and how the weight of different factors changes when choice is constrained (e.g. economic refugees, natural disaster displacement)
Interview or survey community members about their residential location decisions and categorise the factors they name

modes.reason: Using diverse case studies — remote Indigenous community, rural tree change, urban professional, remote mining town — makes visible the range of factors that can be primary in different residential decisions, dismantling the economic default.

nodes.label: Liveability: concept and measurement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the concept of liveability, distinguish between objective and subjective measures, and compare examples of each.
criteria: Defines liveability and distinguishes between objective and subjective measures, providing an example of each.
Explains one limitation of either objective or subjective measures of liveability.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish objective from subjective measures will be unable to evaluate liveability claims in K06 and K08, where they compare places and assess strategies. The whole evaluation framework depends on understanding what kind of evidence is being used.

width.minimum: Students explain what liveability means and distinguish at least one objective measure from one subjective measure.
width.typical: Students discuss the concept of liveability and ways it is measured, comparing objective measures (transportation infrastructure, health services, safety statistics) with subjective measures (people's perceptions, sense of belonging, personal safety feelings).
wider: Critically evaluate a global liveability index (e.g. EIU, Mercer) — examine what indicators are included and excluded, and whose experiences are centred in the measurement approach
Compare how liveability rankings change when subjective community perceptions are given equal weight to objective infrastructure measures
Investigate how liveability measures have changed over time — what does their evolution reveal about changing values?

modes.reason: The objective/subjective distinction requires careful scaffolding — students often believe that quantitative = objective and qualitative = subjective, but many perceptions can be quantified and many objective indicators embed value choices. The reasoning scaffold needs to address the nature of each type, not just the data format.
Critically examining global liveability indices gives students a concrete analytical exercise with real data, making the objective/subjective distinction tangible.

nodes.label: Local access and perceptions of liveability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare their own access to and use of places in their local area and evaluate how this affects perceptions of liveability.
criteria: Identifies at least two local area features that influence perceptions of liveability, distinguishing between objective access and subjective perception.
Compares their own liveability perception with at least one other perspective, explaining what accounts for any difference.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two aspects of their local area that affect their perception of its liveability.
width.typical: Students compare their own access to and use of places and spaces in their local area with classmates and community members, evaluating how different levels of access to the same physical environment produce different perceptions of liveability.
wider: Survey classmates on liveability perceptions and map variation — examine what predicts difference in perception (age, mobility, transport access, cultural background)
Compare a local area's liveability as perceived by young people, elderly residents and people with disability — what spaces are accessible or inaccessible to each group?
Conduct a walkability audit of the local area and relate findings to liveability perceptions

modes.reason: Moving beyond personal experience to compare perceptions across different population groups in the same place makes visible how access determines perception — the central insight of this node.

nodes.label: Environmental quality and residential decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how environmental quality influences decisions about where to live, using examples of specific environmental quality factors.
criteria: Identifies at least two environmental quality factors that influence residential decisions and explains how each operates.
Uses a specific place example to illustrate how environmental quality affects where people choose or choose not to live.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two environmental quality factors and explain how each influences residential decision-making.
width.typical: Students examine the influence of environmental quality — clean land, air and water, views, recreation facilities and favourable climate — on decisions about where to live, using specific Australian place examples.
wider: Analyse the relationship between environmental quality and housing prices in a specific urban market — examine whether environmental quality is reflected in economic value
Examine how environmental degradation (e.g. air pollution in industrial areas, contaminated land) influences residential movement and community response
Investigate how climate change projections are beginning to alter perceptions of environmental quality and residential desirability in coastal and bushfire-prone areas

modes.reason: Using contrasting examples of environmental quality (coastal amenity vs industrial brownfield vs bushfire risk) reveals how the same geographical concept (environmental quality) operates differently depending on the specific environmental characteristics of a place.

nodes.label: Integration: factors, liveability and environmental quality
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain factors that influence residential decisions — integrating economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic factors with liveability measurement and environmental quality analysis.
criteria: Produces an explanation of a residential decision that addresses multiple factor types and explicitly applies the liveability concept.
Distinguishes objective and subjective elements in the liveability analysis.

width.minimum: Students produce an explanation of a residential decision context that addresses at least two factor types and applies the liveability concept.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated explanation of why people make specific residential decisions — combining factor type analysis, objective and subjective liveability measures, and environmental quality considerations — applied to a specific place or population group.
wider: Apply the integrated framework to a complex case: e.g. the decision of a family to move from urban Sydney to a regional town — map all factor types, liveability measures and environmental quality considerations, and explain the decision

Evaluate how the factors that drive residential decisions differ for First Nations Australians (where spiritual and cultural factors may be primary) vs recently arrived migrants (economic and cultural safety factors) in the same city

modes.reason: The standard brings together factor types, liveability measurement, local perception and environmental quality. Integration practises weaving these into a coherent explanation of a real residential decision rather than listing four separate considerations.

descriptors.title: Services, facilities and liveability
descriptors.description: the location and distribution of services and facilities, and implications for liveability of places
descriptors.knowledge: Students have completed K05 — they understand liveability as a concept, can distinguish objective and subjective measures, and know that factors including environmental quality influence residential decisions. They can represent distribution of resources from K02 work. This standard applies distribution analysis specifically to services and facilities and connects it to liveability outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the location and distribution of services and facilities and their implications for liveability.

nodes.label: Comparing services and facilities across settlement types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the distribution and location of services and facilities between different settlement types — urban, rural, remote and very remote.
criteria: Describes the distributional pattern of at least two services or facilities across different settlement types, identifying where provision is greatest and where it is absent.
Uses appropriate geographical language (distribution, concentration, access, provision) to describe service patterns.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot read or interpret a distribution pattern cannot engage meaningfully with the implication analysis in node 2. The distributional analysis is the spatial foundation on which liveability implications are built.

width.minimum: Students compare access to at least two types of service or facility between two different settlement types.
width.typical: Students compare the distribution and location of a range of services and facilities — including clean water, sanitation, education and health services — between urban, rural, remote and very remote settlements, identifying patterns of provision and under-provision.
wider: Map the distribution of a specific service (e.g. hospitals, schools, internet access) across Australia at a national scale and identify patterns of concentration and absence
Compare service distribution in an Australian remote context with a rural context in a country in Asia — identify common patterns and differences in what drives under-provision
Examine the concept of a 'service desert' (an area with very limited access to multiple services simultaneously) and identify examples in Australia

modes.reason: Accurately describing distributional patterns from maps and data requires practice. Students need repeated exposure to service distribution maps with structured observation tasks before they can generate independent pattern descriptions.

Comparing multiple settlement types (not just urban vs rural) and multiple services reveals the cumulative disadvantage of compound under-provision — a place can lack one service or many simultaneously.

nodes.label: Implications of service distribution for liveability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain implications of service and facility distribution for the liveability of places, including for people with limited access.
criteria: Explains at least two ways that service distribution affects the liveability of a specific place, with reference to who is affected and how.
Distinguishes between having a service in a place and being able to access it, identifying at least one access barrier beyond simple location.

width.minimum: Students explain at least two implications of service under-provision for the liveability of a specific place.
width.typical: Students analyse the distribution of services and facilities in different settlement types — using aerial images and data — to identify implications for people, including access to services and availability of facilities, and explain how these implications affect liveability.
wider: Analyse a specific remote or outer suburban area using aerial images and service data — develop a liveability profile and explain how service distribution shapes that profile
Examine how internet and mobile connectivity has altered service access for remote communities — is digital infrastructure now a critical liveability service?
Compare liveability implications of the same service deficit (e.g. no local hospital) in a remote Indigenous community vs an outer suburban area — are the implications equivalent?

modes.reason: The link between distribution and liveability implication requires explicit reasoning: distribution pattern → access condition → liveability effect. Students often jump from 'few services' to 'bad liveability' without explaining the mechanism. Scaffolding the causal chain builds analytical depth.

Comparing the same service deficit in different contexts (remote Indigenous community vs outer suburb) prevents overgeneralisation and reveals how other factors — economic resources, social capital, cultural context — mediate the liveability impact of service under-provision.

nodes.label: Transport and technology as service access enablers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the role transport and technologies play in people's ability to access services and participate in activities in their local area.
criteria: Explains how at least one transport or technology factor affects access to services in a specific settlement type.
Identifies at least one service type where technology can substitute for physical access and one where it cannot.

width.minimum: Students explain how at least one transport or technology factor affects people's access to services in a specific context.
width.typical: Students explain the role transport (roads, public transport, distance) and technologies (internet, telehealth, online education) play in people's ability to access services and participate in community activities — including cases where technology substitutes for physical service access and cases where it cannot.
wider: Examine the digital divide — how does internet access vary by settlement type, income and age in Australia, and what are the liveability implications?
Research the Flying Doctor Service or remote schooling programs as examples of technology-enabled service delivery and evaluate their effectiveness as liveability solutions
Consider the limits of technology substitution — what services require physical presence (medical procedure, school sports, aged care) and what does this mean for remote liveability?

modes.reason: Widening to both transport and technology, and to both enabling and limiting cases, prevents the misconception that technology fully solves service access inequality for remote communities.

nodes.label: Integration: distribution, access and liveability
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain the location and distribution of services and facilities and their implications for liveability — integrating distributional analysis, access factors and liveability outcomes.
criteria: Produces a place-based analysis that addresses service distribution, access, and liveability implications.
Uses appropriate evidence (maps, aerial images, data) to support at least one claim in the analysis.

width.minimum: Students produce an explanation of a specific place that addresses service distribution, an access consideration, and a liveability implication.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated analysis of a specific Australian settlement type that: maps the distribution of key services, explains how transport or technology affects access, identifies implications for liveability, and uses aerial images or data to support the analysis.
wider: Develop a liveability profile of a contrasting pair of Australian places (e.g. inner-city suburb vs remote town) using service distribution data, aerial images, and access analysis — argue which has greater liveability and for whom
Apply the distribution-access-liveability framework to a place in Asia, identifying similarities and differences with the Australian pattern

modes.reason: The standard brings together spatial distribution analysis, access mediation and liveability outcomes. Integration practises applying these three analytical moves simultaneously to a specific place rather than as separate exercises.

descriptors.title: Cultural connectedness to place
descriptors.description: the cultural connectedness of people to places and how this influences their identity, sense of belonging and perceptions of a place, in particular the cultural connectedness of First Nations Australians to Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: Students have completed K05 and K06 — they understand liveability as concept, know that cultural factors influence residential decisions, and can analyse implications of service distribution. From K03 they understand multilayered values (including spiritual/cultural) of water for First Nations Australians. This standard extends that understanding to place identity, belonging and inclusion/exclusion more broadly.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how cultural connectedness to places influences identity, belonging and perceptions, especially for First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Inclusion, exclusion and sense of belonging in places
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different places where people feel included or excluded and explain how this affects perceptions of liveability.
criteria: Identifies at least one example of inclusion and one of exclusion in a specific place, naming the group affected in each case.
Explains how feelings of safety, threat, inclusion or exclusion affect perceptions of a place's liveability.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that belonging is place-specific and group-specific is the foundation for understanding First Nations connectedness to Country/Place in node 2. Without grasping that the same place produces different belonging experiences for different groups, students cannot engage with the specificity and depth of First Nations place relationships.

width.minimum: Students identify at least one example of a place where a group feels included and one where a group feels excluded, explaining how each affects liveability perception.
width.typical: Students identify different places where people feel included or excluded, safe or threatened, and explain how these experiences of belonging or exclusion affect perceptions of a place's liveability — recognising that the same physical place can produce different belonging experiences for different groups.
wider: Examine how the built environment signals inclusion or exclusion — e.g. bilingual signage, accessible design, culturally appropriate facilities — and consider what physical changes signal whose belonging matters

Analyse a specific case of a place that has become associated with inclusion for one group and exclusion for another (e.g. a park that young people use for gathering but where elderly residents feel unsafe)
Research how gentrification alters belonging experiences — long-term residents may be economically displaced from places central to their cultural identity

modes.reason: Students tend to treat safety and inclusion as universal — if a place is safe/inclusive for them, it is for everyone. Explicitly scaffolding the perspective-taking required to understand differential belonging experiences is the key teaching move here.

Using multiple examples across age groups, cultural groups and settlement types ensures students understand that inclusion/exclusion in place is a widespread geographical phenomenon, not an edge case.

nodes.label: Social connection and liveability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the importance of social connectedness and its effect on perceptions of liveability.
criteria: Explains at least two ways that social connectedness affects perceptions of liveability.
Uses a specific place example to illustrate how social connection or disconnection shapes how a place feels to live in.

width.minimum: Students explain at least two ways that social connectedness affects how people perceive the liveability of a place.
width.typical: Students explain the importance of people being socially connected — through community, cultural groups, family and social networks — and explain how presence or absence of social connection affects perceptions of liveability in different place types.
wider: Examine social isolation in different contexts — elderly people in outer suburbs, young people in remote areas, recently arrived migrants in new cities — and compare how geographic context compounds or alleviates social disconnection
Investigate how digital connectivity has altered social connection in place-based communities and whether virtual social connection substitutes for physical co-presence
Analyse how COVID-19 lockdowns provided a large-scale 'natural experiment' in the liveability effects of reduced social connectivity

modes.reason: Examining social connection/disconnection in diverse contexts — remote, urban, elderly, young, newly arrived — prevents students from treating social connectedness as uniform and reveals how place and social context interact.

nodes.label: First Nations Australians: connectedness and belonging to Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss the cultural connectedness and belonging that First Nations Australians have to a range of places through family, Country/Place, dispossession, relocation and employment.
criteria: Explains the cultural connectedness and belonging of First Nations Australians to Country/Place, identifying at least two dimensions of that connection.
Explains how dispossession or relocation has affected First Nations relationships to Country, using specific reference to historical or contemporary experience.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not grasp the depth and specificity of First Nations connectedness to Country — particularly the way dispossession constitutes a liveability harm beyond physical displacement — will be unable to properly evaluate liveability strategies for First Nations communities in K08.

width.minimum: Students explain the cultural connectedness and belonging that First Nations Australians have to Country/Place, using at least one dimension (family, Country, dispossession or relocation).
width.typical: Students discuss the cultural connectedness and belonging that First Nations Australians have to Country/Place through family ties, Country/Place identity, and the ongoing effects of dispossession, relocation and employment on relationships to place — recognising that connections persist across multiple places and are affected but not erased by displacement.
wider: Examine the historical geography of dispossession and relocation for a specific community — trace how policy (missions, reserves, forced removal) altered relationships to Country and the ongoing consequences for place connectedness today
Research how Native Title and land rights frameworks recognise and partly restore First Nations connections to Country — what does legal recognition mean for cultural connectedness?
Examine contemporary First Nations urban identity — how do Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people maintain connection to Country while living far from ancestral lands?

modes.reason: Students may initially understand First Nations connection to Country as analogous to any person's attachment to a home place. The reasoning scaffold needed is to explain how Country relationship is ontological (defines identity and belonging in a fundamental way) rather than merely sentimental — and how dispossession therefore causes a distinctive form of harm.

Examining multiple dimensions of connectedness (family, Country, spiritual, employment) and how dispossession has affected each dimension prevents a one-dimensional understanding of a complex, layered relationship.

nodes.label: Integration: cultural connectedness, identity and liveability perceptions
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain how cultural connectedness to places influences identity, sense of belonging and perceptions of liveability — integrating inclusion/exclusion analysis, social connection and First Nations Country relationships.
criteria: Produces an explanation that connects cultural connectedness to at least two of: identity, belonging, or liveability perception.
Addresses First Nations Australians' connectedness to Country/Place as a specific case within the explanation.

width.minimum: Students produce an explanation connecting cultural connectedness to either identity, belonging or liveability perception for a specific group.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated explanation of how cultural connectedness to places shapes identity, belonging and liveability perceptions — applying this to at least two different groups (e.g. First Nations Australians and another cultural group) and explaining how geographical context affects the nature and depth of those connections.
wider: Develop a comparative analysis of cultural connectedness to the same urban place for two different groups — e.g. a long-term Aboriginal urban community and a recently arrived migrant community — examining how their connections are similar and different in nature and liveability implications
Evaluate how a specific liveability strategy (K08) takes cultural connectedness into account — does it strengthen or threaten the place connections of any group?

modes.reason: The standard draws together inclusion/exclusion, social connection, and First Nations connectedness into a unified explanation of how cultural belonging shapes place perception. Integration practises making these three threads work together in a coherent argument.

descriptors.title: Strategies for liveability
descriptors.description: strategies used to enhance the liveability of a place, including for young people, the aged or those with disability, drawing on studies such as those from Australia or Europe
descriptors.knowledge: Students have completed K05–K07 — they can explain factors influencing residential decisions, analyse service distribution and its liveability implications, and explain how cultural connectedness shapes belonging and place perceptions. This standard is the synthesis point of the liveability unit — applying all prior conceptual work to the evaluation of strategies that improve liveability for specific community groups.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain strategies used to enhance the liveability of a place for different groups in the community.

nodes.label: Identifying liveability enhancement strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify strategies implemented in Australia or Europe to improve the liveability of a place and explain what aspect of liveability each targets.
criteria: Identifies at least two distinct liveability enhancement strategies from Australia or Europe, naming the strategy and the liveability problem it addresses.
Explains what aspect of liveability (physical, social, environmental, access) each strategy targets.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify a range of strategy types will evaluate liveability improvement narrowly (defaulting to infrastructure). This limits the evaluation capacity needed in node 3, where assessing applicability requires understanding which strategies address which liveability dimensions.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two liveability strategies from Australia or Europe and explain what liveability problem each addresses.
width.typical: Students identify strategies implemented in Australia or a country in Europe to improve liveability — including improving public spaces, walkability, transport connections, water disposal and recycling — explaining what each targets and considering applicability to their own locality.
wider: Research a specific European city known for liveability enhancement (e.g. Vienna, Copenhagen, Amsterdam) and analyse which strategies contribute to its high liveability ratings and whether they are transferable to Australian cities

Compare strategies targeting physical infrastructure (transport, public space) with strategies targeting social infrastructure (community programs, cultural facilities) — which approach has greater liveability impact and for whom?
Investigate strategies in Australian cities that have improved liveability for specific groups — e.g. 20-minute neighbourhood planning, age-friendly city programs, disability access audits

modes.reason: Widening to European exemplars alongside Australian cases gives students a richer strategy repertoire and allows them to see liveability enhancement as a field of active planning practice rather than an abstract aspiration.

nodes.label: Diverse community needs and strategy design
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop or describe a strategy to improve an aspect of liveability that takes into account the needs of diverse groups, including young people, the aged, people with disability, or Traditional Owners.
criteria: Identifies the specific liveability needs of at least two different community groups for a proposed or analysed strategy.
Explains how the strategy design addresses or should address those specific needs.

width.minimum: Students explain how at least one community group's specific needs have been or could be addressed by a liveability strategy.
width.typical: Students develop a strategy (or examine an existing one) to improve an aspect of liveability at the local scale, taking into account the needs of at least two diverse groups — including young people, elderly residents, people with disability, or Traditional Owners — and explaining how the strategy addresses group-specific needs.
wider: Develop a bilingual or culturally-responsive signage proposal for a local area in consultation with First Nations Australians or other cultural communities — examine what this signals about whose belonging is recognised

Design an inclusive public space that addresses the specific needs of young people, elderly residents and people with disability simultaneously — where do needs align and where do they create design tensions?
Research Universal Design principles and evaluate how well an existing local space meets them, proposing specific improvements

modes.reason: Designing for diverse groups requires students to adopt multiple perspectives simultaneously. Using fieldwork in a real local space makes the design challenge concrete and prevents abstract generalisation.

nodes.label: Evaluating strategy applicability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a liveability strategy using criteria and decide on its applicability to their own locality.
criteria: Applies at least two named criteria to evaluate a liveability strategy, using evidence to support each assessment.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion about the strategy's applicability to a specific local context, explaining the reasons.

width.minimum: Students apply at least two evaluation criteria to a liveability strategy and reach a reasoned conclusion about its applicability.
width.typical: Students evaluate a strategy to improve liveability using criteria — such as effectiveness for target groups, feasibility in local context, cost, equity of benefit, and environmental impact — and decide on its applicability to their own locality with reasons.
wider: Evaluate the same strategy against different criteria applied by different stakeholders — e.g. a developer, a disability advocate, a Traditional Owner, a young person — examine how criterion selection reflects values and interests
Compare how a strategy designed for a European context would need to be modified for an Australian context — examine what contextual factors would require modification
Develop a ranked set of liveability priorities for the local area and evaluate two or more strategies against those priorities

modes.reason: Criteria-based evaluation requires students to apply criteria consistently and reach a defensible conclusion. Scaffolding the evaluation process — selecting criteria, applying them with evidence, weighing and concluding — prevents evaluations that are really descriptions with a tagged-on opinion.

nodes.label: Integration: liveability strategies and diverse communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain strategies used to enhance the liveability of a place for diverse community groups — integrating strategy identification, needs analysis and evaluation.
criteria: Produces an analysis of a liveability strategy that addresses community group needs, strategy design, and applicability evaluation.
Draws on at least two liveability concepts from K05–K07 in the analysis.

width.minimum: Students produce an analysis of a liveability strategy that identifies targeted groups, explains how the strategy addresses their needs, and evaluates its applicability.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated analysis of a liveability strategy that: identifies the place context, explains the diverse community needs being addressed, describes the strategy and how it targets those needs, evaluates its effectiveness and applicability to the local context, and draws on at least one Australian or European comparative example.
wider: Develop an original liveability improvement proposal for a specific local place — including community needs assessment, strategy design, criteria evaluation and applicability argument — drawing on K05–K08 content throughout

Compare two Australian cities' liveability enhancement approaches (e.g. Melbourne vs Brisbane, or a capital vs a regional city) and evaluate which approach better addresses the needs of the most disadvantaged community groups

modes.reason: K08 is the synthesis standard for the entire liveability unit. The integration node requires students to draw on all liveability concepts — measurement, distribution, cultural connectedness, diverse needs — in a single coherent analysis of a place-based strategy.

descriptors.title: Develop geographical inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop questions for a geographical inquiry related to a phenomenon or challenge
descriptors.knowledge: Students have developed general inquiry questions in F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S01: develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems). This standard requires them to apply question development specifically within a geographical inquiry framework — questions must be oriented to geographical phenomena, use geographical concepts as organisers, and be plannable as a geographical investigation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop questions to guide a geographical inquiry into a phenomenon or challenge.

nodes.label: Geographical questions vs general questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish a geographical inquiry question from a general question, identifying the geographical phenomenon, concept or challenge it targets.
criteria: Identifies at least two features that make a question geographical and applies these to classify example questions.
Transforms at least one general question into a geographical inquiry question, explaining what geographical dimension has been added.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish geographical from general questions will develop inquiry questions that do not orient the investigation geographically. The resulting investigation plan (node 2) will lack geographical focus, making all subsequent skills application disconnected from geographical inquiry.

width.minimum: Students identify what makes a question geographical (targets a spatial phenomenon, process, distribution or place relationship) and classify examples as geographical or non-geographical.
width.typical: Students explain the features that make a question geographical — it investigates a spatial phenomenon, process, place relationship, environmental challenge or human-environment interaction — and practise transforming general questions into geographical questions by grounding them in place, distribution or environmental process.
wider: Examine a set of real geographical inquiry questions from ACARA exemplars or published geographical research and identify what makes each question productive as a geographical inquiry starter
Compare geographical questions at different scales (local, national, global) and explain how scale shapes what evidence is needed to answer the question

Develop a question that uses one of the ACARA geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale, change) as an explicit organiser and explain how the concept shapes the question

modes.reason: The distinction requires explicit attention to what kind of answer a question invites. Geographical questions invite spatial, environmental or place-based analysis — not just any investigation. Scaffolding: what place/process/distribution does this question target? What evidence would answer it?

nodes.label: Developing questions for a specific phenomenon or challenge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or a challenge may arise, producing questions that are specific, investigable and geographically grounded.
criteria: Develops at least two geographical inquiry questions about a specific phenomenon or challenge that are specific and investigable with real evidence.
Explains what geographical phenomenon, process or concept each question targets.
