nodes.hinge_reason: The quality of inquiry questions determines the quality of the investigation. Vague or non-investigable questions produce investigations that cannot generate meaningful evidence or conclusions. All subsequent skills (S02–S06) depend on having a sharp inquiry question to work from.

width.minimum: Students develop at least two investigable geographical questions about a specific phenomenon or challenge, each of which could be pursued with real evidence.
width.typical: Students develop questions to investigate a geographical phenomenon or challenge — e.g. the causes of water scarcity in different places, or the factors affecting liveability — producing questions that are specific, investigable with available evidence, and oriented to geographical concepts (cause, distribution, change, interconnection, sustainability).
wider: Develop a question sequence — an initial question and follow-up questions that deepen or extend the inquiry based on what answers to the initial question might reveal
Develop questions at different scales for the same phenomenon (e.g. water scarcity questions at local, national and global scale) and explain how different questions require different evidence
Compare questions that investigate causes vs questions that investigate impacts vs questions that investigate responses — examine how question type shapes what an investigation can reveal

modes.reason: Developing investigable questions requires iterative refinement — students produce a draft question, test it for specificity and investigability, refine it, and test again. Consolidation through peer critique and teacher feedback cycles builds the precision needed.
Practising question development across both water and liveability contexts — the two major content units — prevents question development being tied to a single topic.

nodes.label: Planning a geographical investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan a geographical investigation, identifying the evidence needed, how it will be collected, and appropriate digital planning tools.
criteria: Produces an investigation plan that specifies the inquiry question, at least two types of evidence needed, and a collection method for each.
Explains how the planned evidence would allow the inquiry question to be answered.

width.minimum: Students produce a basic investigation plan that identifies the inquiry question, the evidence needed to answer it, and at least one collection method.
width.typical: Students plan an investigation of a geographical phenomenon or challenge, using digital planning tools — identifying inquiry questions, evidence needed (statistics, fieldwork data, maps, satellite imagery), collection methods, and analysis approach.
wider: Develop a full investigation plan with timelines, data sources, fieldwork logistics, and analysis methods — evaluate whether the plan is feasible within available time and resources
Compare two possible investigation plans for the same question — evaluate which would produce more reliable or comprehensive evidence
Plan an investigation that triangulates evidence from multiple sources (primary fieldwork + secondary statistics + spatial data) and explain why triangulation strengthens findings

modes.reason: Planning integrates the inquiry question (node 2) with evidence types and collection methods (anticipating S02). The integration move is: question → evidence needed → collection method → analysis approach, as a connected sequence rather than four separate decisions.

descriptors.title: Collect, organise and represent geographical data
descriptors.description: collect, organise and represent data and information from primary research methods, including fieldwork and secondary research materials, using geospatial technologies and digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students have prior data collection and organisation skills from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S02: locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats). This standard introduces geospatial technologies, specialist digital tools, cartographic conventions and the distinction between primary fieldwork methods and secondary research materials in a specifically geographical context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collect, organise and represent geographical data from primary and secondary sources using appropriate geospatial technologies, digital tools and cartographic conventions.

nodes.label: Primary fieldwork methods for geographical data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify appropriate primary research methods for a geographical inquiry, including fieldwork, and use specialised digital tools to collect original materials.
criteria: Identifies at least two primary research methods appropriate to a specific geographical inquiry question and explains what data each produces.
Uses at least one digital tool to support primary data collection and explains why it was selected.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot select appropriate primary methods and tools for a geographical inquiry will produce data that does not match the inquiry question. The mismatch between question, method and data undermines the entire inquiry cycle — analysis and conclusion cannot proceed meaningfully from poorly matched data.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two primary fieldwork methods appropriate to a geographical inquiry and explain what kind of data each produces.
width.typical: Students identify appropriate primary research methods including interview and survey data, photographs of streetscapes, annotated field sketches, diagrams and statistics related to liveability or water — and use specialised digital tools (e.g. survey platforms, mapping apps) to collect original materials from a field context.
wider: Conduct fieldwork using at least two different primary methods (e.g. survey + field sketch + photographs) and reflect on what each method captures and what it misses
Design a fieldwork data collection protocol including the questions, observation prompts and recording formats needed — evaluate the protocol before going to the field
Compare fieldwork data collected using different methods for the same site and identify agreements and discrepancies

modes.reason: Selecting a primary method requires reasoning about what data type the question needs and which method produces that type. Scaffolding: inquiry question → data type needed → method that produces that data type → tool for that method. This chain prevents method selection by familiarity rather than fitness.

nodes.label: Secondary research: finding and selecting relevant materials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect relevant secondary research materials using advanced search functions, evaluating relevance and reliability.
criteria: Locates at least two secondary sources relevant to a geographical inquiry question and explains the criteria used to assess each source's relevance.
Uses at least one advanced search method to find sources and reflects on how it improved search results.

width.minimum: Students locate at least two relevant secondary sources for a geographical inquiry and explain why each is relevant.
width.typical: Students collect relevant secondary research materials — print and online publications, photographs, images, statistical datasets — using advanced search functions (e.g. specific field search operators) and explain the criteria used to assess relevance and reliability.
wider: Compare two secondary sources on the same topic (e.g. two reports on water scarcity in a region) and evaluate their reliability, currency and perspective

Examine the difference between primary and secondary use of the same material — e.g. an aerial photograph used as primary evidence of current land use vs used as secondary evidence from a historical archive
Practise advanced search operators to narrow results to relevant sources and evaluate whether the results are genuinely more useful

modes.reason: Reliable source selection requires repeated practice with explicit criteria. Students need multiple search exercises with structured reflection on what was found and why it was or was not suitable.

nodes.label: Representing data in appropriate geographical formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent geographical data and information in formats appropriate to the data type and inquiry question — including tables, graphs, and geospatial representations.
criteria: Represents geographical data in at least one format (map, table, graph) that is appropriate to the data type and inquiry question.
Applies cartographic conventions (title, scale, north arrow, legend) to any map produced.
nodes.hinge_reason: Data representation is the bridge between collection and analysis. Students who cannot represent data in geographically appropriate formats — particularly spatial representation with cartographic conventions — cannot engage with S03 pattern and trend analysis. A table where a map is needed, or a map without conventions, prevents spatial pattern reading.

width.minimum: Students represent collected data in at least one appropriate format and explain why that format was chosen.
width.typical: Students represent data in appropriate formats — combining primary research data into questionnaires, tables or graphs; representing spatial information using cartographic conventions in maps at different scales using computer mapping tools.
wider: Represent the same dataset in two different formats (e.g. table and choropleth map) and evaluate which better communicates the spatial pattern
Construct a map conforming to full cartographic conventions (title, scale, north arrow, legend, projection note) for a geographical distribution and evaluate its accuracy and readability
Use geospatial software (e.g. Google My Maps, ArcGIS Online) to represent spatial data and reflect on how digital tools alter what can be represented and communicated

modes.reason: Cartographic conventions require repeated practice to apply correctly and consistently. Students need practice constructing maps with all required conventions — not just exposure to examples.
Representing both spatial (map) and non-spatial (graph, table) data, and comparing which format serves which question, builds genuine understanding of representation as a communication choice.

nodes.label: Integration: collect, organise and represent in an inquiry context
nodes.checkpoint: Students collect, organise and represent data from primary and secondary sources using appropriate geospatial and digital tools — producing a coherent evidence base for a geographical inquiry.
criteria: Produces an evidence base using at least one primary and one secondary source, represented in appropriate formats for the inquiry question.
Reflects on one limitation or gap in the evidence base and explains what additional evidence would address it.

width.minimum: Students produce a small evidence base (at least one primary and one secondary source) organised and represented in appropriate formats for a specific inquiry question.
width.typical: Students produce an evidence base for a geographical inquiry that combines primary and secondary data, organises it into appropriate formats, uses geospatial technologies where applicable, and presents it in forms that support analysis of the inquiry question.
wider: Develop a full evidence base for a geographical inquiry using at least three different data sources and two different representation formats — evaluate which combinations produce the most useful analytical base
Reflect on the quality of the evidence base produced: which inquiry questions are well-supported and which have evidence gaps? What would strengthen the base?

modes.reason: The integration node connects the three earlier nodes — method selection, source finding, representation — into a coherent evidence base for a specific inquiry. The performance is the production of evidence fit for purpose, not the demonstration of each skill in isolation.

descriptors.title: Interpret and analyse geographical data
descriptors.description: interpret and analyse geographical data and information to identify similarities and differences, explain patterns and trends and infer relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students have prior skills identifying patterns and trends from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S03: evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, or to infer relationships). This standard extends that to geographical-specific analytical moves: reading spatial data, explaining geographical patterns and trends with reference to geographical processes, and inferring place-based relationships from data.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and analyse geographical data to identify similarities and differences, explain patterns and trends, and infer relationships.

nodes.label: Identifying similarities and differences in geographical data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences in geographical data and information, using specific evidence from maps, images or data.
criteria: Identifies at least two similarities and two differences between geographical datasets or places, citing specific evidence for each.
Avoids vague generalisations — each comparison is grounded in a specific data point, map feature or image detail.
nodes.hinge_reason: Identifying similarities and differences with specific evidence is the foundation for pattern explanation in node 2. Students who make vague comparisons ('one place has more services') without specific evidence cannot transition to explaining spatial patterns — they have no data points to connect into a pattern.

width.minimum: Students identify at least two similarities and two differences in a geographical dataset or between two places, with specific evidence.
width.typical: Students identify similarities and differences in geographical data — e.g. comparing housing density from aerial images of inner vs outer suburbs, or rural vs remote places — using specific evidence from the data and avoiding vague generalisations.
wider: Compare data at multiple scales for the same phenomenon — identify similarities and differences at local, state and national scales
Compare similarities and differences using both quantitative data (statistics) and qualitative data (photographs, field sketches) for the same location pair
Examine a case where aggregate data obscures important local similarities and differences — practise identifying what fine-grained analysis reveals that aggregate analysis hides

modes.reason: Students frequently describe differences without citing specific evidence. Consolidation requires repeated practice extracting specific data points from maps and images as the basis for comparison — not describing general impressions.

nodes.label: Explaining geographical patterns and trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain geographical patterns and trends in data, connecting the pattern to a geographical process or relationship.
criteria: Identifies at least one geographical pattern or trend in data and explains it by reference to a geographical process.
Distinguishes between describing a pattern (what is observed) and explaining it (why it occurs).
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who can identify patterns but not explain them cannot draw geographical conclusions (S04). Pattern description without process explanation is empirically incomplete — it cannot support inference or decision-making.

width.minimum: Students identify at least one geographical pattern or trend in data and explain it by reference to a geographical process or relationship.
width.typical: Students explain patterns and trends in geographical data — e.g. using graphs, weather maps and satellite images to examine temporal and spatial patterns of a hydrological hazard — connecting the pattern to an underlying geographical process (not just naming it).
wider: Distinguish between a pattern (spatial distribution at a point in time) and a trend (change over time) and analyse one example of each for the same phenomenon
Examine a pattern that appears simple but has a complex explanation — e.g. why do some remote areas have higher water costs despite being near water sources? — practising multi-causal explanation
Use two different data formats (e.g. map and graph) to identify the same pattern, and evaluate which format makes the pattern more visible

modes.reason: The move from describing a pattern to explaining it requires a process chain: observed pattern → geographical mechanism → why this pattern exists here and not elsewhere. Explicit scaffolding of this chain prevents students stopping at description.

Practising pattern explanation across both physical (hazard spatial patterns) and human (service distribution patterns) phenomena builds transferable analytical skills and prevents students from learning a single process explanation.

nodes.label: Inferring geographical relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can infer relationships in geographical data and information, explaining the relationship and the evidence base for the inference.
criteria: Infers at least one relationship from geographical data and identifies the evidence that supports the inference.
Notes at least one limitation of the inference or an alternative explanation that the data cannot rule out.

width.minimum: Students infer at least one relationship from geographical data and explain the evidence that supports the inference.
width.typical: Students infer relationships in data and information collected — e.g. using surveys and interviews to identify community attitudes about service distribution in cities vs remote communities — explaining the relationship inferred, the evidence base, and the degree of confidence warranted.
wider: Distinguish between correlation (two things vary together) and causal relationship (one causes the other) in geographical data, and test this distinction on real examples
Infer a relationship from two different data types (quantitative and qualitative) for the same phenomenon and consider whether the two data types produce the same inference
Examine an apparent relationship in data that has an alternative explanation — practise generating and evaluating rival explanations

modes.reason: Students often treat correlation as causation. The reasoning scaffold — pattern observed → relationship inferred → evidence for inference → confidence level → possible alternative explanation — builds epistemic care about inference that is central to geographical analysis.

nodes.label: Integration: interpret and analyse geographical data
nodes.checkpoint: Students interpret and analyse geographical data — identifying similarities and differences, explaining patterns and trends, and inferring relationships — in the context of a geographical inquiry.
criteria: Produces a data analysis that demonstrates at least two of: identifying similarities/differences, explaining patterns/trends, inferring relationships.
Grounds each analytical claim in specific data evidence.

width.minimum: Students produce an analysis of geographical data that demonstrates at least two of the three analytical moves (compare, explain, infer).
width.typical: Students produce an integrated analysis of a geographical dataset that identifies similarities and differences, explains at least one spatial pattern or trend, and infers at least one relationship — presented as a connected analytical argument rather than three separate exercises.
wider: Produce a full data analysis section for a geographical inquiry report that applies all three analytical moves to multiple data sources, evaluates the reliability of the inferences, and identifies gaps
Peer-review another student's data analysis using the three-move framework — provide specific feedback on whether each move is demonstrated with sufficient evidence

modes.reason: The three analytical moves — compare, explain, infer — need to be applied sequentially and cumulatively in a real analysis context. Integration practises moving through all three in response to a geographical dataset rather than applying each in isolation.

descriptors.title: Draw geographical conclusions
descriptors.description: draw conclusions based on the analysis of the data and information
descriptors.knowledge: Students have prior evidence-based conclusion skills from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S05: develop evidence-based conclusions). This standard requires them to draw conclusions specifically in a geographical inquiry context — using geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale, change) as organisers, and connecting conclusions to the impacts of geographical phenomena on people, places and environments.
descriptors.endpoint: Students draw conclusions based on the analysis of geographical data and information.

nodes.label: Geographical concepts as conclusion organisers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use at least one geographical concept (place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale or change) to organise and frame a geographical conclusion.
criteria: Names the geographical concept used to organise the conclusion and explains how it frames the analytical finding.
Produces a conclusion that is structured by a geographical concept, not just a summary of data findings.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who skip the concept organiser step produce conclusions that are empirical summaries ('the data shows X') rather than geographical conclusions ('this distribution pattern shows that sustainability is compromised because…'). The concept organiser is what makes a conclusion geographical rather than generic.

width.minimum: Students identify which geographical concept is most relevant to organising their conclusion and explain why.
width.typical: Students draw on analysis results and use at least one of the concepts of place, space, environment, interconnections, sustainability, scale or change to organise a response to a geographical inquiry question — e.g. using distribution analysis to form conclusions about sustainability of farming, or using location analysis to form conclusions about interconnections between people, place, environment and liveability.
wider: Apply two different geographical concepts to the same analysis and compare the conclusions each organiser generates — examine how concept choice shapes what the conclusion highlights
Develop a conclusion about interconnections that traces a chain: geographical distribution → human access → social outcome — making explicit how the concept of interconnections connects these
Practise applying each of the seven geographical concepts to a single dataset and evaluate which produces the most insightful conclusion

modes.reason: The move from analysis results to a geographically-framed conclusion requires explicit practice with the concept organiser as a tool. Scaffold: analysis finding → which concept applies → how does the concept frame a conclusion → what does the conclusion state?

nodes.label: Explaining impacts on people, places and environments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the impacts of a geographical phenomenon or challenge on people, places and environments, drawing on analysis results.
criteria: Explains at least one impact on people and one impact on places or environments, connecting each to the geographical phenomenon studied.
Uses analysis evidence to support each impact claim.

width.minimum: Students explain at least one impact on people AND one impact on places or environments from their analysis, connected to the geographical phenomenon studied.
width.typical: Students explain the impacts of a geographical phenomenon or challenge on people, places and environments — e.g. impacts of water scarcity on individuals, communities and government; or impacts of declining water quality on people and liveability of places — connecting each impact to the analytical evidence.
wider: Trace a cascade of impacts: initial geographical phenomenon → first-order impact → second-order impact → systemic consequence — e.g. drought → reduced farm income → community service decline → population loss
Compare impacts at different scales — individual, community, government — and explain how scale shapes the nature and severity of impact
Examine cases where impacts are distributed unequally across groups — who bears the impact and why — connecting to broader geographical concepts of equity and sustainability

modes.reason: Explaining impacts across people, places AND environments — not just one category — requires deliberate widening. Students default to human impacts. Using case studies where environmental impacts are primary (water quality, habitat loss) builds fuller impact analysis.

nodes.label: Conclusions as answers to the inquiry question
nodes.checkpoint: Students can produce a geographical conclusion that directly responds to the inquiry question, synthesising analytical findings into a defensible claim.
criteria: Produces a conclusion that directly responds to the inquiry question.
Supports the conclusion with at least two analytical findings, using geographical terminology.

width.minimum: Students produce a conclusion that directly answers the inquiry question and is supported by at least two pieces of analytical evidence.
width.typical: Students produce a geographical conclusion that: directly responds to the inquiry question, synthesises key analytical findings, uses a geographical concept as organiser, and explains impacts on people, places or environments — presented as a coherent claim rather than a list of findings.
wider: Write a conclusion at two different confidence levels — a strong conclusion when evidence is clear and a hedged conclusion when evidence is partial — practising appropriate epistemic language
Develop a counter-argument to a classmate's conclusion using the same data — examine what the same evidence can support if analysed differently
Compare the conclusion reached through quantitative data analysis with the conclusion suggested by qualitative data (e.g. survey results) for the same inquiry — examine whether they agree

modes.reason: Writing a conclusion as a coherent claim rather than a list of findings requires practice. Students need repeated opportunities to draft, receive feedback, and revise conclusions — distinguishing between 'here is what I found' (finding) and 'here is what this means' (conclusion).

descriptors.title: Identify strategies for geographical action
descriptors.description: identify a strategy for action in relation to environmental, economic, social or other factors, and explain potential impacts
descriptors.knowledge: Students have prior skills proposing actions from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S06: propose actions or responses to issues or challenges and use criteria to assess the possible effects). This standard extends that to the geographical context — proposing individual and collective action in response to geographical phenomena, explaining potential impacts, and reflecting on how personal values influence explanation of impacts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify a strategy for action in relation to a geographical phenomenon or challenge and explain its potential impacts.

nodes.label: Individual action in response to geographical phenomena
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose individual action in response to a geographical phenomenon or challenge, supporting the proposal with geographical reasoning.
criteria: Proposes at least one individual action in response to a geographical phenomenon or challenge.
Supports the proposal with geographical reasoning that connects the action to the identified problem.

width.minimum: Students propose at least one individual action in response to a geographical challenge and explain why it would be effective.
width.typical: Students propose individual actions in response to geographical phenomena or challenges — e.g. reducing individual water footprint, choosing active transport for liveability — supporting each proposal with reasons connected to the geographical analysis conducted.
wider: Evaluate the potential impact of scaling individual action — if many individuals took the same action, would it produce meaningful change? What scale of uptake would be needed?
Compare individual action to collective action for the same challenge and evaluate which is better suited to addressing the geographical cause
Examine cases where well-intentioned individual actions have unintended negative impacts — e.g. increased water recycling in one area reducing river flows to downstream users

modes.reason: Individual action proposals often lack connection to the geographical analysis. The reasoning scaffold: geographical finding → mechanism connecting individual action to that finding → why this action addresses the identified cause or condition → expected impact.

nodes.label: Collective action and geographical change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose collective action in response to a geographical phenomenon or challenge, supporting the proposal with reasons and explaining the geographical mechanism through which it would produce change.
criteria: Proposes at least one collective action and explains how it would address a geographical challenge.
Identifies the scale at which the collective action operates and explains why that scale is appropriate.

width.minimum: Students propose at least one collective action and explain how it would address a geographical challenge at a community or policy scale.
width.typical: Students propose collective actions in response to geographical phenomena — e.g. community water conservation guidelines, planning for sustainable and liveable cities — supporting proposals with reasons including expected geographical impacts and mechanisms of change.
wider: Compare two collective actions at different scales (local vs national) addressing the same geographical challenge — examine what scale of action is needed to address a particular cause
Develop a collective action proposal that involves multiple stakeholders — map the different roles, interests and contributions of each stakeholder group
Examine historical examples of collective action that produced geographical change (e.g. water management reforms, urban greening programs) and evaluate what made them effective

modes.reason: Widening to collective actions at different scales — community, municipal, state, national — prevents students from treating all collective action as equivalent and reveals how the scale of the problem determines the appropriate scale of response.

nodes.label: Personal values and explanation of potential impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on how personal values and attitudes influence explanations of potential impacts of actions on geographical phenomena.
criteria: Identifies at least one personal value or attitude that influences their explanation of a potential impact.
Explains how a different value perspective would produce a different assessment of the same impact.

width.minimum: Students identify at least one way their personal values or experiences influence how they explain a potential impact.
width.typical: Students reflect on the influence of personal values and attitudes on explanations of potential impacts — e.g. how availability of technology and infrastructure shapes what is perceived as a liveable place; how cultural and economic values lead to different assessments of water use priorities — producing an explanation that is aware of its own value-basis.
wider: Examine the same proposed action from two different value perspectives (e.g. economic development vs environmental conservation) and explain how each perspective produces a different impact assessment
Compare the impact explanation produced by a community directly affected by a geographical challenge with the explanation produced by a policymaker or researcher — examine the sources of difference
Reflect on how geographical positionality (where you live, your cultural background, your economic situation) shapes which impacts are visible and which are invisible

modes.reason: Value-awareness in impact explanation requires students to step outside their own perspective and identify its premises. Scaffolding: what values or assumptions underlie my impact explanation? Who might assess impacts differently and why?

nodes.label: Integration: strategy, impact and values
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify a strategy for action in relation to a geographical challenge and explain its potential impacts — integrating individual and collective dimensions and value-awareness.
criteria: Produces a strategy proposal with at least two potential impacts explained.
Reflects on at least one value dimension that shapes the impact explanation.

width.minimum: Students produce a strategy proposal (individual or collective) and explain at least two potential impacts, noting one value dimension that influences the impact explanation.
width.typical: Students produce an integrated strategy proposal that: identifies a geographical challenge, proposes individual and/or collective action, explains potential impacts across multiple dimensions, and reflects on how values shape the impact explanation — presented as a coherent, reasoned proposal rather than separate components.
wider: Develop a strategy proposal that includes both individual and collective components, explains potential impacts at multiple scales, and explicitly acknowledges competing values among different stakeholders
Evaluate the strategy using criteria from K08 (effectiveness, feasibility, equity, environmental impact) and revise the proposal based on the evaluation

modes.reason: The standard brings together individual action, collective action and value-awareness into a single strategy proposal with impact explanation. Integration practises producing this as a connected geographical argument rather than three separate tasks.

descriptors.title: Create geographical descriptions and explanations
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and responses, using geographical knowledge and methods, concepts, terms and reference sources
descriptors.knowledge: Students have prior communication skills from F–6 HASS (AC9HS6S07: present descriptions and explanations, drawing ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources, and using relevant terms and conventions). This standard raises the bar specifically for geographical communication — incorporating geographical methods (maps, graphs, data representations), geographical concepts, specialised terminology, and reference to sources as integrated elements of geographical writing and presentation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and responses using geographical knowledge and methods, concepts, terms and reference sources.

nodes.label: Geographical descriptions with concepts and terminology
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create geographical descriptions that use accurate terminology, reference geographical concepts, and connect the audience to the topic.
criteria: Produces a geographical description that uses at least three geographical terms accurately.
References at least one geographical concept explicitly in the description.

width.minimum: Students produce a geographical description that uses at least three accurate geographical terms and references at least one geographical concept.
width.typical: Students create descriptions that connect the audience to a geographical topic and use geographical concepts and terms accurately — e.g. describing a preferred liveability strategy using terms such as distribution, accessibility, walkability, sustainability, and concepts such as place or interconnections.
wider: Compare a geographical description written for a specialist audience (planners, geographers) with one written for a general community audience — examine how terminology use and concept explanation differ
Evaluate the precision of geographical terminology in a description — identify any terms used imprecisely and revise for accuracy
Analyse a published geographical description (e.g. from a geography journal, planning document) and identify how concept use and terminology contribute to its persuasiveness

modes.reason: Accurate and consistent use of geographical terminology requires practice and feedback. Students frequently use technical terms loosely. Consolidation through targeted vocabulary exercises and peer review of terminology precision builds reliable usage.

nodes.label: Geographical explanations supported by research findings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct geographical explanations that use research findings (data, maps, statistics) to support ideas.
criteria: Produces a geographical explanation that integrates at least two research findings as evidence within the explanation (not just appended).
Explains how each piece of evidence supports the geographical idea being argued.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot integrate research findings into explanations produce claims-without-evidence, which fails the basic requirement of geographical communication. This is the skill that distinguishes geographical explanation from opinion, and it is required by all subsequent assessment tasks.

width.minimum: Students produce an explanation that uses at least two research findings as evidence and connects them to the geographical idea being explained.
width.typical: Students construct explanations using research findings to support ideas — e.g. data on water usage over time and at different places, or information about liveability indexes — ensuring that evidence is integrated into the explanation rather than listed separately.
wider: Construct an explanation using evidence from at least three different source types (quantitative data, map, qualitative interview/survey) and evaluate how the diversity of evidence types strengthens the explanation
Revise an explanation that makes claims without evidence — add appropriate research findings and evaluate how the revision changes the persuasiveness of the explanation
Analyse the role of maps as evidence in a geographical explanation — examine how spatial data is different from statistical data as an evidence type

modes.reason: The move from presenting evidence and then making a claim (list-then-argue) to integrating evidence within an explanation (evidence-embedded argument) requires explicit practice. Consolidation through multiple explanation drafting and revision cycles builds this integration.

Practising evidence integration across both water and liveability content — and across different evidence types (maps, statistics, survey data) — prevents students from treating evidence integration as specific to one topic or data format.

nodes.label: Geographical representations as communication tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop geographical responses that use geographical methods — maps, data representations — to communicate conclusions and support arguments.
criteria: Includes at least one geographical representation in a response and explains how it supports the argument.
Integrates the representation into the text of the response rather than presenting it as a separate appendix.

width.minimum: Students include at least one geographical representation (map, graph, data display) in a response and explain how it supports the argument being made.
width.typical: Students develop conclusions using geographical methods to represent data and information — e.g. a map showing water usage and scarcity in Australia, a map representing liveability indicators — integrating the representation into the response as evidence rather than decoration.
wider: Develop a response that uses multiple map types (distribution map, choropleth, flow map) for the same geographical topic and evaluate which best communicates the argument
Evaluate the communication effectiveness of a geographical representation (map or graph) and revise it to better serve the argument
Create a multi-modal geographical response (text + map + graph + photographs) and evaluate how the modes work together

modes.reason: Widening to multiple representation types and evaluating their fit for the argument being made builds understanding that geographical representation is a communication choice, not just a technical skill.

nodes.label: Integration: create complete geographical responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and responses that integrate geographical knowledge, methods, concepts, terminology and reference sources — producing coherent geographical communication.
criteria: Produces a geographical response that includes description, explanation supported by evidence, and at least one geographical representation.
Uses geographical terminology accurately and consistently throughout.

width.minimum: Students produce a geographical response that includes description, explanation, at least one representation, and uses geographical terminology consistently.
width.typical: Students produce a complete geographical response — written, visual or multimodal — that integrates: accurate geographical description with terminology, explanation supported by research findings, at least one geographical method or representation, and references to sources — presenting the response as a coherent geographical communication.
wider: Produce a complete geographical inquiry report that integrates all elements across all sections — research question, evidence base, analysis, conclusion, strategy — as a professional quality geographical document
Evaluate a peer's geographical response against the four elements of the standard (description, explanation, methods, terminology) and provide structured feedback

modes.reason: The standard brings together description, explanation, representational methods and terminology into a single coherent response. Integration practises producing all elements as a unified geographical communication rather than assembling separate components.

descriptors.title: Geomorphological processes
descriptors.description: geomorphological processes that produce different landscapes and significant landforms
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain how water connects and changes places as it moves through environments (AC9HG7K01), and the causes and impacts of atmospheric/hydrological hazards (AC9HG7K04). They have not yet encountered tectonic, volcanic, or rock-weathering processes at this scale.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain geomorphological processes — including tectonics, volcanism, folding, faulting, weathering, erosion, transportation and deposition — that produce different landscapes and significant landforms.

nodes.label: Landscape diversity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the diversity of landscape types at the global and national scale, including wetlands, grasslands, forests, and deserts.
criteria: Identifies and names at least three distinct landscape types with a located example for each.
Describes at least one distinguishing feature that differentiates each landscape type.

width.minimum: Students describe at least three landscape types with one example location each.
width.typical: Students describe a range of landscape types (wetlands, grasslands, forests, hot and cold deserts) with national and international examples, explaining what distinguishes each type visually and environmentally.
wider: Compare landscape distributions across multiple continents, identifying climate–landscape relationships.
Examine how landscape classification systems differ (e.g., ecological vs geomorphological framings).
Investigate transition zones between landscape types and why boundaries are rarely sharp.

nodes.label: Endogenic processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how tectonics, volcanism, folding and faulting produce major landforms.
criteria: Names and explains at least two endogenic processes (e.g., folding, volcanism) and links each to a named landform.
Distinguishes endogenic processes (driven by internal Earth energy) from surface processes.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students conflate endogenic and exogenic processes, or treat all landforms as surface erosion products, they cannot accurately explain the formation of major landscapes in Node 3 or the hazard origins in AC9HG8K05.

width.minimum: Students explain one endogenic process (tectonic, volcanic, fold or fault) with a named landform example.
width.typical: Students explain how plate tectonics drives volcanism, folding and faulting, linking each process to a named landform example (e.g., MacDonnell Ranges — folding; Great Sumatran Fault — faulting; Krakatoa — volcanism).
wider: Compare landforms produced by convergent vs divergent plate boundaries.
Investigate how the same tectonic setting can produce different landform types (e.g., both mountains and rift valleys).
Examine how volcanic activity produces landscape diversity beyond just volcanic cones — lava plains, calderas, geothermal landscapes.

modes.reason: Students need a clear conceptual model distinguishing internal (endogenic) from external (exogenic) forces before they can correctly attribute landform origins. A process-to-landform reasoning chain — plate boundary type → stress/movement → resulting structure — prevents conflation.

nodes.label: Weathering processes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how chemical and physical weathering break down rock to shape landforms, including the role of rock type.
criteria: Explains at least one chemical and one physical weathering process, identifying the conditions that drive each.
Links rock type to differential weathering outcomes in a named landscape or landform.
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding weathering as a prerequisite to erosion and deposition is needed for Node 4. Students who treat erosion as the only surface process will produce incomplete process chains when explaining landform formation.

width.minimum: Students explain one type of chemical weathering and one type of physical weathering with a landform or landscape example.
width.typical: Students explain chemical weathering (oxidation, solution) and physical weathering (exfoliation, frost wedging), relating each to rock type (sedimentary, igneous, metamorphic) and a selected landform such as Fraser Island or the Twelve Apostles.
wider: Investigate how differential weathering rates between rock types produce distinctive landform features (e.g., tors, inselbergs).
Compare weathering processes in tropical vs arid climates and their contrasting landform outcomes.
Examine karst landscapes as a case study of chemical weathering at landscape scale.

modes.reason: Using multiple rock types and climate contexts helps students avoid exemplar lock-in where they treat sandstone + wind as the only weathering story. Breadth across rock types and climates builds a transferable process model.

nodes.label: Erosion, transportation and deposition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how erosion, transportation and deposition by water and wind shape landforms, using a selected local-scale example.
criteria: Describes the sequence of erosion, transportation and deposition by a named agent in relation to a specific landform.
Explains how the characteristics of the landform reflect the dominant process agent(s).

width.minimum: Students explain how one agent (water or wind) erodes, transports and deposits material to shape a named landform.
width.typical: Students explain the sequence of erosion → transportation → deposition by water and wind, applying this to a selected local-scale landform (e.g., Fraser Island formed by wind, waves and ocean currents; Twelve Apostles formed by coastal erosion and wave action).
wider: Compare the relative roles of water and wind as agents in landform formation in contrasting climate zones.
Investigate how human modifications (vegetation clearing, dams) alter natural erosion and deposition regimes.
Examine time scales — how the same processes that operate daily also explain large-scale landscape formation over geological time.

nodes.label: Process integration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how multiple geomorphological processes interact to produce landscapes, selecting and applying appropriate process explanations to named landforms at different scales.
criteria: Selects and names at least two geomorphological processes relevant to a chosen landform.
Explains how these processes interact or sequence to produce the landform's characteristics.
Locates the landform and identifies the scale at which the explanation operates.

width.minimum: Students explain the formation of one selected landform by identifying the dominant processes involved and how they interact.
width.typical: Students explain how endogenic and exogenic processes together produce a landscape or landform, applying process-based reasoning to examples at national and local scale. They distinguish between structural origins (tectonics, folding) and surface modification (weathering, erosion) in a coherent formation explanation.
wider: Compare two landforms formed by contrasting process combinations (e.g., volcanic island modified by weathering vs sedimentary landform shaped by erosion).
Investigate how the same process produces different outcomes in different contexts — e.g., water erosion in humid vs arid settings.
Explore how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples explain landform formation through Dreaming stories, considering what geographic knowledge these narratives encode.

modes.reason: Students need to coordinate process vocabulary and causal reasoning from Nodes 1–4 into a coherent formation explanation. The integration task — explaining a named landform using multiple processes — is where fragmented knowledge becomes geographic explanation.

descriptors.title: Landscape distribution
descriptors.description: the location and distribution of Australia's distinctive landscapes and significant landforms
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain water distribution at the national scale and have located water resources on maps (AC9HG7K02). They have not yet mapped the distribution of landform types or related landscape patterns across Australia.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the location and distribution of Australia's distinctive landscapes and significant landforms, including their significance to First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Locating Australian landscapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate and name distinctive Australian landscapes and significant landforms on a map.
criteria: Accurately locates and labels at least three distinctive landscapes or significant landforms on a map of Australia.
Describes the spatial distribution pattern (e.g., deserts concentrated in the interior, rainforests in the north).
nodes.hinge_reason: Spatial location is the foundation for all comparison and significance work in Nodes 2–3. Students who cannot accurately locate landscapes will be unable to make meaningful distribution comparisons or relate First Nations connections to specific places.

width.minimum: Students locate at least three distinctive landscapes or significant landforms on a map of Australia.
width.typical: Students represent the distribution of distinctive Australian landscapes (deserts in Central Australia, tropical rainforests in the north) and significant landforms (Uluru, Blue Mountains) on a map, describing the spatial pattern.
wider: Compare the distribution of Australian landscapes with those of another country, identifying similarities and differences in the pattern.
Investigate why certain landscape types cluster in particular parts of Australia, linking climate zones to landscape distribution.
Examine how mapping technology (satellite imagery, GIS) has changed how we document landscape distribution.

modes.reason: Mapping and locating require repeated practice with cartographic tools. Students need to use maps actively — not just read them — before they can represent distributions confidently.

nodes.label: What makes landscapes iconic
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe what makes Australian landscapes and landforms iconic, including their distinctive visual and environmental characteristics.
criteria: Describes at least two characteristics that make a selected landscape or landform distinctive or iconic.
Compares at least one Australian landscape type with an equivalent landscape in another country.

width.minimum: Students describe at least one iconic landscape or landform and explain what distinguishes it.
width.typical: Students identify and describe the characteristics that make selected Australian landscapes and landforms iconic — physical form, rarity, scale, distinctiveness — and compare the distribution of Australian landscapes with those of another country.
wider: Examine how 'iconicity' is socially constructed — what criteria make a place iconic and who decides?
Compare iconic landscape features in Australia with analogous features internationally (e.g., Australian desert vs Mongolian steppe).
Investigate how tourism industries shape and amplify the iconic status of certain landscapes.

modes.reason: Examining iconic landscapes across multiple contexts — different regions of Australia and internationally — prevents students from treating one example as definitively 'what iconic looks like' and builds capacity for comparative geographic thinking.

nodes.label: Significance to First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the significance of a landform important to First Nations Australians, including its name, meaning and cultural/spiritual significance.
criteria: Names and describes a landform significant to a First Nations Australian community, including its First Nations name and meaning.
Explains at least two dimensions of significance (cultural, spiritual, ecological, historical) that the community associates with the place.

width.minimum: Students explain the significance of one landform to a First Nations Australian community, including its name and meaning.
width.typical: Students explain the significance of a landform important to First Nations Australians (e.g., Three Sisters/Blue Mountains, Budj Bim, Uluru-Kata Tjuta), including the names, meanings and layered significance (cultural, spiritual, ecological) that the community associates with the place.
wider: Examine how First Nations place names encode geographic and cultural knowledge about landscapes and landforms.
Compare how the same place is understood differently by First Nations communities and mainstream tourism industries.
Investigate how native title and land rights legislation intersects with the recognition of First Nations connections to iconic landscapes.

modes.reason: Using multiple First Nations examples — from different Country and different types of significance — prevents reduction to a single exemplar and honours the diversity of First Nations relationships to landscapes.

descriptors.title: Values of landscapes
descriptors.description: the spiritual, aesthetic and cultural value of landscapes and landforms for people, including Country/Place of First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain the economic, cultural, spiritual and aesthetic value of water for people including First Nations Australians (AC9HG7K03), and the cultural connectedness of people to places (AC9HG7K07). They have not yet extended this framework to landscapes and landforms broadly.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the spiritual, aesthetic and cultural value of landscapes and landforms for people, including the multilayered meanings of Country/Place for First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: Types of landscape value
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish and describe spiritual, aesthetic and cultural values as distinct ways people value landscapes.
criteria: Defines and distinguishes spiritual, aesthetic and cultural values of landscapes, providing an example of each.
Explains how a specific landscape is valued in at least two different ways by the same or different groups.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students collapse all value types into a single undifferentiated 'people like it' framing, they cannot explain the distinct and layered significance of Country/Place for First Nations Australians in Node 2.

width.minimum: Students identify and describe at least two types of landscape value (spiritual, aesthetic, cultural) with an example each.
width.typical: Students describe spiritual, aesthetic and cultural values as distinct but overlapping dimensions of how people relate to landscapes, providing examples of each from different cultural contexts (e.g., Mt Fuji in Japan — aesthetic and spiritual; Yellow Mountains in China — aesthetic and cultural).
wider: Examine how economic value relates to and sometimes conflicts with spiritual, aesthetic and cultural values.
Compare how the same landscape can hold different value types simultaneously for different groups.
Investigate how tourism commodifies aesthetic landscape value and what this means for spiritual and cultural values.

modes.reason: Students need a clear schema for distinguishing value types — what counts as spiritual vs aesthetic vs cultural — before they can apply these distinctions to the more complex First Nations context. A value-type framework built here carries the whole standard.

nodes.label: Country/Place and First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the multilayered meanings of landscapes and landforms for First Nations Australians, including Dreaming stories and the material, cultural and spiritual dimensions of Country/Place.
criteria: Explains at least two dimensions of First Nations Australians' connection to a named Country/Place.
Describes how Dreaming stories or Creation stories give meaning to a specific landscape or landform.

width.minimum: Students explain at least one dimension of the special connection First Nations Australians have to Country/Place, with a named example.
width.typical: Students examine how Dreaming stories and Torres Strait Islander Creation stories give meaning to Country/Place, and describe the multilayered meanings (material, cultural and spiritual wellbeing) associated with landscapes and significant landforms for First Nations Australians.
wider: Examine how Country/Place meanings are transmitted across generations through oral tradition, ceremony and land management practice.
Compare how Dreaming stories encode geographic knowledge (seasonal patterns, species locations, water sources) alongside spiritual meaning.
Investigate how First Nations communities navigate tensions between sharing cultural knowledge publicly and protecting sacred knowledge.

modes.reason: Using multiple First Nations examples — different Country, different story traditions — prevents reduction to a single exemplar and models the diversity of First Nations relationships to landscape across Australia.

nodes.label: Landform formation and First Nations knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the formation of a landform and connect this to the special significance First Nations Australians hold for that Country/Place.
criteria: Explains the physical formation of a named landform using geomorphological process language.
Connects the physical landform to the cultural, spiritual or material significance it holds for a First Nations community.

width.minimum: Students explain the physical formation of a landform and identify its significance to a First Nations community.
width.typical: Students explain the formation of a significant landform (geomorphological explanation) and connect this to the special connections First Nations Australians have to that Country/Place, showing how physical and cultural knowledge of the same landscape can co-exist and enrich understanding.
wider: Compare the geomorphological explanation of a landform with a Dreaming story account, examining what each reveals that the other does not.
Investigate how First Nations ecological knowledge of landforms (e.g., water sourcing, fire management) is being integrated into contemporary land management.
Examine how the tourism industry represents both the geomorphological and cultural significance of iconic sites like Uluru.

modes.reason: This node asks students to hold two knowledge systems — physical formation and cultural significance — in relation without collapsing one into the other. The integrative move is the intellectual work of this descriptor.

descriptors.title: Human activity and landscapes
descriptors.description: the interconnections between human activity and geomorphological processes, and ways of managing distinctive landscapes
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain strategies to manage water sustainability (AC9HG7K02) and have examined responses to hydrological hazards (AC9HG7K04). They have not yet examined how human activity directly drives or modifies geomorphological processes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the interconnections between human activity and geomorphological processes, and evaluate ways of managing distinctive landscapes including contributions from First Nations Australian knowledges.

nodes.label: Interconnection as a concept
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what 'interconnection' means in the context of human activity and natural processes, and identify examples where human activity modifies geomorphological processes.
criteria: Explains interconnection as a relationship where human activity modifies natural processes and vice versa.
Identifies at least one human activity and describes how it alters a specific geomorphological process.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat human impact as external and one-directional (humans affect nature, not vice versa) cannot explain the bidirectional interconnections required by this descriptor, and will produce incomplete explanations in Nodes 2–3.

width.minimum: Students explain what interconnection means and identify one example of human activity modifying a geomorphological process.
width.typical: Students explain the concept of interconnection between human activity and the environment, identifying how activities such as tourism, land clearing, mining or urban development alter erosion, sedimentation and landscape stability, with located examples.
wider: Map the chain of interconnections from one human activity through to multiple environmental effects.
Examine how interconnections operate at different scales — local activity producing regional or national-scale landscape change.
Investigate feedback loops where landscape degradation creates conditions for further human modification.

modes.reason: The concept of interconnection as bidirectional and multidirectional needs explicit scaffolding. A cause-chain reasoning structure (activity → process change → landscape outcome → feedback) prevents the linear 'humans damage environment' oversimplification.

nodes.label: Human activity and erosion/sedimentation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the interconnections between specific human activities (tourism, land clearing, mining, river regulation) and the quality of geomorphological environments.
criteria: Explains the interconnection between a named human activity and a specific geomorphological process, describing the resulting environmental effects.
Uses location-specific evidence to support the explanation.

width.minimum: Students explain one human activity and its effects on a geomorphological environment, identifying the process(es) modified.
width.typical: Students explain the interconnections between at least two types of human activity (e.g., overuse of tourist tracks, land clearing for palm oil, mining, river regulation/dams) and the quality of geomorphological environments, identifying the processes affected and the environmental consequences.
wider: Compare the scale of environmental impact of different human activities — which types of activity produce the most significant geomorphological change?
Investigate how the effects of human-modified erosion and sedimentation are distributed unevenly, affecting some communities more than others.
Examine specific case studies: Three Gorges Dam effects on the Yangtze River system, or Murray-Darling management.

modes.reason: Using multiple activity types and contexts builds a repertoire of interconnection examples, preventing students from treating tourism overuse as the only mechanism of human-landscape modification.

nodes.label: Managing distinctive landscapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain ways of managing distinctive landscapes, including the contribution of First Nations Australian knowledges to landscape management.
criteria: Explains at least one strategy for managing a distinctive landscape and identifies the problem it addresses.
Describes the contribution of First Nations Australian knowledges to the management of at least one landscape.

width.minimum: Students identify one management strategy for a distinctive landscape and explain how it addresses a geomorphological or environmental issue.
width.typical: Students explain strategies used to manage distinctive landscapes (e.g., track management in bushland, land rehabilitation after mining, riparian vegetation management) and identify the contribution of First Nations Australian knowledges (e.g., Indigenous Peoples' Knowledge incorporated into management of Kakadu, Uluru, the Great Barrier Reef, the Snowy Mountains).
wider: Evaluate the effectiveness of different management approaches — comparing government-led vs community-led vs co-management models.
Examine how First Nations land management practices (e.g., cultural burning) are being integrated into contemporary environmental management frameworks.
Investigate cases where management strategies have failed and analyse the reasons.

modes.reason: Management strategies require students to connect human activity (Node 2) with geomorphological processes (Node 1 and K01) and the value of landscapes (K03). The integration point synthesises knowledge, cultural significance and management reasoning together.

descriptors.title: Geomorphological hazards
descriptors.description: the causes and impacts of a geomorphological hazard on people, places and environments, and the effects of responses
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain causes and impacts of atmospheric/hydrological hazards and community/government responses (AC9HG7K04). They now extend this cause-impact-response framework to geomorphological hazards (volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, landslides, avalanches).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the causes and impacts of a geomorphological hazard on people, places and environments, and the effects of responses including prevention, mitigation and preparedness strategies.

nodes.label: Causes of geomorphological hazards
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the geomorphological causes of at least one hazard type.
criteria: Names and explains the geomorphological cause(s) of at least one hazard type.
Links the hazard to an underlying geomorphological process (e.g., tectonic movement, slope instability).
nodes.hinge_reason: If students treat hazards as random events rather than outcomes of specific geomorphological processes, they cannot explain why particular places are at risk or why particular responses are effective — the core of Nodes 2 and 3.

width.minimum: Students explain the causes of one geomorphological hazard (volcanic eruption, earthquake, tsunami, landslide or avalanche).
width.typical: Students explain the geomorphological causes of selected hazard types, linking hazard type to the underlying processes — tectonic movement for earthquakes and tsunamis, volcanic pressure for eruptions, slope instability for landslides and avalanches.
wider: Compare the causal mechanisms of two hazard types (e.g., earthquake vs landslide), identifying what they share and what is distinct.
Investigate how the frequency and magnitude of hazard events relate to their geomorphological setting.
Examine how climate change is altering the frequency or distribution of geomorphological hazards (e.g., permafrost thaw and landslides).

modes.reason: Students need to connect geomorphological process knowledge from K01 to hazard causation. A process-to-hazard reasoning chain (plate boundary setting → stress type → hazard event) prevents treating hazard as an isolated phenomenon.

nodes.label: Impacts on people, places and environments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the environmental, economic and social impacts of a geomorphological hazard at the local scale.
criteria: Describes at least two types of impact (environmental, economic or social) of a named hazard on a specific place.
Explains how the characteristics of the place (e.g., location, infrastructure, economic development) influence the scale of impacts.

width.minimum: Students describe at least two impacts (environmental, economic or social) of a named geomorphological hazard on a specific place.
width.typical: Students examine the environmental (landscape change, biodiversity loss), economic (loss of industry, unemployment, infrastructure damage) and social (wellbeing, displacement, community vulnerability) impacts of a selected hazard at the local scale, using a specific case study.
wider: Compare impacts of the same hazard type in places with different levels of economic development and infrastructure.
Examine how vulnerability to hazard impacts is unevenly distributed within a community.
Investigate how human activities have heightened the impact of a hazard — land clearing increasing landslide risk, coastal development increasing tsunami impact.

modes.reason: Examining impacts across multiple dimensions (environmental, economic, social) and different community contexts prevents single-dimension impact analysis and builds the multi-factor reasoning students need for evaluating responses.

nodes.label: Responses and their effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of responses to geomorphological hazards, applying the principles of prevention, mitigation and preparedness.
criteria: Applies at least one principle (prevention, mitigation or preparedness) to explain how the harmful effects of a named hazard can be reduced.
Explains the effects of a management response on people, places or environments.

width.minimum: Students explain one response to a geomorphological hazard and its intended effect.
width.typical: Students explain the principles of prevention, mitigation and preparedness as a framework for hazard response, applying them to a case study hazard and evaluating how the harmful effects of the hazard can be reduced. They reflect on how human activity has heightened vulnerability and how management strategies address this.
wider: Compare the effectiveness of prevention, mitigation and preparedness responses for different hazard types.
Examine how early warning systems have changed hazard outcomes in specific cases.
Investigate how community capacity and governance affect the quality of hazard response.

modes.reason: Evaluating responses requires students to bring together causal understanding (Node 1), impact analysis (Node 2) and knowledge of management principles into a coherent assessment of what works and why.

descriptors.title: Urbanisation and its impacts
descriptors.description: causes of urbanisation and its impacts on places and environments, drawing on a study from a country such as the United States of America, and its implications
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain factors that influence where people live including liveability and environmental quality (AC9HG7K05), and strategies to enhance liveability (AC9HG7K08). They have not yet examined urbanisation as a process with causes and spatial impacts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the causes of urbanisation and its impacts on places and environments, drawing on a country study, and explain the implications of these impacts.

nodes.label: Urban growth vs urbanisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between urban growth and urbanisation, and explain push-pull forces that drive population movement toward urban areas.
criteria: Correctly distinguishes urban growth from urbanisation with examples of each.
Identifies and categorises at least two push factors and two pull factors driving urbanisation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate urban growth with urbanisation, or treat population movement as purely economic, will produce shallow explanations of urbanisation impacts. The conceptual distinction and the push-pull model underpin all subsequent analysis in this standard.

width.minimum: Students define and distinguish urban growth from urbanisation, and identify at least two push-pull factors.
width.typical: Students explain the difference between urban growth (increase in the size of an urban area) and urbanisation (increase in the proportion of population living in urban areas), and explain how push-pull forces contribute to internal and international population movements that drive urbanisation.
wider: Examine how the relative weighting of push vs pull factors differs between internal and international migration contexts.
Compare urbanisation trajectories in a developed country (USA) and a developing country, identifying structural differences.
Investigate how digital connectivity is changing the traditional push-pull model of urbanisation.

modes.reason: The urban growth / urbanisation distinction requires clear definitional work, and the push-pull model needs systematic unpacking so students can apply it analytically rather than listing factors without structure.

nodes.label: Scales of urbanisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between large cities and megacities, and explain urban corridor formation, drawing on examples at the national scale.
criteria: Defines megacity and names at least one example, explaining what distinguishes it from a large city.
Locates urban settlements at the national scale and describes the broad pattern of urban concentration.

width.minimum: Students define megacity and distinguish it from a large city, with at least one located example.
width.typical: Students distinguish between large cities and megacities (population ≥10 million), describe their growth patterns and explain urban corridor formation (e.g., Boston–Washington corridor), drawing on Australian capital city growth and a US case study.
wider: Compare megacity growth patterns in the Global North (e.g., Los Angeles) with those in the Global South (e.g., Lagos, Mumbai).
Investigate what problems emerge specifically at megacity scale that are not present in large cities.
Examine urban corridor formation as a distinct urban form — what drives it and what are its infrastructure implications?

nodes.label: Economic conditions and urban change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how changes in economic conditions affect the characteristics of urban places, including growth, decline and renewal.
criteria: Explains how at least one economic condition has changed the characteristics of a named urban place.
Identifies whether the economic change produced growth, decline or transformation in the urban place.

width.minimum: Students explain one way that economic conditions have changed the characteristics of an urban place.
width.typical: Students explain how economic conditions (tourism boom, resource decline, deindustrialisation, urban renewal investment) affect the characteristics of urban places, using examples of population growth in coastal communities, decline in regional areas, and urban renewal districts.
wider: Compare the urban character of a growth community and a declining community in the same country.
Examine gentrification as an economic-urban process — its causes and the differential effects on existing residents.
Investigate how government policy (infrastructure investment, zoning) shapes economic-driven urban change.

modes.reason: Using multiple economic scenarios — growth, decline, renewal — prevents students from treating economic urbanisation as only a growth story and builds capacity to explain divergent urban trajectories.

nodes.label: Impacts of urbanisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how urbanisation produces positive and negative impacts on the quality of the environment and on economic and social opportunities.
criteria: Explains at least two types of impact of urbanisation (economic, social or environmental) using evidence from a country study.
Distinguishes between positive and negative impacts of urbanisation on the quality of environment.

width.minimum: Students explain at least one positive and one negative impact of urbanisation.
width.typical: Students explain the connections between urbanisation and economic and social opportunities (university access, employment, cultural infrastructure) and the negative environmental impacts (increased carbon emissions, water consumption, habitat loss, impervious surface expansion), drawing on a country study.
wider: Examine how urban environmental impacts are unevenly distributed across different communities within a city.
Compare the environmental footprint of high-density and low-density urban forms.
Investigate how the scale of urbanisation (megacity vs regional city) changes the nature and severity of environmental impacts.

modes.reason: Students need to integrate economic opportunity explanations (Node 3) with environmental impact analysis to produce a balanced, multi-factor account of urbanisation's implications — the full demand of this descriptor.

descriptors.title: Urban distribution
descriptors.description: differences in the distribution of urban settlements and urban concentration in Australia compared with another country such as the United States of America, and their implications
descriptors.knowledge: Students explain the location and distribution of services and facilities and liveability implications (AC9HG7K06). They have applied basic spatial analysis at local/urban scales. They have not yet compared urban distribution patterns at the national scale across countries.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain differences in the distribution and concentration of urban settlements in Australia compared with another country, and interpret the relationship between population density and proximity to urban centres.

nodes.label: Representing urban distribution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate and represent the distribution of urban settlements in Australia and another country (e.g., USA), identifying similarities and differences.
criteria: Locates and labels major urban settlements in Australia and another country on a map.
Describes at least two differences in the distribution pattern of urban settlements between the two countries.
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot read and represent distribution patterns at the national scale, they cannot explain the causes of urban concentration (Node 2) or interpret population density gradients (Node 3). Spatial literacy at national scale is the prerequisite.

width.minimum: Students locate major urban settlements in Australia and one other country on a map, describing a broad distribution pattern.
width.typical: Students represent the location of urban settlements in Australia and the United States of America, identifying similarities and differences in distribution — e.g., coastal concentration in Australia, more even interior distribution in the USA — and use maps to describe the spatial pattern.
