Investigate the economic and social impacts on a place (e.g. Manila, Bangalore) of becoming a global business service hub — connect to K07-K08 trade and production themes

modes.reason: This node integrates transport/information networks (Node 2) and digital connectivity (Node 3) into a real-world outcome: the geographic redistribution of service work enabled by technology. The teaching investment is on connecting the infrastructure concepts to their economic geography consequences.

descriptors.title: Tourism, leisure and place impacts
descriptors.description: the effects on places of people's travel, recreational, cultural or leisure choices, and the strategies for managing the impacts on these places
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how people's activities affect the characteristics of places (Y7-8). They have not examined tourism and leisure as a structured driver of environmental, economic and social change, nor examined management plans that integrate cultural and scientific knowledge to address these impacts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the causes of global tourism growth and its environmental, economic and social impacts on places, predict how future trends may affect places, and examine management strategies that integrate cultural and scientific knowledge to manage these impacts.

nodes.label: Causes and growth of global tourism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss the causes of global tourism growth
criteria: Identifies at least three distinct causes of global tourism growth
Explains how at least two causes are interconnected
Connects causes to the volume and global reach of tourist movement

width.minimum: Identify at least three causes of global tourism growth (e.g. increased disposable income, cheaper air travel, improved communications, globalisation)
width.typical: Explain how economic, technological and social factors have combined to drive global tourism growth; connect causes to the scale of international tourist movement
wider: Analyse how social media and travel platforms have changed the distribution of tourist demand — which places attract more tourists as a result, and why?
Compare the causes of mass tourism growth with the rise of niche tourism (e.g. ecotourism, pilgrimage tourism) — explain what different demand drivers operate
Examine how COVID-19 disrupted global tourism and what this revealed about the economic dependencies tourism creates

modes.reason: Causes of tourism growth are multi-factor. Students who identify only one or two causes (usually 'more money and cheaper flights') miss the social and technological dimensions. Multiple contexts surface the full range.

nodes.label: Environmental, economic and social impacts of tourism
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the environmental, economic and social impacts of tourism on places and predict how future trends may affect these impacts
criteria: Identifies at least one environmental, one economic and one social impact of tourism
Explains the mechanism of each impact rather than just naming it
Makes a prediction about how a future tourism trend will affect a place
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish environmental, economic and social impacts — and explain their mechanisms — cannot evaluate whether management strategies address the right impact type in Node 3. Conflating all impacts as generically 'bad for the environment' prevents strategy evaluation.

width.minimum: Identify at least one environmental, one economic and one social impact of tourism on a named place; explain the mechanism of each impact
width.typical: Explain the environmental (habitat degradation, pollution, carbon footprint), economic (income, employment, dependency) and social (cultural change, displacement, commodification) impacts of tourism on places popular with tourists; predict how space tourism or post-COVID recovery may affect places
wider: Examine pilgrimage tourism (e.g. Mecca, Vatican City, Varanasi) as a distinct case — explain how religious tourism produces different impact profiles compared with mass leisure tourism
Analyse how overtourism affects a specific place — identify which impacts are reversible and which are not
Predict how space tourism could affect near-Earth orbital environments — extend the impact framework to a new frontier

modes.reason: Impact categorisation (environmental/economic/social) is the organising framework for this descriptor and for S05 strategy evaluation. Students who cannot distinguish impact types with mechanism explanations produce undifferentiated impact lists. Scaffolding the three-category structure with mechanism for each ensures students have the analytical framework Node 3 requires.

Pilgrimage and space tourism are both named in the elaborations as prediction contexts. These extend the impact framework beyond the familiar leisure tourism case and give advancing students genuinely different impact profiles to analyse.

nodes.label: Management strategies integrating cultural and scientific knowledge
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how management plans integrate cultural and scientific knowledge and experience to manage the effects of people's travel and leisure choices
criteria: Identifies at least one management strategy for a tourist place
Explains how the strategy addresses a specific impact identified in Node 2
Identifies how the strategy integrates cultural and/or scientific knowledge

width.minimum: Identify at least one management strategy for a tourist place; explain how it addresses a specific impact from Node 2; identify whether it uses cultural, scientific or both types of knowledge
width.typical: Examine how management plans such as that for Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park integrate cultural knowledge and experience, scientific knowledge and past governance experience to manage the effects of tourism; explain how this integration produces better management outcomes than either alone
wider: Compare the management approaches of two tourist places with different cultural and environmental contexts — explain why their management strategies differ
Examine how past governance failures at a tourist site (e.g. Uluru climbing ban history) shaped the current management approach — what was learned?
Evaluate whether a specific management strategy (e.g. visitor quotas, cultural protocols, zoning) addresses the root cause of an impact or its symptoms

modes.reason: This node integrates tourism causes (Node 1) and impact types (Node 2) with management logic — strategies must address specific impacts using appropriate knowledge types. Uluru-Kata Tjuta is the elaboration's named case and is ideal for demonstrating cultural-scientific knowledge integration. Teaching investment should ensure students connect the strategy back to the impact it addresses.

descriptors.title: Trade interconnections at all scales
descriptors.description: the ways that places and people are interconnected with other places through trade in goods and services, at all scales
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand that places are interconnected through movement of people, goods and ideas (Y7-8). They have not examined the mechanisms and scale variations of trade interconnections systematically, nor traced how these change over time at local, national and global scales.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine how and why places are interconnected through trade in goods and services at local, national and global scales, and identify examples of how trade interconnections change over time.

nodes.label: Local trade: businesses selling and buying across places
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify products and services that businesses in their local area sell to or buy from other places
criteria: Identifies at least two products/services local businesses sell to other places
Identifies at least two products/services local businesses buy from other places
Distinguishes between businesses trading locally, nationally and globally

width.minimum: Identify at least two products or services that local businesses sell to other places and at least two they buy from other places
width.typical: Examine a range of local businesses — identify what they sell to and buy from other places; explain what factors determine whether a business sells locally, nationally or globally
wider: Map the trade connections of three local businesses at different scales — compare the geographic extent of their interconnections
Investigate how local farmers' market products connect to local, national and global supply chains simultaneously
Examine how digital platforms (e.g. Etsy, eBay) have changed the scale at which local producers can trade

modes.reason: Starting with local examples makes the abstract concept of trade interconnection concrete. Examining multiple local businesses — not just one — gives students a range of scale experiences to compare.

nodes.label: National, regional and global trade interconnections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine how and why places are interconnected nationally, regionally and globally through trade in goods and services
criteria: Identifies trade interconnections at national, regional and global scales
Explains at least two reasons why places trade at different scales
Gives specific examples from Australia's trade relationships
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding why places trade — comparative advantage, resource endowment, market demand — is prerequisite for explaining how interconnections change over time in Node 3 and why production impacts fall where they do in K08. Students who can only describe that trade happens without explaining why cannot trace the logic of changing interconnections.

width.minimum: Identify how places are interconnected through trade at national, regional and global scales; explain at least two reasons why places trade across scales
width.typical: Explain why places specialise in particular goods or services and how comparative advantage, resource endowment and market demand drive trade interconnections at national, regional and global scales; give examples from Australia and its trading partners
wider: Analyse why Australia exports particular goods (iron ore, coal, agricultural products) but imports others — explain using resource endowment and comparative advantage
Examine regional trade agreements (e.g. ASEAN, Pacific trade agreements) — explain how agreements shape the geography of trade interconnections
Investigate the role of global cities (e.g. Singapore, Hong Kong) as trade hubs — explain how their location and infrastructure concentrate trade interconnections

modes.reason: The 'how and why' framing in the descriptor signals that description alone is insufficient. Students who list trade examples without explaining the mechanisms (why does Australia export iron ore rather than steel?) cannot answer the 'why' component. Scaffolding the comparative advantage and resource endowment logic builds the explanatory depth the descriptor requires.

Covering local, national, regional and global scales prevents students from conflating scale levels. Each scale has different trade logic, and students who understand only one level cannot generalise.

nodes.label: Change in trade interconnections over time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify examples of change in interconnections between places and people through trade over time at local, national and global scales
criteria: Identifies at least one example of changed trade interconnection at local, national and global scales
Explains what drove the change in each case
Uses temporal language correctly (e.g. 'since', 'over time', 'historically')

width.minimum: Identify at least one example of how trade interconnections have changed over time at the local, national and global scale
width.typical: Explain how and why trade interconnections have changed over time at local, national and global scales — consider how changing technologies, geopolitics, environmental conditions or consumer preferences have altered trade relationships; give examples at each scale
wider: Trace how a specific trade relationship has changed over time (e.g. Australia-China trade in resources or food) — explain what drove the change and how it affected both places
Examine how global supply chain restructuring during COVID-19 altered trade interconnections — what changed at local, national and global scales?
Investigate how environmental factors (e.g. climate change, resource depletion) are beginning to alter the geography of trade interconnections

modes.reason: Change over time is best understood through specific cases at each scale. Students who generalise without grounding in a specific case ('trade has globalised') cannot explain why particular interconnections changed. Covering at least one example at each scale level anchors the generalisation.

descriptors.title: Production, consumption and sustainability
descriptors.description: the impacts of the production and consumption of goods on places throughout the world, and strategies to manage sustainability in these places
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe how production and consumption affect places (Y7-8). They have examined trade interconnections in K07. They have not analysed full supply chains end-to-end, evaluated the environmental effects across a supply chain, or examined sustainability management strategies for production and consumption impacts at scale.
descriptors.endpoint: Students examine the environmental, economic and social effects of production and consumption on places worldwide, and examine and evaluate sustainability strategies used to manage these impacts.

nodes.label: Effects of production on people, places and environments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the effects on people, places and environments of mining, farming, forestry and the production of manufactured goods
criteria: Identifies at least two production types and their effects on places
Distinguishes between environmental, economic and social effects
Names specific affected groups or places rather than speaking in generalities

width.minimum: Identify at least two production types (mining, farming, forestry, manufacturing); explain one environmental, economic or social effect of each on the place of production
width.typical: Explain the environmental, economic and social effects of mining, farming, forestry or manufactured goods production on the places where they occur; identify who is affected and how
wider: Compare the effects of two different production types (e.g. mining vs forestry) on the same type of place — explain what differs in their environmental footprints
Examine the cumulative effects of multiple production activities in a single region — explain how effects interact
Investigate how the effects of production in low-income countries differ from those in high-income countries — explain using regulation, labour conditions and environmental standards

modes.reason: The descriptor lists four production types (mining, farming, forestry, manufactured goods). Students who examine only one have an incomplete picture of the range of impact types. Multiple production contexts ensure the node's building block function for the supply chain analysis in Node 2.

nodes.label: Environmental effects across the product supply chain
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the environmental effects of the production and distribution of consumer products on places at each stage of the supply chain
criteria: Traces at least three stages of a product supply chain
Identifies an environmental effect at each stage and the place where it occurs
Explains why environmental effects are distributed across different places in the supply chain
nodes.hinge_reason: The supply chain framing — tracing effects across production, distribution and consumption stages — is the key analytical move for this standard and for evaluating strategies in Nodes 3-4. Students who can only describe effects at one stage cannot explain why particular places are disproportionately affected or evaluate whether a strategy addresses the right stage of the chain.

width.minimum: Trace at least three stages of a product supply chain; identify an environmental effect at each stage
width.typical: Trace a full product supply chain (e.g. e-waste: mining → production → sales → disposal) and explain the environmental effects on the places where raw materials are extracted, products are made and waste is received
wider: Map the geographic spread of supply chain environmental effects — which countries bear extraction costs, which bear waste costs, and why?
Analyse the global oil supply chain from extraction to waste — explain the environmental effects at each stage and in both extraction (West Asia) and consumer (Australia) locations
Investigate the concept of 'externalities' — explain why environmental costs are often borne by places different from those that benefit economically

modes.reason: Supply chain analysis requires students to trace across stages and identify where impacts occur geographically, not just what impacts exist. Students who describe impacts without geographic sequencing cannot explain why e-waste effects fall in developing countries while consumer benefits accrue in developed ones. Scaffolding the stage-by-stage geographic trace builds this analytical structure.

The elaboration provides two supply chain cases: e-waste and global oil. Using both gives students contrasting supply chain structures — discrete manufactured goods versus a continuous resource commodity — and prevents over-generalisation from one case.

nodes.label: Global oil supply chain: extraction to waste
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the environmental, economic and social impacts of the global oil supply chain and identify how impacts could be sustainably managed
criteria: Identifies at least two environmental, economic or social impacts of the oil supply chain
Locates impacts geographically (distinguishing extraction vs consumption locations)
Identifies at least one management strategy and explains what impact it addresses

width.minimum: Identify where oil is extracted (West Asia), processed and consumed (including Australia); explain at least two environmental, economic or social impacts across the chain
width.typical: Evaluate the environmental, economic and social impacts of the global oil supply chain from extraction (West Asia), processing, and sale to waste disposal in Australia and West Asia; identify how these impacts could be sustainably managed
wider: Compare the impacts of oil extraction and the impacts of oil consumption — which places bear environmental costs and which bear economic benefits?
Analyse how oil spills at different stages of the supply chain (extraction, transport, refinery, end use) differ in their environmental footprints and management challenges
Evaluate the extent to which current management strategies for the oil supply chain address extraction impacts versus consumption impacts

modes.reason: The descriptor's 'evaluate' command term signals that students must go beyond description to weigh impacts against criteria. Students who list impacts without evaluating their relative significance or tracing their geographic distribution are not yet at this node's checkpoint. Scaffolding the evaluation framework (what criteria distinguish serious from minor impacts?) builds the analytical depth needed.

nodes.label: Waste management strategies and sustainability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine waste management strategies used by governments and identify implications for sustainability
criteria: Identifies a specific waste management strategy used by an Australian government
Explains what sustainability dimension the strategy addresses
Identifies at least one sustainability implication (environmental, economic or social) of the strategy

width.minimum: Identify at least one waste management strategy used by a local, state or national government in Australia; explain what sustainability dimension (environmental, economic, social) it addresses
width.typical: Examine a waste management strategy used in an Australian city or regional centre (e.g. waste reduction, recycling programs, circular economy approaches); identify the environmental, economic and social sustainability implications; connect to supply chain logic from Node 2
wider: Evaluate a specific waste management strategy against all three sustainability criteria — environmental, economic and social — and identify trade-offs
Compare waste management approaches in different Australian cities or between Australia and an Asian country — explain why approaches differ
Investigate extended producer responsibility policies — explain how shifting waste management costs back to producers changes the supply chain logic

modes.reason: This node integrates production effects (Node 1), supply chain logic (Node 2) and oil supply chain evaluation (Node 3) into a management analysis. Waste management strategies only make sense as responses to specific impacts at specific supply chain stages. Teaching investment should connect the strategy directly back to the impact it addresses in the supply chain.

descriptors.title: Developing geographical inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop a range of questions for a geographical inquiry related to a phenomenon or challenge
descriptors.knowledge: Students can develop geographical questions to guide inquiry and plan investigations at a range of scales (Y7-8). They are building towards refining questions using geographical concepts and multi-scale digital planning tools. At Y9, the move is from generating initial questions to sharpening focus through geographical concepts and scale.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and modify a range of questions that sharpen the focus of a geographical inquiry using concepts and scale, and plan an investigation using digital tools.

nodes.label: Generating initial inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a range of questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or why a challenge has arisen
criteria: Develops at least three questions that investigate different dimensions of a phenomenon or challenge
Questions are open and investigable (not yes/no)
Questions address at least two of: causes, impacts, connections, management
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot generate a range of investigable questions from different angles, they cannot refine and sharpen these into a coherent inquiry plan in Node 2. A single question or description-only questions collapse the inquiry into a report task and block all subsequent phases of work.

width.minimum: Develop at least three questions that investigate a geographical phenomenon or challenge from different angles (e.g. what, why, how, who is affected)
width.typical: Develop a range of questions for a geographical inquiry that investigate causes, impacts, connections and management dimensions of a phenomenon or challenge; ensure questions are open and investigable
wider: Evaluate a set of questions for geographical focus — identify which questions are genuinely geographical and which are too general or not investigable
Develop questions for both a biome and an interconnections topic — compare how the same question types operate differently across different phenomena
Develop questions at different levels of complexity — identify which questions scaffold the investigation and which are the driving research question

modes.reason: Question generation is a procedural capability that improves with practice across multiple phenomena. Students who develop questions for only one topic have a fragile repertoire. Building range across biome and interconnection topics — as the elaborations suggest — ensures the capability transfers.

nodes.label: Sharpening questions using concepts and scale
nodes.checkpoint: Students can modify questions to sharpen the focus of an investigation using geographical concepts or scale of study
criteria: Modifies at least one question to include a geographical concept or scale specification
Explains how the modification sharpens the inquiry focus
Produces a question that is more focused and investigable than the original
nodes.hinge_reason: Questions that lack geographical concept focus or clear scale produce unfocused investigations. If students cannot sharpen a question, their planning in Node 3 will lack the disciplinary focus needed to select appropriate tools and sources. An unsharpened question makes the investigation plan arbitrary.

width.minimum: Modify at least one question from Node 1 to sharpen its focus using a geographical concept (e.g. scale, interconnection, sustainability) or a specified scale of study
width.typical: Develop and modify questions to sharpen inquiry focus by integrating geographical concepts and specifying scale (e.g. national scale, local scale); show how the modified question produces a more focused investigation than the original
wider: Compare how the same question operates differently at local versus global scale — explain what changes and what stays the same
Modify a broad question into a sequence of focused sub-questions that could structure an investigation
Evaluate the difference between concept-sharpened and content-narrowed questions — explain why adding a geographical concept produces a different kind of question than narrowing to a specific example

modes.reason: Question modification is a metacognitive move — students must reflect on what their original question is actually asking, identify what is missing (geographical concept, scale specification), and reconstruct it. Scaffolding the diagnostic step — 'what is this question missing?' — builds the reflective reasoning the modification requires.

nodes.label: Planning a multi-scale investigation using digital tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan an investigation of a geographical phenomenon using digital tools at a range of scales
criteria: Identifies the phenomenon, scale(s) and digital tools in an investigation plan
Connects tool selection to the scale and question type
Explains how the plan addresses the sharpened questions from Node 2

width.minimum: Outline an investigation plan that identifies: the phenomenon, the scale(s) of study, at least two digital tools to be used, and what data or information will be collected
width.typical: Plan a geographical investigation of a biome modification or place connection topic using digital tools; specify the scale(s) of investigation, the tools to be used (e.g. GIS, mapping platforms, digital data sources), and how the investigation will address the sharpened questions from Node 2
wider: Develop an investigation plan that uses different digital tools for different scales — explain why each tool is appropriate for its scale
Anticipate methodological challenges in the plan — what data might be difficult to find, what scale transitions are problematic?
Evaluate two possible investigation plans for the same question — explain which is more feasible and would produce better geographical data

modes.reason: The investigation plan integrates the sharpened questions from Nodes 1-2 with tool selection and scale decisions. Teaching investment should focus on the connection: the digital tools chosen should be appropriate for the scale and the question type, not selected arbitrarily. A plan where tool choice is disconnected from the question has not reached this checkpoint.

descriptors.title: Collecting, representing and comparing geographical data
descriptors.description: collect, represent and compare data and information from primary research methods, including fieldwork and secondary research materials, using geospatial technologies and digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can collect, represent and compare geographical data using a range of methods and tools (Y7-8). At Y9, the moves are: evaluating sources for relevance and reliability, creating multi-variable visual representations, and constructing cartographically-compliant special purpose maps using geospatial technologies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collect primary and secondary data, evaluate sources for relevance and reliability, create multi-variable visual representations using digital tools, and construct cartographically-compliant special purpose maps.

nodes.label: Primary research methods including fieldwork
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify appropriate primary research methods including fieldwork to collect original geographical materials
criteria: Identifies at least two primary research methods and the data each produces
Explains when each method is appropriate for a geographical inquiry
Justifies method selection for a specific inquiry topic

width.minimum: Identify at least two primary research methods (e.g. fieldwork observation, photography, field sketches, surveys, interviews); explain what geographical data each produces and when each is appropriate
width.typical: Identify and use primary research methods including fieldwork to collect original materials relevant to a geographical inquiry (e.g. aerial photograph comparison, field sketches documenting biome alteration, surveys on technology use); justify method selection for the inquiry
wider: Compare what different primary methods reveal about the same phenomenon — explain what fieldwork observation captures that a survey cannot, and vice versa
Evaluate the feasibility of different primary methods for Y9 inquiry topics — which are accessible for students and which require modification?
Design a fieldwork protocol for documenting biome alteration over time using repeated photography and field sketches — specify what would be compared and how

modes.reason: Primary method selection requires students to build a working repertoire of method types and their appropriate uses. Students who only know one method cannot make justified choices. The elaboration's range of examples (aerial photographs, field sketches, surveys) signals the need for repertoire across method types.

nodes.label: Collecting and evaluating secondary research materials
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect relevant secondary research materials using targeted criteria and evaluate them for relevance and reliability
criteria: Collects at least two secondary sources using targeted search criteria
Evaluates each source for relevance to the inquiry question
Evaluates each source for reliability using at least two explicit criteria
nodes.hinge_reason: Source evaluation is prerequisite for all downstream data interpretation and conclusion-drawing in S03-S04. Students who collect sources without evaluating them use unreliable or irrelevant data to draw conclusions, undermining the entire investigation. Phase collapse here (accepting any source as equally valid) cascades through every subsequent analysis phase.

width.minimum: Collect at least two secondary sources using targeted search criteria; evaluate each source for relevance (Does it address the inquiry question?) and reliability (Who is the author? Is it referenced?)
width.typical: Collect secondary research materials online using targeted criteria relevant to an inquiry (e.g. biome modification, digital divide); evaluate each source for relevance and reliability using explicit criteria including author expertise, referencing and currency
wider: Compare the relevance and reliability of a government report, a news article and a peer-reviewed source on the same topic — explain what each is appropriate for
Investigate how the same phenomenon is represented differently in sources from different countries or organisations — explain what this reveals about reliability and perspective
Develop a source evaluation rubric for a Y9 geography inquiry — specify criteria and weighting for relevance and reliability

modes.reason: Relevance and reliability evaluation requires students to interrogate sources against explicit criteria rather than accept them uncritically. Students who cannot articulate the criteria (What makes a source relevant? What makes it reliable?) cannot apply them. Scaffolding the two-question diagnostic — relevance test, then reliability test — builds the evaluative procedure.

Evaluating multiple source types (government, news, peer-reviewed) against the same criteria gives students comparative calibration — they develop a sense of the reliability spectrum rather than treating evaluation as a pass/fail binary.

nodes.label: Creating multi-variable visual representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create multi-variable visual representations of geographical data using digital tools
criteria: Creates a visual representation displaying at least two variables
Identifies what the representation reveals about geographical patterns
Selects an appropriate representation type for the data

width.minimum: Create at least one visual representation of multi-variable geographical data (e.g. a complex graph, table or diagram); identify the variables displayed and what the representation reveals
width.typical: Create multi-variable visual representations using digital tools — e.g. a temperature-precipitation-biome graph, a data comparison table, a cross-section showing soil horizons; explain what the representation reveals about geographical patterns
wider: Create a visual representation that shows a relationship between two variables — explain how the choice of representation type (graph, table, diagram) affects what the relationship reveals

Construct a 3D diagram or flow diagram that shows process interactions (e.g. oil spill impacts on aquatic food production, subsistence farmer daily activity) — explain why a 2D representation would be insufficient
Evaluate a data visualisation made by someone else — identify what it communicates well and what it obscures

modes.reason: Multi-variable representation requires students to match representation type (graph, table, cross-section, flow diagram) to data type and analytical purpose. Building a range of representation types ensures students can select appropriately for different data structures.

nodes.label: Constructing cartographically-compliant special purpose maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the spatial distribution of geographical phenomena by constructing special purpose maps that conform to cartographic conventions
criteria: Constructs a map with at least four cartographic conventions correctly applied
Represents the spatial distribution of a geographical phenomenon accurately
Map title and legend correctly describe what is shown

width.minimum: Construct a special purpose map that includes at least four cartographic conventions (title, scale, legend, north arrow, border); represent the spatial distribution of at least one geographical phenomenon
width.typical: Construct a cartographically-compliant special purpose map showing the relationship between biomes and world food production or another geographical phenomenon; apply all required cartographic conventions; explain what the spatial distribution revealed by the map shows
wider: Construct a map using GIS software — explain how digital tools change the process of map construction and what they enable that manual maps cannot
Compare two maps of the same phenomenon at different scales — explain what each reveals and what each obscures
Evaluate a published map for cartographic quality — identify conventions met and violations, and explain the impact on map readability

modes.reason: Cartographic conventions are a precision task — errors in scale, legend or orientation are directly assessable and produce misleading maps. Students need practice producing complete maps under the full convention checklist, not just awareness that conventions exist. Repeated production with feedback is the appropriate response at this node.

descriptors.title: Evaluating data: generalisations, patterns and relationships
descriptors.description: evaluate geographical data and information to make generalisations and predictions, explain patterns and trends and infer relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify patterns and trends in geographical data (Y7-8). At Y9, the moves are: making and justifying generalisations from data, making predictions from trends, and inferring causal relationships between variables.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate geographical data to make justified generalisations and predictions, explain patterns and trends with reference to geographical factors, and infer relationships between causes and impacts represented in data.

nodes.label: Making generalisations from data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can make generalisations about trends from geographical data
criteria: Makes at least one generalisation that goes beyond restating individual data points
Identifies specific evidence from the data that supports the generalisation
Qualifies the generalisation appropriately (e.g. 'in most cases', 'with some exceptions')
nodes.hinge_reason: Generalisation is the bridge between raw data and pattern explanation. Students who cannot make a justified generalisation produce data summaries rather than analysis, and cannot make predictions or infer relationships in Nodes 2-3. If students cannot move from 'the data shows X' to 'we can therefore say Y generally', the subsequent analytical moves in this standard are inaccessible.

width.minimum: Make at least one generalisation from a dataset or survey; explain what evidence from the data supports the generalisation
width.typical: Make and justify generalisations about geographical trends from data sources such as questionnaires, interviews or quantitative datasets; identify evidence that supports and evidence that qualifies the generalisation
wider: Compare generalisations made from a qualitative source (e.g. interviews about food access) with generalisations from a quantitative source (e.g. food production statistics) on the same topic — explain what each type of data reveals
Identify when a generalisation is over-broad — find a data point that doesn't fit and explain what it reveals about the limitations of the generalisation
Evaluate two generalisations about the same trend (e.g. from different data sources) — explain which is better supported and why

modes.reason: Generalisation requires students to synthesise across data points rather than read off individual values. The reasoning scaffold — 'what pattern appears across multiple data points?' then 'what does that allow us to say generally?' — needs explicit modelling. Students who describe individual data points rather than synthesising them have not crossed this node's threshold.

nodes.label: Explaining patterns and trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain a geographical pattern or trend with reference to geographical factors
criteria: Identifies at least one pattern or trend in geographical data
Explains the pattern with reference to at least one geographical factor
Uses geographical data vocabulary (trend, distribution, pattern) correctly

width.minimum: Identify at least one pattern or trend in data; explain it with reference to at least one geographical factor
width.typical: Explain geographical patterns and trends in data (e.g. locations of food scarcity from hunger index maps, transport network distribution from survey data) using relevant geographical factors; connect the explanation to the inquiry question
wider: Compare pattern explanations across scales — explain why the same trend appears differently at local versus global scale
Use multiple data sources to triangulate a pattern explanation — explain how different sources support or complicate the explanation
Explain a pattern that has an unexpected feature — identify what additional factor or exception the data reveals beyond the main trend

modes.reason: Pattern explanation requires students to move from 'I can see X in the data' to 'X occurs because of geographical factor Y'. Students who describe patterns without explaining them have not reached this node. The causal step — connecting the pattern to a geographical mechanism — needs explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Inferring relationships between causes and impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain relationships between causes and impacts of factors represented in data
criteria: Identifies at least one causal relationship between variables in data
Explains the mechanism connecting the cause to the impact
Distinguishes between a relationship that shows correlation and one that shows causation

width.minimum: Identify at least one causal relationship between two variables shown in data; explain the mechanism connecting cause to impact
width.typical: Explain relationships between causes and impacts of geographical factors represented in data (e.g. GPS and GIS use → precision fertiliser application → yield increase + reduced run-off; GPS mapping → tourist transport choices → tourist distribution); distinguish correlation from causal relationship
wider: Identify a relationship in the data that could be correlation rather than causation — explain what additional evidence would be needed to confirm causation
Trace a multi-step causal chain in the data (e.g. technology adoption → precision farming → reduced environmental impact → sustained productivity) — explain each link
Compare two datasets and explain why the same causal factor produces different impacts in different geographical contexts

modes.reason: Inferring relationships requires students to distinguish correlation from causation and to articulate the mechanism connecting cause to impact. Students who confuse the two or who cannot articulate a mechanism cannot evaluate strategies in S05 or draw conclusions in S04. Scaffolding the mechanism step — 'what process connects X to Y?' — is the critical analytical move.

descriptors.title: Justifying conclusions
descriptors.description: evaluate data and information to justify conclusions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can draw conclusions from geographical data (Y7-8). At Y9, the moves are: drawing conclusions about the impact of a geographical challenge on people, places and environments; and justifying conclusions by reflecting on the perspectives and reasons behind those perspectives.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate data and information to draw and justify conclusions about geographical challenges, reflecting on environmental, economic and social perspectives and the reasons for these perspectives.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions about geographical challenges
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions about the impact of a geographical challenge on people, places and environments
criteria: States at least one conclusion about a geographical challenge's impacts
Identifies the specific data or evidence that supports the conclusion
Distinguishes the conclusion from a restatement of the data
nodes.hinge_reason: Drawing a supported conclusion — clearly distinguishing claim from evidence — is prerequisite for justifying conclusions in Node 2. Students who cannot make this distinction either restate data as conclusions (no analytical move) or make claims unsupported by evidence. Both patterns prevent meaningful perspective-reflection in Node 2.

width.minimum: Draw at least one conclusion about a geographical challenge from data; identify the impact on people, places or environments that the conclusion addresses
width.typical: Draw conclusions about the environmental, economic and social impacts of a geographical challenge (e.g. food species decline and food security, cyberattacks on technological interconnections) from multiple data sources; clearly distinguish the conclusion from the data that supports it
wider: Draw conclusions at different scales — explain how a conclusion about local impacts differs from a conclusion about national or global impacts of the same challenge
Compare conclusions drawn from two different data sources about the same challenge — explain where they converge and diverge
Identify the limits of what can be concluded from available data — explain what the data cannot support

modes.reason: The conclusion-drawing move requires students to synthesise multiple data sources into a claim that goes beyond the data while being supported by it. This is different from summarising data. Scaffolding the distinction between 'the data shows' and 'we can therefore conclude' — and asking students to show the inferential step — builds the analytical move.

nodes.label: Justifying conclusions through perspective reflection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can justify conclusions by reflecting on perspectives identified and the reasons for these perspectives
criteria: Identifies at least two perspectives on a geographical challenge
Explains the reasons behind each perspective (not just states that they exist)
Shows how perspective reflection qualifies or strengthens the conclusion from Node 1

width.minimum: Identify at least two different perspectives on a geographical challenge; explain the reasons for each perspective; show how perspective-awareness strengthens or qualifies a conclusion
width.typical: Justify conclusions about a geographical challenge by identifying environmental, economic and social perspectives and explaining the reasons for each; show how consideration of multiple perspectives (e.g. on disappearing arable land or ecotourism) produces a more robust or qualified conclusion
wider: Identify a case where two perspectives on the same challenge produce contradictory conclusions — explain how to resolve or acknowledge the contradiction
Reflect on how your own perspective as a student in Australia may shape what you find to be a persuasive conclusion — identify what perspectives are harder to access from this position
Evaluate a published conclusion — identify whose perspectives are represented and whose are absent, and explain how this affects the conclusion's validity

modes.reason: This node integrates the conclusion from Node 1 with the perspective-reflection move required by this descriptor. The work is not about listing perspectives but about showing how perspective-awareness changes or qualifies the conclusion drawn from data. Teaching investment should focus on the connection between perspective identification and conclusion revision.

descriptors.title: Developing and evaluating strategies
descriptors.description: develop and evaluate strategies using environmental, economic or social criteria; recommend a strategy and explain the predicted impacts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can propose actions and explain reasons for them (Y7-8). At Y9, the moves are: evaluating strategies against environmental, economic and social criteria; making a recommendation from alternatives; explaining predicted outcomes; and reflecting on personal values.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and evaluate strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria, recommend a strategy, explain its predicted impacts, and reflect on how personal values influence predicted outcomes.

nodes.label: Proposing individual and collective strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose individual and collective strategies for addressing a geographical challenge and support each with reasons
criteria: Proposes at least one individual and one collective strategy
Supports each strategy with at least one reason explaining how it addresses the challenge
Distinguishes between what individual and collective action can achieve

width.minimum: Propose at least one individual and one collective strategy for a geographical challenge; explain why each would address the challenge
width.typical: Propose a range of individual actions (e.g. reducing food wastage, reducing environmental impact in tourist places) and collective actions (e.g. organisational food security initiatives, labour practice improvements) for addressing a geographical challenge; support each with reasoned justification
wider: Compare the scale of impact of individual versus collective strategies for the same challenge — explain what individual action cannot achieve alone
Identify who would need to act for each strategy to be effective — explain how collective action problems arise when individual and collective incentives diverge
Develop a strategy that combines individual and collective action — explain how the two levels reinforce each other

modes.reason: Students need a working repertoire of strategy types at different scales (individual, community, organisational, government) to evaluate and select from in Nodes 2-3. Students who can only propose one type of strategy have an underdeveloped evaluative toolkit.

nodes.label: Evaluating strategy effectiveness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of a strategy in relation to environmental, economic and social criteria
criteria: Applies at least two of the three criteria (environmental, economic, social) to evaluate a strategy
Provides evidence-based judgement for each criterion applied
Identifies at least one trade-off or limitation in the strategy
nodes.hinge_reason: Evaluation against explicit criteria is the prerequisite for recommendation in Node 3 — without criterion-based evaluation, the recommendation has no rational basis. Students who say a strategy 'is good' without applying criteria cannot explain predicted impacts or compare alternatives, collapsing the recommendation into preference rather than justified judgement.

width.minimum: Apply at least two of the three criteria (environmental, economic, social) to evaluate one strategy; explain what the evaluation reveals about the strategy's effectiveness
width.typical: Evaluate the effectiveness of a strategy against environmental, economic and social criteria (e.g. assessing SDG Goal 2 food security progress, evaluating a national park management plan's implementation); identify which criteria the strategy meets, partially meets or does not address
wider: Identify trade-offs in a strategy evaluation — a strategy may perform well against one criterion while performing poorly against another
Apply the same three criteria to evaluate two competing strategies for the same challenge — compare the evaluation outcomes
Evaluate a strategy's effectiveness at different scales — does it perform differently at local, national or global scale?

modes.reason: Criterion-based evaluation is a structured reasoning task. Students commonly apply criteria in name only ('this is good environmentally because it's sustainable') without substantive evidence. Scaffolding the full evaluation cycle — criterion stated, evidence identified, judgement made — builds the evaluative rigour that recommendation requires.

Applying the same criteria to different strategies, or the same strategy across scales, prevents students from assuming that good performance on one criterion generalises. Trade-off identification is only possible when students can see strategies performing differently across criteria.

nodes.label: Recommending a strategy and predicting impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recommend a strategy and explain its predicted outcomes and impacts
criteria: States a clear strategy recommendation
Justifies the recommendation with reference to the evaluation criteria from Node 2
Explains at least two predicted outcomes or impacts of the recommended strategy

width.minimum: Recommend one strategy with a reasoned justification; explain at least two predicted outcomes or impacts of implementing the strategy
width.typical: Recommend a strategy for a geographical challenge (e.g. improving food quality and cultural acceptability, reducing global hazardous waste movement) and explain its predicted outcomes and impacts across environmental, economic and social dimensions; connect the recommendation to the evaluation from Node 2
wider: Address likely counterarguments to the recommended strategy — explain why the recommendation stands despite the limitations identified in evaluation
Predict second-order impacts — what might change as a result of the strategy's first-order effects?
Compare two possible recommendations and explain why one is preferable given the evaluation criteria from Node 2

modes.reason: Recommendation integrates the strategy repertoire from Node 1 and the criterion-based evaluation from Node 2 into a justified choice. The recommendation must be explicitly grounded in the evaluation — a recommendation that ignores the evaluation has not integrated the prior nodes.

nodes.label: Reflecting on personal values and predicted outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on the influence of personal values and attitudes on predicted outcomes and impacts
criteria: Identifies at least one personal value that influences a predicted outcome
Explains how a different value would produce a different prediction
Connects the values reflection back to the strategy recommendation from Node 3

width.minimum: Identify at least one personal value or attitude that influences a predicted outcome; explain how a different value or attitude might produce a different prediction
width.typical: Reflect on how personal values (e.g. preference for locally produced food, commitment to recycling) influence predicted outcomes and impacts; explain how different values lead to different predictions about the same strategy
wider: Examine how cultural background or geographic position might shape what values are held and what outcomes are predicted — connect to S04 perspective reflection
Identify where a value judgement is embedded in an apparently objective predicted impact — explain what would change if the value were different
Reflect on how the values implicit in a government or organisational strategy differ from personal values — explain what this reveals about whose interests are prioritised

modes.reason: Values-reflection requires metacognitive awareness — students must step back from their prediction and ask what value it assumes. Students who cannot identify the embedded value cannot reflect on how different values produce different predictions. Scaffolding the identification step — 'what do I have to believe is important for this prediction to follow?' — builds the reflective capacity.

descriptors.title: Creating geographical descriptions and explanations
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and responses, using geographical knowledge and geographical tools as appropriate, and concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can create descriptions and explanations using geographical knowledge and tools (Y7-8). At Y9, the moves are: applying geographical concepts and terms in structured responses; using data representations (maps, graphs, images) and research findings as evidence; and calibrating tone appropriately to audience.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and responses using geographical concepts and terms, incorporating and acknowledging research findings, using geographical tools as evidence, and applying tone appropriate to audience.

nodes.label: Applying geographical concepts and terms in responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop responses using geographical concepts and terms accurately
criteria: Uses at least three geographical concepts correctly in a response
Applies concepts as analytical frameworks, not just as vocabulary
Uses geographical terminology accurately throughout
nodes.hinge_reason: Geographical concepts are the organising framework that distinguishes geographical responses from general descriptions. Students who cannot use concepts correctly as analytical tools rather than as vocabulary produce responses that meet the description command but not the geographical knowledge requirement. This blocks the explanation and research-incorporation moves in Nodes 2-3.

width.minimum: Use at least three geographical concepts (e.g. scale, place, interconnection, sustainability, environment) and five geographical terms correctly in a response
width.typical: Develop a response using geographical concepts (scale, place, environment, interconnection, change, sustainability) and correct geographical terminology; apply concepts as organising frameworks rather than as vocabulary inserts
wider: Evaluate a peer response for conceptual accuracy — identify where concepts are used correctly as frameworks and where they are name-dropped without conceptual function
Use two related concepts together in one explanation (e.g. scale and interconnection; environment and sustainability) — explain how the concepts interact rather than using each independently
Apply the same concept across two different content areas (e.g. use 'interconnection' to analyse both biome modification and trade) — explain what the concept reveals in each case

modes.reason: Building a working vocabulary of geographical concepts and terms requires repeated use across different content areas, not memorisation in one context. Applying concepts across biome, interconnection and trade content builds the transferable conceptual toolkit the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Using representations and research findings as evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create descriptions using representations of data and research findings as evidence
criteria: Incorporates at least one data representation into a response as supporting evidence
References and acknowledges at least one research finding
The representation is connected to the claim it supports, not inserted separately

width.minimum: Create a response that incorporates at least one data representation (map, graph, diagram, table, photograph) and references at least one research finding; acknowledge the source
width.typical: Create a description using maps, photographs, diagrams, graphs, tables or satellite images as evidence for geographical claims; incorporate and acknowledge research findings from secondary sources
wider: Evaluate how well a data representation functions as evidence for a specific claim — explain what the representation shows and what it cannot prove
Compare two representations of the same phenomenon (e.g. a map and a graph of biome distribution) — explain what each adds as evidence
Construct a response where the structure is driven by the research findings rather than by a predetermined argument — explain how findings shape the response

modes.reason: The elaboration lists multiple representation types (maps, photographs, diagrams, graphs, tables, satellite images). Students who use only one type have a limited evidence repertoire. Exposure to multiple representation types in multiple content contexts builds the flexibility the descriptor requires.

nodes.label: Tone, audience and structured argument
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create explanations that apply tone appropriate to the audience and present a reasoned argument
criteria: Applies a consistent tone appropriate to an identified audience throughout
Structures the response with a clear position, reasoning and conclusion
Integrates geographical concepts and research-based evidence into the argument

width.minimum: Create a response with a consistent tone appropriate to an identified audience; structure the response with a clear position, supporting reasoning and a conclusion
width.typical: Create an explanation with audience-appropriate tone (e.g. authoritative tone for a management proposal, accessible tone for a public information piece) and reasoned argument — for example, a case for reducing food wastage or a management plan for a tourist hotspot
wider: Produce two versions of the same response for different audiences — explain how the tone, vocabulary and structure of each differs
Evaluate a published geographical response for tone-audience fit — identify where tone choices strengthen or undermine the argument
Draft a response where the tone must balance authority (for a professional audience) with accessibility (for a general public audience) — explain the trade-offs

modes.reason: This node integrates geographical concepts (Node 1), research-grounded evidence (Node 2), and structured argument with audience awareness. The response is the whole product — nodes 1 and 2 supply the content and evidence, this node supplies the communicative form. Teaching investment should ensure the three elements work together, not appear as separate layers in the response.

descriptors.title: Human-induced changes and sustainability
descriptors.description: the human-induced changes that challenge the sustainability of places and environments
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the effects on environments of human alteration of biomes (AC9HG9K02), challenges to sustainable food production and management strategies (AC9HG9K04), and the impacts of production and consumption on places with sustainability strategies (AC9HG9K08). They can describe human-environment interconnections and identify sustainability challenges at a general level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the nature of human-induced environmental changes that challenge the sustainability of places and environments, and identify tensions between conflicting perspectives of individuals, communities and governments on sustainable practices.

nodes.label: Nature and types of human-induced environmental change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what human-induced environmental change is and describe the major types — including water and atmospheric pollution, loss of biodiversity, and degradation of land and aquatic environments.
criteria: Students identify at least two distinct types of human-induced environmental change and describe what makes each type a challenge to sustainability
Students explain the difference between a human-induced change and a natural environmental variation
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot distinguish between types of human-induced change and their mechanisms, they cannot accurately explain which environmental functions (resource, service, spiritual) are threatened in AC9HG10K04, and their sustainability discussions (K01, K02) will conflate causes with effects.

width.minimum: Identify and describe at least two types of human-induced environmental change using one studied context.
width.typical: Explain the nature of multiple types of human-induced environmental change (pollution, biodiversity loss, land/aquatic degradation) using a range of local, national and global examples.
wider: Investigate a specific large-scale environmental degradation case (e.g. Great Barrier Reef bleaching, Amazon deforestation) to trace the interactions between multiple change types
Research historical human-induced changes and compare rates and types of change over time to identify acceleration trends
Examine the ecological concept of tipping points and what it means for the reversibility of human-induced change

modes.reason: Students frequently conflate human-induced change with natural variability. Invest in an explicit framework distinguishing change types by mechanism (extraction, pollution, alteration) and affected system before moving to sustainability implications.
Exposure to varied change types across aquatic, atmospheric and terrestrial systems prevents students from treating one type (e.g. pollution) as representative of all human-induced change.

nodes.label: Sustainability as a concept — environmental functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the concept of sustainability in relation to environmental functions (resource, service, spiritual) and articulate why human-induced changes threaten those functions.
criteria: Students explain what sustainability means in relation to at least one environmental function, using correct terminology
Students connect a specific human-induced change to a threat to a named environmental function
nodes.hinge_reason: The concept of sustainability as applied to environmental functions is foundational for K02 (world views) and K04 (management strategies). Students without a working definition of sustainability cannot evaluate whether management strategies are adequate or assess trade-offs between world views.

width.minimum: Define sustainability in the context of at least one environmental function and explain how a studied human-induced change threatens it.
width.typical: Explain sustainability across resource, service and spiritual environmental functions; connect specific types of human-induced change to threats to each function category.
wider: Compare contested definitions of sustainability (weak vs strong sustainability, anthropocentric vs ecocentric) and evaluate their implications for management decisions
Investigate how First Nations Australians' concepts of Country/Place embed a notion of sustainability that integrates resource, service and spiritual functions
Examine international frameworks (e.g. UN Sustainable Development Goals, planetary boundaries) as formal attempts to operationalise sustainability

modes.reason: Sustainability is used loosely in everyday contexts. Students need explicit scaffolding that ties the concept to environmental function categories — resource provision, ecological services, cultural/spiritual value — before applying it critically.
Exposing students to sustainability across different function types (not just resource) broadens their capacity to apply the concept in K02 world views discussions and K04 case studies.

nodes.label: Conflicting perspectives on sustainable practices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the tensions between conflicting perspectives of individuals, communities, governments and businesses regarding the use of sustainable practices.
criteria: Students identify at least two stakeholder groups with differing perspectives on a sustainability practice and explain the basis of the disagreement
Students explain why resolving sustainability tensions is complex, with reference to at least one specific conflict example

width.minimum: Describe at least two different stakeholder perspectives on one sustainability issue, identifying the source of tension between them.
width.typical: Identify and explain tensions between the perspectives of individuals, communities, businesses and governments on sustainable practices across at least two contexts; explain why perspectives differ (values, priorities, economic interests, legal frameworks).
wider: Analyse a real governance dispute (e.g. state vs federal conflict over water allocation, community vs developer conflict over land use) to trace how institutional power shapes which perspectives prevail
Compare how different legal systems resolve sustainability conflicts — for example, rights-based approaches vs market-based mechanisms vs regulatory approaches
Investigate cases where community-led sustainability initiatives succeeded or failed in shifting government policy, identifying leverage points

modes.reason: Exposure to multiple sustainability conflicts across different stakeholder configurations (individual/community, community/government, government/business) prevents students from assuming one conflict type is representative of all.

descriptors.title: Environmental world views
descriptors.description: the environmental world views of people and their implications for environmental management
descriptors.knowledge: Students can explain conflicting stakeholder perspectives on sustainability (AC9HG10K01) and understand human-induced environmental change types. They have engaged with interconnections between human activity and environments (AC9HG9K02, AC9HG9K08) and understand that different people have different relationships to place.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss the influence of people's environmental world views (human-centred and earth-centred) regarding environmental management and explain how world views shape choices of management methods.

nodes.label: Human-centred and earth-centred world views
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between human-centred (anthropocentric) and earth-centred (ecocentric) environmental world views and explain what each implies about the relationship between humans and the environment.
criteria: Students define both human-centred and earth-centred world views using correct terminology
Students identify at least one management approach associated with each world view and explain the connection
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish these world views cannot explain why different stakeholders choose different management methods in K04, nor can they discuss whether environmental change is 'necessarily a problem' — a question whose answer depends entirely on one's world view.

width.minimum: Define both world view types and describe one management approach associated with each.
width.typical: Explain the philosophical basis and practical implications of human-centred and earth-centred world views; link each to concrete management approaches such as resource extraction vs conservation, economic development vs protected areas.
wider: Investigate intermediate world views such as stewardship ethics or biocentric ethics that complicate the binary, evaluating how each positions human responsibility
Examine how legal frameworks in different countries encode world views — for example, rights of nature legislation in Ecuador or New Zealand vs resource-rights regimes
Compare how Indigenous world views differ from both human-centred and earth-centred Western frameworks, particularly regarding relational ontologies

modes.reason: The human-centred/earth-centred distinction is conceptually slippery — students often assume everyone shares their own world view. Use explicit comparison frameworks (value source, moral standing of nature, justification for management) to make the distinction concrete before applying it.

nodes.label: World views and causes of environmental issues
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare differences in people's views about the causes of an environmental issue, explaining how world view shapes the identification of causes.
criteria: Students explain how two stakeholders with different world views identify different causes for the same environmental issue
Students use the terms 'human-centred' and 'earth-centred' correctly when analysing cause attribution

width.minimum: Compare two different perspectives on the causes of one environmental issue, tracing how each perspective reflects a different world view.
width.typical: For at least one environmental issue of personal, national and global importance, compare perspectives from human-centred and earth-centred stakeholders; explain how each world view leads to a different identification of causes and responsible parties.
wider: Analyse media coverage of a single environmental issue from outlets reflecting different world views, identifying how framing choices (headline, quoted sources, language) encode particular world views
Investigate how scientific consensus on an environmental issue (e.g. climate attribution) intersects with or conflicts with different world view frameworks
Compare how communities in different countries assign cause and responsibility for the same global environmental issue based on historical, economic and cultural factors

modes.reason: Analysing cause attribution across multiple issues and stakeholder groups prevents students from applying the world view framework mechanically to a single case.

nodes.label: World views and management choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss whether environmental change is necessarily a problem and explain how people's world views shape their choices of management methods.
criteria: Students explain how a specific world view leads to a specific management approach (or non-intervention) using correct terminology
Students discuss, with evidence, why people holding different world views may disagree on whether an environmental change requires management

width.minimum: Explain how at least one world view leads to a specific management choice, and discuss whether all stakeholders view the change as a problem requiring management.
width.typical: Discuss multiple management methods (environmental, economic, regulatory, community-based) in terms of the world views they reflect; explain why not all stakeholders agree that a given change is a problem requiring intervention.
wider: Evaluate a specific environmental management decision at national or international scale — identifying which world views are reflected in the chosen strategy and which are marginalised
Investigate cases where communities chose not to manage or reverse an environmental change, examining the world view basis for that choice
Compare how different cultural or religious traditions within a single country produce divergent views on whether and how to manage a specific environmental change

modes.reason: This node integrates world view identification, cause attribution and management choice into a coherent explanatory chain. Students need to coordinate all three moves — a teacher signal to make the connections explicit rather than treating each move as separate.

descriptors.title: First Nations custodial responsibility and environmental management
descriptors.description: First Nations Australians' approaches to custodial responsibility and environmental management in different regions of Australia
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand the spiritual and aesthetic value of landscapes for First Nations Australians (AC9HG8K03) and have engaged with environmental world views including distinctions between anthropocentric and other frameworks (AC9HG10K02). They have developed awareness of Country/Place as a concept in earlier years.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain First Nations Australians' approaches to custodial responsibility and environmental management in different regions of Australia, including the influence of cultural values, the role of First Nations Park Rangers, and First Nations models of sustainability.

nodes.label: Custodial responsibility and cultural values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what custodial responsibility means for First Nations Australians and identify the influence of cultural values — including continuity of cultural practices, management of Country/Place, and land tenure — on how environments are managed.
criteria: Students explain custodial responsibility using the concept of obligations to Country/Place, distinguishing it from general environmental care
Students identify at least two cultural values that influence how a specific First Nations community manages their environment
nodes.hinge_reason: If students understand custodial responsibility only as a synonym for 'caring for country' without grasping the cultural and obligations-based nature of the concept, they will misrepresent First Nations approaches in K04 management comparisons and reproduce shallow or tokenistic analysis.

width.minimum: Define custodial responsibility and explain its basis in cultural values for at least one Country/Place with reference to a specific community or region.
width.typical: Explain how cultural values (continuity of practices, obligations to Country/Place, land tenure systems) shape custodial responsibility across different regions; identify how custodial responsibility differs from mainstream environmental management approaches.
wider: Investigate how land tenure arrangements (native title, co-management agreements, IPA — Indigenous Protected Areas) interact with custodial responsibility in different Australian regions
Research how custodial knowledge is transmitted across generations and what happens to environmental management when this transmission is disrupted
Compare custodial responsibility frameworks in different First Nations regions of Australia (e.g. arid, tropical, coastal) to identify shared principles and context-specific practices

modes.reason: Custodial responsibility is a concept grounded in relational ontology that differs fundamentally from both anthropocentric stewardship and ecocentric conservation. Students need a framework that distinguishes obligations-based management (custodial responsibility) from interest-based management (mainstream approaches) before applying it to regional cases.

Custodial responsibility is expressed differently across different regions, Country/Places and communities. Exposure to multiple regional examples prevents reductive generalisation about 'what Aboriginal people do'.

nodes.label: First Nations Park Rangers and cultural knowledge in practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the role of First Nations Australian Park Rangers and how their cultural knowledge and practices contribute to the management of Country/Place and environments.
criteria: Students describe what First Nations Park Rangers do, identifying at least one cultural practice that is central to their management approach
Students explain how cultural knowledge contributes to environmental outcomes, not merely as background but as an active management input

width.minimum: Describe the role of First Nations Rangers in managing a specific Country/Place, explaining how at least one cultural knowledge practice informs their management approach.
width.typical: Explain the role of First Nations Rangers across multiple contexts; describe how cultural knowledge practices (fire management, species monitoring, water management, seasonal practices) are integrated with contemporary conservation techniques.
wider: Investigate the Savanna Burning Carbon Farming Initiative as a case where traditional fire management practices are formally integrated with environmental markets
Research a specific Ranger group — such as the Firesticks Alliance or the Rangers of the Kakadu National Park — and evaluate how their dual knowledge system functions in practice
Examine documented cases where First Nations knowledge has changed mainstream scientific understanding of an Australian ecosystem

modes.reason: The Ranger programme varies significantly across Australia — arid, tropical, coastal, riverine contexts each involve different practices. Students benefit from two or more case examples to avoid treating one Ranger group as representative.

nodes.label: First Nations models of sustainability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain First Nations Australians' models of sustainability, including specific practices such as fire management, land care, species protection and community capacity building, and explain how these contribute to broader conservation.
criteria: Students explain at least two First Nations sustainability practices in concrete terms, not just as labels
Students explain how First Nations models of sustainability contribute to conservation outcomes beyond the immediate community

width.minimum: Explain at least two specific sustainability practices from First Nations models and describe how each contributes to environmental outcomes.
width.typical: Explain First Nations models of sustainability including obligations to Country/Place, fire management, removal of invasive species, protection of threatened species and capacity building; connect each to broader conservation outcomes and explain how these contribute to national and international sustainability frameworks.
wider: Evaluate how formal recognition of First Nations sustainability models (e.g. in national park co-management agreements, state environmental legislation) has changed management outcomes in specific regions
Compare First Nations sustainability models in Australia with Indigenous environmental management approaches in other countries (e.g. Māori kaitiakitanga in Aotearoa New Zealand)
