Investigate the evidence base for specific First Nations practices — e.g. mosaic burning effects on biodiversity — and evaluate how Western science is engaging with and validating this knowledge

modes.reason: This node integrates custodial responsibility, Ranger practice and sustainability frameworks into a coherent account of First Nations environmental management as a knowledge system that contributes to conservation. The teaching signal is to make the integration explicit — not to treat practices as isolated examples.

descriptors.title: Environmental change: causes, effects and management strategies
descriptors.description: causes and effects of a change in an identified environment at a local, national or global scale, and strategies to manage sustainability
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand human-induced environmental changes and sustainability (AC9HG10K01), environmental world views (AC9HG10K02), and First Nations custodial approaches (AC9HG10K03). They have engaged with sustainability strategies for biomes (AC9HG9K04) and urban places (AC9HG8K09), providing a prior framework for evaluating management strategies.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the causes and effects of a change in an identified environment and propose and compare strategies to manage sustainability, drawing on environmental, economic and social criteria and considering trade-offs and the perspectives of different stakeholders.

nodes.label: Identifying context and describing causes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a specific environmental change context, describe its causes, and explain the impacts on the sustainability of the environment's functions.
criteria: Students identify a specific environmental change context and describe at least two causes with their mechanisms
Students explain the impact of the change on at least one environmental function using correct geographical terminology
nodes.hinge_reason: Without an accurate and specific account of causes and affected environmental functions in their studied context, students cannot evaluate whether proposed strategies actually address the right problem — the entire evaluation chain (nodes 2–3) depends on the cause-effect analysis being correct.

width.minimum: Describe the causes of environmental change in one identified context and explain impacts on at least one environmental function (resource, service or spiritual).
width.typical: Describe the causes of environmental change in a studied context across local, national or global scale as appropriate; explain impacts on multiple environmental functions including resource provision, ecological services, and cultural or spiritual value.
wider: Investigate a complex multi-causal environmental change case (e.g. Murray-Darling Basin water stress, Great Barrier Reef bleaching) tracing the interaction of natural and human factors at different scales

Analyse how scale of study changes the apparent causes and effects — for example, localised agricultural runoff vs national water policy vs global climate change as causes of the same environmental change
Examine an environmental change case in a developing country context and compare the causes and affected environmental functions with an equivalent change in Australia

modes.reason: Students often list causes without tracing causal mechanisms or explaining which environmental functions are affected and how. Scaffolding the cause → mechanism → function impact chain explicitly prevents superficial cause listing.

nodes.label: World views and strategy development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise how people's world views influence how management strategies are developed and implemented, and identify who is involved in strategy decision-making.
criteria: Students identify at least two stakeholders involved in developing a management strategy and explain how their different world views influence the strategy they support
Students identify at least one trade-off that decision-makers face and explain how different stakeholders evaluate that trade-off differently

width.minimum: Identify at least two stakeholder groups involved in developing a management strategy for the studied context and explain how their world views influence the strategies they support.
width.typical: Explain how Traditional Owners, communities, developers, governments and NGOs use environmental, economic and social criteria when making decisions; show how world view (human-centred vs earth-centred) shapes which criteria are prioritised and what trade-offs are accepted.
wider: Analyse a documented governance process (e.g. an environmental impact assessment, a resource management tribunal) to trace how different stakeholder world views are weighted in formal decision-making
Investigate a case where First Nations Traditional Owners' world views and management priorities diverged from government or NGO approaches, examining how the tension was or was not resolved

Compare decision-making criteria for environmental management in two different national governance systems (e.g. Australia vs India) examining how institutional structures encode different world views

modes.reason: Students need exposure to multiple stakeholder configurations — not just community vs government — to build a flexible understanding of how world views shape strategy development in different governance contexts.

nodes.label: Proposing and comparing management strategies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose strategies to manage the effects of environmental change and compare strategies in terms of environmental, economic and social criteria, including cross-national comparison where appropriate.
criteria: Students propose at least one management strategy and evaluate it against at least two criteria (environmental, economic, social)
Students explain a trade-off involved in their proposed strategy and acknowledge why different stakeholders may evaluate the trade-off differently

width.minimum: Propose at least one management strategy for the studied context and evaluate it against at least one criterion (environmental, economic or social).
width.typical: Propose and evaluate multiple strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria; compare strategies in Australia with strategies in another country for human-induced environmental change, using stated criteria and acknowledging trade-offs.
wider: Compare three strategy types — environmental (marine reserves, national parks), spatial (corridors, urban planning) and holistic (addressing past and present causes) — evaluating the criteria each type is best suited to address
Evaluate the effectiveness of a real implemented strategy over time using before/after evidence, identifying what was achieved and what remained unresolved
Develop and justify a prioritised strategy recommendation that explicitly addresses the different criteria and trade-offs involved, including acknowledgment of First Nations approaches where relevant

modes.reason: This node integrates cause-effect analysis, world view awareness and multi-criteria evaluation into a strategy proposal. The teacher signal is to make the connections explicit: a good strategy proposal flows directly from the cause-effect analysis (Node 1) and accounts for the stakeholder world views identified in Node 2.

Strategy comparison requires applying consistent criteria across cases — students often compare incomparable things (effectiveness vs cost vs acceptability) without acknowledging they are using different criteria. Scaffold the criteria framework before asking for comparison.

descriptors.title: Measuring human wellbeing and development
descriptors.description: the methods used to measure spatial variations in human wellbeing and development, and how these can be applied to determine differences between places at the global scale
descriptors.knowledge: Students have examined causes of urbanisation and its impacts on places (AC9HG8K06), reasons for and effects of migration (AC9HG8K08), and interconnections between places through trade and consumption (AC9HG9K07-K08). They understand that places differ in economic and social conditions but have not yet used formal measurement indices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify the UN Sustainable Development Goals relevant to human wellbeing, compare different measurements of human wellbeing including GDP, HDI and PQLI, and interpret and explain trends in human wellbeing in a developed and a developing country over time.

nodes.label: Concepts of human wellbeing and development
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what human wellbeing and development mean as geographical concepts, identifying the UN Sustainable Development Goals relevant to human wellbeing.
criteria: Students define human wellbeing as encompassing more than economic conditions, identifying at least two non-economic dimensions
Students identify at least three SDGs relevant to human wellbeing and explain what each targets
nodes.hinge_reason: If students understand human wellbeing only as economic prosperity, they will misinterpret multi-dimensional indices in Node 2 and cannot explain why different measures produce different country rankings.

width.minimum: Define human wellbeing and development as distinct concepts and identify at least three SDGs relevant to wellbeing.
width.typical: Explain human wellbeing as a multi-dimensional concept encompassing economic, social, environmental and political dimensions; identify the SDGs most relevant to wellbeing (health, education, poverty, inequality, clean water) and explain what each targets.
wider: Investigate the Capability Approach (Amartya Sen, Martha Nussbaum) as an alternative conceptual framework for human wellbeing and evaluate how it differs from GDP-based development thinking
Examine critiques of 'development' as a concept — including post-development and degrowth perspectives — and assess their implications for how wellbeing is measured
Explore how the SDG framework was developed and which countries or stakeholders had the greatest influence on the goals selected, examining whose definition of wellbeing it reflects

modes.reason: Students often reduce wellbeing to wealth. Explicit conceptual work establishing wellbeing as multi-dimensional (economic, social, environmental, political) before introducing measurement indices prevents persistent conflation of wealth with wellbeing.

nodes.label: Measurement methods: GDP, HDI, PQLI and their trade-offs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare different measurements of human wellbeing — including GDP, HDI and PQLI — explaining what each measures, how they differ, and what rankings of selected countries reveal.
criteria: Students describe what GDP, HDI and at least one other index measure, identifying the dimensions each captures
Students compare rankings of at least two countries across two different indices and explain the reason for a ranking difference
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot explain why different measures produce different rankings and what that difference means, they cannot interpret spatial variation data in K06 or explain intra-national inequality in K07.

width.minimum: Describe what GDP and at least one composite index (HDI or PQLI) measure and compare rankings for two countries, explaining one difference between the rankings.
width.typical: Compare GDP, HDI and PQLI for a range of countries including Australia, India and a Pacific country; explain trends in different measurements and explain why a country may rank differently across indices.
wider: Evaluate more recent composite measures such as the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) or Happy Planet Index against GDP and HDI, assessing what each adds
Investigate anomalies — countries that rank much higher on HDI than GDP (or vice versa) — and explain the political, historical or social factors that produce the divergence
Examine gender-disaggregated wellbeing data (e.g. Gender Development Index, GII) and evaluate what the disaggregation reveals that composite indices obscure

modes.reason: Students often treat indices as interchangeable and conclude that a 'better' measure is simply a more accurate version of the same thing. An explicit comparison framework showing what each index includes/excludes and why is essential before spatial analysis.
Comparing indices across a range of countries (including countries that diverge in their relative rankings) is the primary way to develop understanding of what each index captures and what it misses.

nodes.label: Trends in wellbeing at global scale
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret and explain trends in human wellbeing in a developed and a developing country over time, applying wellbeing indices at the global scale.
criteria: Students interpret wellbeing data for two countries over time, identifying at least one trend
Students explain the trend with reference to at least one economic, social or political factor

width.minimum: Interpret a graph or table of wellbeing data for two countries over time and describe at least one trend, offering an explanation for that trend.
width.typical: Interpret and explain trends in human wellbeing for Australia and a country in Asia or the Pacific over time, identifying convergence or divergence patterns and explaining the economic, social and political factors driving the trends.
wider: Examine global wellbeing trend data to identify regions showing fastest improvement and those showing stagnation or decline, explaining the structural factors behind divergent trajectories
Investigate the relationship between aid flows, foreign investment and wellbeing trends in a specific developing country — evaluating which interventions correlate with sustained improvement
Research how global shocks (pandemics, financial crises, climate events) differentially affect wellbeing trajectories in developed vs developing countries

modes.reason: This node integrates conceptual understanding of wellbeing, index literacy and data interpretation into a coherent trend analysis. Students need to connect what the index measures to what the trend means — not just read the data but explain it in terms of the dimensions the index captures.

descriptors.title: Spatial variations in wellbeing: regional and national scale
descriptors.description: reasons for, and consequences of, spatial variations in human wellbeing at a regional and national scale, drawing on studies such as from within India or another country in Asia
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare wellbeing measurements using GDP, HDI, PQLI and other indices at global scale (AC9HG10K05). They understand urbanisation causes and effects (AC9HG8K06) and internal/international migration patterns (AC9HG8K08), which are relevant to within-country wellbeing variation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and describe the causes and consequences of spatial inequality in human wellbeing within India or another country in Asia, interpreting spatial data on wellbeing to identify regions of high and low wellbeing and explaining similarities and differences.

nodes.label: Spatial patterns of wellbeing within a country
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret spatial data on human wellbeing within India or another Asian country to identify regions of high and low wellbeing, describing the spatial pattern.
criteria: Students identify regions of high and low wellbeing in a studied country from spatial data, using geographic references
Students describe the spatial pattern (e.g. rural-urban gradient, regional concentration) observed in the data
nodes.hinge_reason: Spatial pattern description is foundational — if students cannot read the geographic distribution of wellbeing variation, they cannot identify which regions require explanation in Node 2 or connect consequences to the right regions.

width.minimum: Interpret a map or spatial dataset showing wellbeing variation within one country and describe the spatial pattern (e.g. urban/rural, coastal/inland, regional concentration).
width.typical: Interpret and analyse spatial data on wellbeing in India or another Asian country using measures such as MPI, HDI sub-national data, or equivalent; identify regions of high and low wellbeing and describe the spatial pattern and its key characteristics.
wider: Compare spatial patterns of wellbeing in two Asian countries, explaining how different historical, geographical and political factors produce different spatial patterns
Use geospatial technologies to map and analyse multi-variable wellbeing data within a country, identifying clustering or spatial autocorrelation in the distribution
Investigate how spatial patterns of wellbeing within a country have changed over time in response to development policies, migration or economic shifts

modes.reason: Students often describe data without identifying the spatial dimension — noting that some regions are low without articulating the geographic pattern (rural/urban, north/south, coastal/inland). Explicitly scaffold spatial description before explanation.

nodes.label: Causes of spatial inequality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the economic, social, technological, political and environmental causes of spatial variations in wellbeing within India or another Asian country compared to Australia.
criteria: Students identify at least two types of causes (drawing from economic, social, technological, political or environmental) of spatial inequality in the studied country
Students explain how each identified cause contributes to the spatial pattern of wellbeing variation

width.minimum: Identify at least two causes of spatial inequality in wellbeing within the studied country and explain how each contributes to the spatial pattern observed.
width.typical: Describe economic (uneven investment, industrial concentration), social (education access, healthcare distribution), technological (connectivity gaps), political (historical marginalisation, policy focus) and environmental (climate, resource access) causes of spatial wellbeing inequality; compare causes in India or another Asian country with causes in Australia.
wider: Investigate how colonial history shaped current spatial inequalities — examining how British colonial infrastructure development in India produced long-lasting geographic economic concentrations
Analyse a specific policy or investment decision (e.g. Special Economic Zones, infrastructure corridors) and evaluate its effects on the spatial distribution of wellbeing
Examine intersectionality in causes — how caste, gender and geography interact in India to compound wellbeing disadvantage in specific regions

modes.reason: Cause identification is enriched by comparison — seeing that different countries have different spatial inequality profiles driven by different cause combinations builds understanding of causation as complex and contextual, not universal.

nodes.label: Consequences of spatial inequality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret and analyse measures of wellbeing, identify the consequences of inequality, and make inferences about wellbeing levels at different scales.
criteria: Students identify at least two consequences of spatial wellbeing inequality for people in low-wellbeing regions
Students make an inference about wellbeing in a specific region or context using data evidence, not assertion

width.minimum: Describe at least two consequences of spatial wellbeing inequality for people in low-wellbeing regions of the studied country.
width.typical: Interpret and analyse measures including MPI, PFI, FSI and similar; describe consequences of inequality at multiple scales (individual, community, national); make inferences about wellbeing in specific contexts (e.g. rural Rajasthan vs urban Mumbai; local vs national scale for child labour).
wider: Investigate feedback loops — how low wellbeing in a region produces further disadvantage (e.g. brain drain, infrastructure underinvestment, political marginalisation) — tracing the self-reinforcing mechanisms of spatial inequality

Examine how specific consequences of spatial inequality (e.g. rural-urban migration pressure, political instability, environmental degradation) create externalities that affect even high-wellbeing regions
Compare the consequences of spatial inequality in India with consequences of indigenous/remote disadvantage in Australia (linking to K07), identifying structural parallels and differences

modes.reason: This node integrates spatial pattern reading (Node 1), cause analysis (Node 2) and consequence identification into a coherent inequality analysis. Students need to connect the geographic pattern to its causes and then to its human consequences — a three-step chain that requires explicit scaffolding.

descriptors.title: Spatial variations in wellbeing in Australia
descriptors.description: reasons for, and consequences of, spatial variations in human wellbeing in Australia, including for First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand spatial wellbeing variations at the regional/national scale using international cases (AC9HG10K06) and are familiar with wellbeing measurement tools (AC9HG10K05). They have engaged with First Nations custodial approaches (AC9HG10K03) and Australia's internal migration and urban/rural dynamics (AC9HG8K06, AC9HG8K08).
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the reasons for and consequences of spatial variations in human wellbeing in Australia, including identifying causes for First Nations Australians' wellbeing data and explaining how a person's wellbeing is influenced by where they live, with reference to interconnections of environmental, economic, social and technological factors in at least two different places.

nodes.label: Spatial patterns of wellbeing in Australia
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the spatial pattern of wellbeing variation within Australia, identifying areas of higher and lower wellbeing and recognising the particular pattern for First Nations Australians.
criteria: Students describe the spatial distribution of wellbeing in Australia, identifying at least two geographically distinct places with different wellbeing profiles
Students identify the wellbeing gap between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians using at least one specific data point or measure
nodes.hinge_reason: The spatial pattern provides the foundation for cause identification — if students do not first establish what the pattern is and where the variation sits geographically, their causal explanations will be generic rather than place-specific.

width.minimum: Describe wellbeing variation across at least two different Australian places (e.g. urban and remote) using at least one data source.
width.typical: Interpret and analyse similarities, differences, patterns and trends in wellbeing data across Australian places including urban, regional and remote; identify the particular wellbeing profile of First Nations Australians compared to non-Indigenous Australians.
wider: Map spatial wellbeing data across Australian states/territories or statistical areas, identifying clustering patterns and geographic gradients
Examine how wellbeing data for First Nations Australians varies within the First Nations population — for example, between urban, regional and remote communities — avoiding a single national average
Trace how the spatial distribution of wellbeing in Australia has changed over recent decades, identifying which regions have experienced improvement and which have stagnated

modes.reason: Students often jump to causes (remote areas are disadvantaged because they are far away) without first establishing the data picture. Scaffold data reading before explanation — what does the data actually show about spatial variation?

nodes.label: Causes of wellbeing variation — environmental, economic, social, technological
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the environmental, social, economic and technological factors that influence wellbeing and create spatial variation across Australian places, including factors specific to First Nations Australians' wellbeing.
criteria: Students explain at least two factors from different domains (environmental, economic, social, technological) that contribute to wellbeing variation between named Australian places
Students explain at least one factor specific to First Nations Australians' wellbeing, connecting it to a historical or structural cause

width.minimum: Identify and explain at least two factors from different domains (e.g. one economic, one social) that contribute to wellbeing variation between two Australian places.
width.typical: Explain how environmental (access to resources, climate), social (health and education services), economic (employment, income) and technological (ICT access) factors interact to create wellbeing variation across Australian places; explain the additional and intersecting factors that shape First Nations Australians' wellbeing, including Closing the Gap initiatives.
wider: Investigate how historical policies (stolen generations, land alienation, forced relocation) created structural disadvantages that persist as causes of current wellbeing gaps for First Nations Australians
Examine the concept of the 'tyranny of distance' as a driver of regional disadvantage in Australia and evaluate policy responses that have attempted to address it
Analyse a specific remote community's wellbeing profile and trace the full factor set — geographical, historical, economic, social — that produces that profile

modes.reason: Factor analysis is enriched by comparing two very different Australian places — e.g. a remote First Nations community vs an outer suburban area vs a regional town — to show that the same factor domain (e.g. economic) operates very differently in different geographic contexts.

nodes.label: Place, interconnection and wellbeing outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how a person's wellbeing is influenced by where they live, with reference to interconnections of environmental, economic, social and technological factors in at least two different Australian places.
criteria: Students explain how at least two interconnected factors shape a person's wellbeing in a specific Australian place
Students identify how the wellbeing experience differs between at least two different Australian places and explain the geographical basis of that difference

width.minimum: Explain how interconnections between at least two factors (e.g. economic and social) shape wellbeing outcomes for people in one specific Australian place.
width.typical: Explain how a person's wellbeing is shaped by their place through the interconnection of environmental, economic, social and technological factors; demonstrate this for at least two different Australian places, including consideration of ways to improve wellbeing of remote First Nations communities including community-proposed approaches.
wider: Develop a detailed interconnection web for a specific place showing how multiple factors interact and compound — identifying which factor interactions are most significant for wellbeing outcomes
Investigate and evaluate specific strategies proposed or implemented by First Nations communities themselves to improve wellbeing, assessing how community agency shapes outcomes

Compare how two different government policy approaches to regional wellbeing in Australia have fared — for example, comparing place-based investment strategies with targeted individual support schemes

modes.reason: This node integrates spatial pattern reading, factor analysis and the geographical concept of place into a holistic account of wellbeing as place-shaped. Students need to connect the factors identified in Node 2 into a coherent explanation of how interconnections produce a place-specific wellbeing outcome.
The descriptor requires at least two different places — the comparison is integral, not optional. Teaching should ensure students have genuine comparative material, not just a single case study.

descriptors.title: Organisational responses to improve human wellbeing
descriptors.description: responses of international and national government and non-government organisations to improve human wellbeing in Australia, within India and another country in the Pacific
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand causes and consequences of wellbeing variation at global scale (AC9HG10K05), within a country in Asia (AC9HG10K06), and within Australia including for First Nations Australians (AC9HG10K07). They are positioned to evaluate organisational responses against the causes identified in those earlier standards.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and explain responses of government and non-government organisations to improve human wellbeing in Australia, India and a Pacific country, evaluating programs against their objectives and outcomes.

nodes.label: Types of organisations and their approaches
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the types of organisations that respond to wellbeing issues — international (e.g. UN agencies), national government (e.g. AusAID equivalents), and non-government (e.g. World Vision, Red Cross) — and explain how their mandates and approaches differ.
criteria: Students distinguish between at least two types of organisations (government, NGO, international) by mandate and approach
Students explain how an organisation's type shapes what it can and cannot do to improve wellbeing

width.minimum: Describe the role of at least two different types of organisation (e.g. one government, one NGO) and explain how their approach to improving wellbeing differs.
width.typical: Identify and describe the different mandates, funding sources, target populations and methods of international government organisations, national government programs and NGOs; explain how the type of organisation shapes the approach taken.
wider: Examine tensions between different organisational types — for example, where government programs and NGO programs in the same country or community have conflicting priorities or methods
Investigate how organisations coordinate (or fail to coordinate) in complex humanitarian or development contexts — examining the UN coordination architecture for a specific crisis
Research the growth of social enterprise and community-led organisations as a third approach between government and NGO models, with examples from Australia's First Nations sector

modes.reason: Students often conflate government programs and NGOs, or assume all aid organisations do the same thing. An explicit framework distinguishing types by mandate, funding, accountability and target population prevents blurring that undermines evaluation in Node 2.

nodes.label: Programs and their objectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the objectives and outcomes of specific programs to reduce wellbeing inequality in Australia, India and a Pacific country.
criteria: Students identify at least one specific program in each of the three contexts (Australia, India/regional, Pacific) and describe its objectives
Students explain what each program targets and who the intended beneficiaries are

width.minimum: Describe one specific program in at least one country context, identifying its objectives and what it targets.
width.typical: Identify and explain programs in each of the three mandated contexts (Australia — including First Nations wellbeing; India or regional inequalities; Pacific country); describe program objectives, target populations and intended outcomes for each.
wider: Research how AusAID's objectives and methods evolved over time and compare its approach to wellbeing improvement with that of an equivalent bilateral aid agency (e.g. USAID, DFID/FCDO)
Investigate the evidence base for a specific NGO program (e.g. World Vision's Zonal Health Program, Red Cross WASH programs) by examining reported outcomes data
Examine community-proposed ways to improve First Nations wellbeing in Australia and compare these with government-initiated programs, identifying points of alignment and divergence

modes.reason: The descriptor requires three country contexts — students need genuine engagement with programs in each, not a single case study applied across all three. The teaching signal is to ensure coverage of all three contexts with sufficient specificity.

nodes.label: Evaluating program effectiveness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of programs to improve wellbeing, connecting program outcomes to the causes of wellbeing inequality identified in earlier standards.
criteria: Students evaluate a program against its stated objectives, identifying at least one strength and one limitation with evidence
Students connect the program's approach to at least one identified cause of wellbeing inequality, explaining whether or not the program addresses that cause

width.minimum: Evaluate the effectiveness of one program against its stated objectives, identifying at least one strength and one limitation.
width.typical: Evaluate programs in terms of whether they address the identified causes of wellbeing inequality; consider whether outcomes match objectives; acknowledge limitations of evaluation data (selectivity, short-term framing, aid dependency risks).
wider: Apply a consistent evaluation framework (e.g. OECD-DAC criteria: relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, sustainability) to compare two programs in the same region
Investigate a program that has been independently evaluated and compare self-reported outcomes with external evaluation findings — examining the gap and what produces it
Explore critiques of aid and development programs more broadly — evaluating whether program approaches address structural causes of inequality or focus on symptoms

modes.reason: Program evaluation integrates understanding of wellbeing causes (K05-K07) with program analysis — a good evaluation requires students to connect the program's approach to the actual drivers of the wellbeing issue it addresses. The teaching signal is to make this connection explicit rather than treating evaluation as stand-alone.

descriptors.title: Develop geographical inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop a range of questions for a geographical inquiry related to a phenomenon or challenge
descriptors.knowledge: At Y9, students developed a range of questions for geographical inquiry (AC9HG9S01). At Y10 the added complexity is working with multi-scale phenomena and linking questions across scales (local, national, global) using geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale, change) to sharpen focus.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop a range of relevant questions to investigate a geographical phenomenon or challenge, modifying and refining questions to incorporate geographical concepts and scale of study, and planning an investigation across multiple scales using digital tools.

nodes.label: Generating relevant questions for a geographical phenomenon
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a range of relevant questions to investigate why a geographical phenomenon has changed or a challenge may arise.
criteria: Students generate at least three questions about a phenomenon that are geographically framed, not just generally curious
Students' questions together address multiple aspects of the phenomenon (nature, distribution, causes, consequences, responses)
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot generate questions that are geographically framed rather than generically curious, the entire inquiry they conduct will lack geographical direction — data collection (S02), analysis (S03) and conclusion (S04) all flow from the question quality.

width.minimum: Generate at least three questions about one geographical phenomenon or challenge, ensuring the questions are geographically relevant (not generic).
width.typical: Develop a range of relevant questions that together address multiple dimensions of a geographical phenomenon or challenge — covering what, why, where, how and with what consequences; ensuring questions are grounded in geographical concepts.
wider: Develop question sets for two contrasting phenomena (e.g. environmental sustainability and human wellbeing) and compare the inquiry structures, evaluating which questions are most productive for geographical investigation
Investigate how professional geographers frame inquiry questions and compare professional research questions with student-generated questions for the same topic
Generate questions that deliberately cross scales (local, national, global) for the same phenomenon and evaluate how scale change reshapes the inquiry

modes.reason: Students often generate questions that could apply to any discipline ('What is the problem? How bad is it? What should we do?'). Scaffold geographical question framing explicitly — what makes a question geographical is that it involves place, space, scale, environment or interconnection.

nodes.label: Refining questions using concepts and scale
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop and modify questions to sharpen the focus of an investigation using geographical concepts and scale of study.
criteria: Students modify at least one question to incorporate a named geographical concept, explaining how the concept sharpens the inquiry focus
Students produce a refined question that specifies a scale of study and explain what kind of data that scale requires

width.minimum: Take a broad question and modify it to incorporate at least one geographical concept (place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale, change) and a specific scale of study.
width.typical: Develop and modify a set of inquiry questions so that each incorporates a geographical concept and addresses a specified scale (local, national, global); explain how the concept and scale sharpens the question's focus and what kind of data it calls for.
wider: Develop parallel versions of the same question at three different scales and explain how each version calls for different data, methods and sources
Investigate how geographical concepts function as analytical lenses — taking one concept (e.g. interconnection) and exploring how it reshapes the questions that can be asked about a phenomenon
Evaluate a set of student-generated questions against criteria of focus, researchability and geographical relevance, revising weak questions with explicit justification

modes.reason: Practising question refinement across multiple phenomena and concepts builds the transferable skill — students who have only refined questions for one phenomenon may be unable to apply the process to a new topic.

nodes.label: Planning a multi-scale investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can plan an investigation of a phenomenon at a range of scales using digital tools.
criteria: Students produce an investigation plan that addresses the phenomenon at two or more scales, identifying at least one data source per scale
Students explain how their planned investigation would answer at least two of their refined inquiry questions

width.minimum: Outline a plan for investigating one phenomenon at two or more scales, identifying data sources for each scale.
width.typical: Plan an investigation of a phenomenon across local, national and/or global scales using digital tools; identify appropriate data sources, methods and questions for each scale; explain how findings at each scale will be integrated.
wider: Plan an investigation that involves both primary data collection (fieldwork, survey) and secondary data sources, specifying how each will be used and how they will be compared
Evaluate a completed geographical investigation plan — identifying strengths and gaps in question coverage, scale consideration and data source selection
Design a digital tool-supported investigation plan for a phenomenon where geospatial technologies (GIS, satellite imagery, interactive mapping) are central to data collection or analysis

modes.reason: An investigation plan integrates question development, scale selection and method planning. Students need to see how each question implies a method and data source — the plan is the explicit connection point between inquiry questions and research design.

descriptors.title: Collect, represent and compare geographical data
descriptors.description: collect, represent and compare data and information from primary research methods, including fieldwork and secondary research materials, using geospatial technologies and digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: At Y9, students collected, represented and compared data using primary and secondary methods, geospatial technologies and digital tools (AC9HG9S02). At Y10 the additional complexity involves evaluating sources for relevance, reliability and bias, respecting First Nations consultation protocols, and representing multi-variable data using geospatial and digital tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collect data from primary and secondary research methods, evaluate sources for relevance, reliability and bias, respect First Nations consultation protocols where relevant, and represent multi-variable data using geospatial technologies and digital tools.

nodes.label: Primary research methods including fieldwork
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and use primary research methods, including fieldwork, to collect original materials relevant to their inquiry.
criteria: Students identify a primary research method appropriate to their inquiry and describe how it would be used
Students acknowledge First Nations consultation protocols when planning investigations that involve First Nations communities

width.minimum: Identify at least one primary research method appropriate to the inquiry and describe how it would be used to collect original data.
width.typical: Identify primary methods (survey, interview, fieldwork observation) and explain their use in collecting data for geography inquiry; apply at least one method; identify and respect First Nations consultation protocols when planning investigations involving First Nations communities.
wider: Design and conduct a fieldwork-based investigation, including choice of location, data recording protocol and analysis of collected data
Investigate how primary data collection protocols differ when working with First Nations communities — examining what ethical consultation looks like in practice and why it matters

Compare the advantages and limitations of different primary methods (survey vs interview vs observation) for the same research question, evaluating which would produce more reliable or representative data

modes.reason: Students benefit from experience with more than one primary method — exposure to survey, interview and observation contexts builds understanding of what each method is suited for.

nodes.label: Evaluating sources for relevance, reliability and bias
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate primary and secondary research materials for relevance, reliability and bias, including identifying different types of bias.
criteria: Students evaluate a source for relevance, reliability and bias using evidence from the source
Students explain how a specific type of bias (information or selection) affects what a source tells them and what it omits
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot evaluate sources, they will use unreliable or biased data in their analysis (S03) and draw conclusions (S04) built on a weak evidentiary foundation — the entire subsequent inquiry chain is compromised by weak source evaluation.

width.minimum: Evaluate one source using at least two criteria (relevance, reliability or bias) and explain the evaluation with evidence from the source.
width.typical: Evaluate primary and secondary sources for relevance (currency, fit to inquiry), reliability (authorship, referencing, expertise) and bias (information bias, selection bias); compare findings from primary research with secondary research for relevance and reliability.
wider: Analyse how bias operates differently in quantitative data (selection bias in sampling) vs qualitative sources (framing and perspective bias) — developing a multi-type bias evaluation framework
Evaluate sources specifically related to First Nations communities or aid programs where power dynamics shape what is published and from whose perspective
Investigate how media sources on environmental or wellbeing issues reflect particular world views, applying the bias evaluation framework to identify not just error but perspective

modes.reason: Students often treat relevance and reliability as the same thing, or conflate 'I agree with this' with 'this is reliable'. An explicit framework distinguishing the three criteria — with a worked example applying all three to the same source — prevents undifferentiated source assessment.
Practising source evaluation across different source types (news, academic, NGO reports, government data, community-produced) builds a more flexible and accurate evaluation toolkit.

nodes.label: Representing multi-variable data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent multi-variable data using geospatial technologies and digital tools.
criteria: Students represent data from at least two variables using a digital tool, producing a representation that accurately reflects the data
Students explain what their data representation shows and what geographical pattern or relationship it reveals

width.minimum: Represent data from at least two variables using an appropriate digital tool, explaining what the representation shows.
width.typical: Represent multi-variable data using geospatial technologies (e.g. scatterplots showing correlation between two geographic variables such as literacy and GDP per capita) and digital tools (pie graphs, tables, digital photographs); select representation types appropriate to the data and the question.
wider: Create a geospatial map showing spatial distribution of two or more wellbeing variables across a country or region, using GIS or a mapping tool to identify spatial patterns
Evaluate a range of representation types for the same dataset — explaining which representation most effectively communicates the geographical pattern and why
Design and produce a multi-panel data visualisation that combines geospatial mapping with statistical representations to tell a coherent geographical story

modes.reason: Students need to build a repertoire of representation types — not just know that multiple types exist, but have practised using several. Each representation type is suited to different data structures and questions.

descriptors.title: Evaluate data to generalise, explain patterns and infer relationships
descriptors.description: evaluate geographical data and information to make generalisations and predictions, explain patterns and trends and infer relationships
descriptors.knowledge: At Y9, students evaluated geographical data to make generalisations and predictions, explain patterns and trends and infer relationships (AC9HG9S03). At Y10 the same descriptor applies with the implicit expectation that students apply it to more complex data sets — including geospatial technology outputs, multi-variable data and cross-national comparisons — that match the Y10 content strand complexity.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate geographical data and information to develop generalisations, explain patterns and trends in complex datasets including geospatial outputs, and infer relationships between key environmental or wellbeing indicators at the national scale.

nodes.label: Developing generalisations from data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop generalisations from geographical data and information, critically analysing text and images for meaning and significance.
criteria: Students develop at least one generalisation that makes an inferential claim rather than describing a single data point
Students ground their generalisation in specific evidence and acknowledge at least one limitation of the generalisation
nodes.hinge_reason: Generalisation is the inferential move that links raw data to geographical argument — without it, pattern explanation and relationship inference (nodes 2 and 3) are merely description without analytical payload.

width.minimum: Analyse one geographical data source or image and develop at least one generalisation grounded in the evidence.
width.typical: Critically analyse text, data and images for meaning and significance; develop generalisations that go beyond description — making a claim about a geographical pattern that the data supports, and acknowledging what the data does not show.
wider: Develop competing generalisations from the same dataset and evaluate which is better supported, identifying the reasoning steps that distinguish a strong from a weak generalisation

Analyse contrasting images (e.g. before/after deforestation satellite images, contrasting nightlife North/South Korea) and develop generalisations about what the contrast reveals at a geographical level
Investigate how generalisations function in geographical argument — what makes a generalisation too broad or too narrow to be analytically useful

modes.reason: Students often confuse generalisation with description ('the map shows that area X has low HDI') rather than making an inferential claim ('areas with lower HDI tend to be rural and landlocked, suggesting that resource access and connectivity are systematic factors'). Scaffold the description → inference → generalisation chain.

nodes.label: Explaining patterns and trends
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain geographical patterns and trends in data, including trends in complex and multi-variable datasets.
criteria: Students identify a pattern or trend in a dataset and provide a causal explanation using at least one geographical factor
Students distinguish between a description of the pattern and an explanation of why the pattern exists

width.minimum: Identify a pattern or trend in a geographical dataset and offer an explanation for that pattern using at least one geographical factor.
width.typical: Explain patterns and trends in geographical data with reference to multiple causal factors — including why spatial or temporal patterns show the distribution they do and what factors account for the trend; apply to both environmental sustainability and wellbeing contexts.
wider: Analyse a pattern that contradicts a common expectation (e.g. a country with high GDP but low HDI, or a protected area with declining biodiversity) and explain the anomaly
Examine how the apparent pattern changes depending on the scale of data aggregation — e.g. national level vs subnational level vs local level for the same variable
Explain a trend over time (e.g. HDI trajectory, biodiversity index change) identifying the policy, economic or environmental events that correspond to inflection points in the trend

modes.reason: Practising pattern explanation across both environmental and wellbeing data types builds transferability — the analytical move is the same but the factor vocabulary differs, and students need experience in both.

nodes.label: Inferring relationships between indicators
nodes.checkpoint: Students can infer relationships between key environmental or wellbeing indicators at the national scale, using geospatial technology applications where appropriate.
criteria: Students identify a relationship between two indicators and explain the basis for inferring it from the data
Students evaluate the strength of the inferred relationship, acknowledging alternative explanations or confounding factors

width.minimum: Identify a likely relationship between two geographical indicators (e.g. air quality and population density, adult literacy and HDI) and explain the basis for inferring the relationship.
width.typical: Infer relationships between multiple environmental or wellbeing indicators at national scale; use geospatial technology applications to create maps showing the relationship spatially; evaluate the strength of the inferred relationship with reference to data evidence.
wider: Distinguish between correlation and causation in a geographical relationship — identifying a case where two indicators correlate but are both caused by a third factor rather than each other
Use a scatterplot or bivariate map to visualise a relationship between two indicators and evaluate what the visualisation reveals and conceals about the relationship
Investigate a relationship between an environmental indicator and a wellbeing indicator at national scale — tracing the mechanism that connects them

modes.reason: Relationship inference integrates generalisation, pattern explanation and data visualisation (from S02) into a coherent analytical conclusion. Students should explicitly connect the relationship they infer to the patterns they have explained and the data they have used.

descriptors.title: Justify geographical conclusions
descriptors.description: evaluate data and information to justify conclusions
descriptors.knowledge: At Y9, students evaluated data to justify conclusions (AC9HG9S04). At Y10 the same descriptor is applied with the expectation that conclusions integrate at least two geographical concepts as organisers and that justification examines whether the reasons given are adequate for the conclusion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students draw conclusions using at least two geographical concepts as organisers and examine whether and how the reasons given justify the conclusion reached, across sustainability and wellbeing contexts.

nodes.label: Conclusions grounded in geographical concepts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions using at least two geographical concepts (place, space, environment, interconnection, sustainability, scale, change) as organisers for their reasoning.
criteria: Students draw a conclusion about a geographical phenomenon and identify at least two concepts that organised their reasoning
Students explain how each concept shaped what they looked for in the data, not just what label applies
nodes.hinge_reason: Using concepts as genuine organisers rather than decorative labels is the distinguishing feature of disciplinary geographical argument. If students simply name concepts without using them analytically, their conclusions are not geographically reasoned — and justification (Node 2) has nothing substantive to build on.

width.minimum: Draw a conclusion about one geographical phenomenon using at least two named geographical concepts as organising ideas.
width.typical: Draw conclusions using at least two geographical concepts as organisers; explain how each concept contributes to the conclusion's reasoning — not just listed as labels but functioning as analytical lenses that shape what the data means.
wider: Compare conclusions drawn when using different concept pairings for the same data — evaluating how the choice of concepts shapes the analytical direction
Develop a framework for selecting which concepts are most appropriate for a given inquiry and explain the analytical justification for the selection
Examine how professional geographical conclusions in reports, articles or policy documents deploy concepts as organisers, comparing professional and student-level conclusion structures

modes.reason: Students often append concept names to conclusions without integrating them ('this shows interconnection because things are connected'). Scaffold concept-as-organiser thinking: the concept should shape what you look at, what counts as evidence, and what the conclusion claims — not just label a pre-formed conclusion.

nodes.label: Evaluating the justification for a conclusion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine the reasons given for a specific decision or conclusion and explain how these reasons have or have not justified the conclusion.
criteria: Students evaluate whether reasons given for a conclusion are adequate, identifying at least one strength and one gap or weakness
Students explain how interconnected factors (at least two types) were or were not accounted for in the justification

width.minimum: Examine one conclusion or decision and evaluate whether the reasons given adequately justify it, identifying at least one strength and one weakness in the justification.
width.typical: Examine the reasoning behind decisions related to sustainability management or wellbeing improvement; evaluate whether the reasons given are sufficient, appropriate and internally consistent; identify where interconnected factors (environmental, economic, social, political, technological) are accounted for or overlooked.
wider: Evaluate a geographical decision from a policy document or case study — tracing the explicit and implicit reasoning, identifying assumptions, and assessing whether the conclusion follows from the evidence and arguments given
Construct an alternative conclusion from the same data and evidence, explaining what different reasoning steps would be required to reach it
Investigate a case where a decision was made and later revised — examining what new evidence or reasoning caused the revision and what that reveals about the original justification

modes.reason: Practising justification evaluation across both sustainability and wellbeing contexts builds the transferability of the critical reasoning skill — students who have only evaluated one type of conclusion may not apply the skill to a new context.

descriptors.title: Develop, evaluate and recommend strategies
descriptors.description: develop and evaluate strategies using environmental, economic or social criteria; recommend a strategy and explain the predicted impacts
descriptors.knowledge: At Y9, students developed and evaluated strategies using environmental, economic or social criteria, recommended a strategy and explained predicted impacts (AC9HG9S05). At Y10 the same descriptor applies with greater complexity: explicit reflection on personal values, evaluation of collective as well as individual action, and integration with First Nations traditional practices.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop and evaluate both individual and collective strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria; recommend a strategy with explained predicted impacts; reflect on personal values and their influence on strategy choices.

nodes.label: Developing strategies — individual and collective
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose both individual and collective strategies for addressing a geographical challenge, supporting each with reasons.
criteria: Students propose at least one individual and one collective strategy, providing reasons for each
Students identify who has responsibility for implementing each proposed strategy

width.minimum: Propose at least one individual and one collective strategy for a geographical challenge, providing reasons for each.
width.typical: Propose and describe both individual actions (e.g. reducing ecological footprint) and collective actions (e.g. community programs, volunteering, policy advocacy) for a geographical challenge; explain the reasoning behind each strategy and identify who is responsible for implementation.
wider: Investigate specific organisations that students could engage with collectively — Red Cross, Red Crescent, environmental NGOs — and evaluate what individual participation in collective action achieves
Compare the scale and type of impact achievable through individual vs collective action for the same challenge, identifying where individual action is most and least effective
Research a case where grassroots collective action led to policy change, tracing the pathway from individual decisions to collective impact at a systems level

modes.reason: Students often focus on individual action as the primary response to geographical challenges. Exposure to collective action models — including First Nations community-led approaches — broadens the strategy repertoire.

nodes.label: Evaluating strategies against criteria
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the effectiveness of a strategy using environmental, economic and social criteria, reflecting on whether the strategy achieves its aims.
criteria: Students evaluate a strategy against at least two criteria from different domains, providing evidence for their evaluation
Students identify at least one trade-off in the strategy — where meeting one criterion compromises another
nodes.hinge_reason: Multi-criteria evaluation is the basis for the recommendation in Node 3 — if students evaluate using only one criterion or apply criteria without evidence, their recommendation will not be genuinely justified and the final integration node cannot produce a defensible geographical conclusion.

width.minimum: Evaluate one strategy against at least two criteria (environmental, economic or social), identifying evidence of effectiveness and limitations.
width.typical: Evaluate strategies using environmental, economic and social criteria; reflect on whether environmental degradation has been reduced or wellbeing improved; explain reasons for decisions including traditional practices (e.g. firestick farming) and grassroots aid implementations.
wider: Apply a systematic multi-criteria evaluation framework to compare two strategies for the same challenge, producing a reasoned recommendation based on the comparison
Examine cases where evaluation evidence for a strategy is contested — identifying why different evaluators reach different conclusions using the same criteria

Evaluate a strategy involving First Nations traditional practices (e.g. firestick farming, water management) against environmental, cultural and social criteria — explaining how traditional practices are validated as effective strategies

modes.reason: Students often evaluate using one preferred criterion (usually environmental or economic) and ignore the others. Scaffold simultaneous three-criteria evaluation explicitly — including acknowledgment that criteria may point in different directions and that trade-offs are a feature, not a problem to be resolved.

nodes.label: Recommending a strategy with predicted impacts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recommend a strategy, explain the predicted impacts, and reflect on how personal values and attitudes influence the strategy choice.
criteria: Students recommend a strategy and explain at least two predicted impacts (one intended, one possible unintended or trade-off consequence)
Students reflect on at least one personal value that influenced their strategy choice, explaining the connection

width.minimum: Recommend one strategy, explain at least two predicted impacts, and reflect on how at least one personal value influenced the choice.
width.typical: Recommend a strategy supported by reasons from the evaluation; explain predicted environmental, economic and social impacts; reflect on how personal values and attitudes — including sustainability values, social justice values or cultural values — influenced the strategy choice.
wider: Develop a recommendation that explicitly addresses the trade-offs identified in Node 2 — explaining how the recommended strategy prioritises some criteria over others and why
Reflect on how a different value position would lead to a different strategy recommendation — making the value-strategy connection explicit and non-deterministic
Apply sustainable design principles to an urban or built environment strategy and explain how the design principles reflect specific values about wellbeing, environment and community

modes.reason: A strategy recommendation integrates criteria evaluation, predicted impact analysis and value reflection into a coherent geographical argument. The teaching signal is to make each component explicit in the recommendation — not a bare recommendation, but one that shows the evaluative reasoning and value position behind it.

descriptors.title: Create geographical descriptions, explanations and responses
descriptors.description: create descriptions, explanations and responses, using geographical knowledge and geographical tools as appropriate, and concepts and terms that incorporate and acknowledge research findings
descriptors.knowledge: At Y9, students created descriptions, explanations and responses using geographical knowledge, tools, concepts and terms (AC9HG9S06). At Y10 the same descriptor applies with added complexity: explicit use of tone appropriate to purpose and audience (including authoritative tone), formal use of structural features, and integration of geospatial data representations as part of the response.
descriptors.endpoint: Students create descriptions, explanations and responses that use appropriate structural features, incorporate geographical knowledge and tools, deploy concepts and terms accurately, acknowledge research findings, and apply tone appropriate to purpose and audience.

nodes.label: Structural features and purposeful organisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a description or explanation for a purpose using structural features to organise ideas, findings, impacts and actions.
criteria: Students produce a response with at least two structural features that support the organisation of ideas for the stated purpose
Students explain how the structural choices they made support the reader's understanding

width.minimum: Produce a structured written response with at least two identifiable structural features (e.g. sub-headings, introduction, body, conclusion) that organise the content for its purpose.
width.typical: Create a description for a specific purpose using structural features — sub-headings, logical sequencing, topic sentences — to organise ideas, findings, impacts and actions; align the structure to the purpose and audience.
wider: Evaluate the structural choices in a model geographical response — explaining why certain structural features serve the purpose and audience of that text

Produce two versions of the same content using different structural approaches for different audiences (e.g. a formal report for a government audience vs a community information document) and explain the structural differences
Analyse how geospatial data representations (maps, graphs, tables) are integrated into the structure of a response to support the argument, not just illustrate it

modes.reason: Structural choices are audience and purpose dependent — students benefit from practising structures for different text types (report, explanation, proposal, description) to build flexible writing repertoire.

nodes.label: Incorporating geographical knowledge, tools and concepts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present conclusions using geospatial technologies and digital tools, incorporating geographical knowledge, concepts and terms that reflect and acknowledge research findings.
criteria: Students incorporate at least one geospatial or digital tool output accurately into a response, explaining what it shows
Students use at least two geographical concepts or terms accurately and acknowledge research findings that support their claims

width.minimum: Include at least one geospatial or digital tool output as part of a response, and use at least two geographical concepts or terms accurately, with acknowledgement of research sources.
width.typical: Present conclusions using geospatial technologies and digital tools (e.g. HDI trend graphs, wellbeing maps, GIS outputs); use geographical concepts and terms accurately and consistently; acknowledge research findings that support each major claim.
wider: Create a response that integrates multiple data representations (map, graph, table) into a coherent argument — explaining what each representation contributes to the overall explanation
Evaluate the data representations in a published geographical report for their accuracy, relevance and argumentative function, then produce an improved version
Produce a response where geospatial data visualisations are specifically designed to reveal a spatial relationship or trend that supports the central claim

modes.reason: Building a repertoire of geospatial and digital tool outputs that students can accurately incorporate in responses requires practice across multiple tool types — each tool type has conventions for integration into written responses.

nodes.label: Applying tone appropriate to purpose and audience
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop an explanation using an authoritative tone appropriate to purpose and audience, referring to data representations and research findings when explaining a strategy or phenomenon.
criteria: Students produce a response with an identifiable and consistent tone appropriate to the stated purpose and audience
Students refer to at least one data representation or research finding in their explanation, integrating it into the argument rather than simply appending it

width.minimum: Produce a response that demonstrates an identifiable tone choice (e.g. authoritative, persuasive, informative) appropriate to the stated purpose and audience.
width.typical: Develop an explanation using an authoritative tone, with reference to representations of data and research findings; adjust tone appropriately when explaining strategies to improve sustainability or wellbeing to different audiences; maintain consistency between tone, purpose and content.
wider: Produce the same content with two different tones for two different audiences — evaluating how vocabulary, sentence structure and hedging language shift with audience
Analyse tone in a policy document and a community information text about the same geographical issue, identifying the linguistic features that produce each tone
Evaluate when authoritative tone is and is not appropriate in geographical communication — examining contexts where more provisional or dialogic language is more honest or more effective

modes.reason: Tone is the final integrating element of geographical communication — it requires students to coordinate structural choices, concept use, data integration and language register into a coherent text that achieves its communicative purpose. The teaching signal is that tone is not a separate layer added at the end, but a quality that runs through all the decisions made in producing the text.
